statements.text: U. PREAMBLE AND GENERAL PRINCIPLES

statements.heading: U.1. Introduction
statements.text: In the name of Aḷḷāh, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ʾAbū ʿAmr ʿUṯmān b. Saʿīd b. ʿUṯmān, the teacher of recitation—may God be pleased with him—said: Praise be to God, the unique in eternity, the bestower of blessings, the creator of creation through His power, the director of affairs through His wisdom, whose command cannot be thwarted, whose judgement cannot be overruled, for He is swift in reckoning. I praise Him for all His blessings. I thank Him for the succession of His bounties and favours. I ask Him that He be abundant in His favours and plentiful in His kindness. May God bless the giver of good news, the warner, the illuminating lamp, our Prophet Muḥammad, may God bless him and his virtuous and pure family, and may He bring them much peace. Now, you have asked me—may God instruct you well—to compose for you a summary on the ways of the seven readers of the provinces—may God have mercy on them—so that its comprehension will come within reach, its memorisation will become easy, its study will become light, containing those transmissions and paths that are well-known and broadly propagated among the reciters, and that are sound and established among the foremost masters of yore. So, I have responded to what you have asked and applied myself to the composition which you wished in the way that you wanted. I have adopted an approach of brevity, summary and avoidance of length and repetition; I have chosen straightforward words and cut back the interpretations; I have pointed out things in a way which conveys the facts without being exhaustive, in order that they may be arrived at with ease and that their memorisation may be within reach. I mention for each one of the readers two transmissions. So, I mention: 1. For Nāfiʿ the transmission of Qālūn and Warš; 2. For Ibn Kaṯīr the transmission of Qunbul and al-Bazzī from their teachers from him; 3. For ʾAbū ʿAmr the transmission of ʾAbū ʿUmar [al-Dūrī] and ʾAbū Šuʿayb [al-Sūsī] from al-Yazīdī from him; 4. For Ibn ʿĀmir the transmission of Ibn Ḏakwān[1] and Hišām from their teachers from him; 5. For ʿĀṣim the transmission of ʾAbū Bakr and Ḥafṣ; 6. For Ḥamzah the transmission of Ḫalaf and Ḫallād from Sulaym from him; 7. For al-Kisāʾī the transmission of ʾAbū ʿUmar [al-Dūrī] and ʾAbū al-Ḥāriṯ from him.[2] So, these are 14 transmissions from them which are the ones recited and relied upon. When the transmissions from them disagree, I mention the transmitter by his name and leave out the name of his master. If they agree, I mention the master by his name. If Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kaṯīr agree, I say “the two of the holy cities read” and if ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī agree, I say “the Kufans read,” seeking for a rough approximation for students, and desiring simplification for beginners. And upon God—mighty and majestic is He—I depend, to Him I hold fast, in Him I put my trust. He is sufficient for me and to Him I turn in repentance. First, I will begin this book of mine with the mention of the names of the reciters, and the transmitters from them, their lineage, their patronyms, the date of their death, their countries, and the transmission path (back to the Prophet) of their recitation and naming their teachers, the transmission path of our own recitation to them, and the names of those who conveyed it to us from them in riwāyah (‘transmission of specific variants’) and tilāwah (‘a full recitation of the Qurʾān to the teacher’). Then I will proceed to mention their manners and disagreements, if God Almighty wills it. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This is a reference to Sībawayh (1988, IV:202) who explicitly tells us that ʾAbū ʿAmr reads it with an ultrashort vowel, not with no vowel.

statements.heading: U.2. The Names of the Readers, the Two Transmitters Transmitting from Each, Their Lineage, Their Countries, Their kunyahs and Their Death
U.2.1. Nāfiʿ the Medinan
statements.text: He is Nāfiʿ b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʾAbī Nuʿaym, client of Ǧaʿūnah b. Šaʿūb al-Layṯī, ally of Ḥamzah b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, originally from Isfahan. His patronym was ʾAbū Ruwaym. It was also said that it was ʾAbū al-Ḥasan and it was also said that it was ʾAbū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He died in Medina in the year 169 AH. Qālūn is ʿĪsā b. Mīnā al-Madanī al-Zuraqī, client of the Zuhrīs, and he was a teacher of Arabic. His patronym was ʾAbū Mūsā and Qālūn was his agnomen. He transmitted that Nāfiʿ had given him that agnomen due to his excellence in his reading because qālūn in the language of the Byzantines means ‘good’.[3] He died in Medina around the year 220 AH. Warš is ʿUṯmān b. Saʿīd al-Miṣrī. ʾAbū Saʿīd is his patronym and Warš his agnomen, and he was given the agnomen for what was said about the intensity of his whiteness.[4] He died in Egypt in the year 197 AH.

footnotes.text: This is one of the alternative names of Sūrat al-Šūrā (Kandil 1992, 51).

statements.heading: U.2.2. Ibn Kaṯīr the Meccan
statements.text: He is ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. Kaṯīr al-Dārī, client of ʿAmr b. ʿAlqamah al-Kinānī. Al-Dārī means ‘the perfume seller’. His patronym was ʾAbū Maʿbad. He is from among the successors (i.e., the generation after the companions of the Prophet). He died in Mecca in the year 120 AH. Qunbul is Muḥammad b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Muḥammad b. Ḫālid b. Saʿīd b. Ǧurǧah al-Makkī al-Maḫzūmī. His patronym is ʾAbū ʿUmar and his agnomen is Qunbul; it is said that they were a people of a house at Mecca known as the Qanābilah. He died in Mecca after[5] the year 280 AH. Al-Bazzī is ʾAḥmad b. Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. al-Qāsim b. Nāfiʿ b. ʾAbī Bazzah, the muezzin, the Meccan, client of the Banū Maḫzūm. His patronym is ʾAbū al-Ḥasan and he is known as al-Bazzī. He died after 240 AH. Qunbul and al-Bazzī transmitted the reading from Ibn Kaṯīr through a chain of transmission (i.e., they were not his direct students).

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

statements.heading: U.2.3. ʾAbū ʿAmr the Basran
statements.text: He is ʾAbū ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlāʾ b. ʿAmmār b. ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. al-Ḥuṣayn b. al-Ḥāriṯ b. Ǧulhum b. Ḫuzāʿī b. Māzin b. Mālik b. ʿAmr b. Tamīm. It was said that his name was Zabbān, or al-ʿUryān, or Yaḥyā, or that his patronym was his name, or that it was something other than that. He died in Kufa in the year 154 AH. ʾAbū ʿUmar is Ḥafṣ b. ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ṣuhbān al-ʾAzdī al-Dūrī the grammarian. Al-Dūr is a place in Baġdād. He died in Mecca[6] around 150 AH. ʾAbū Šuʿayb is Ṣāliḥ b. Ziyād b. ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. ʾIsmāʿīl al-Rustubī al-Sūsī. They both transmitted his reading from ʾAbū Muḥammad Yaḥyā b. al-Mubārak al-ʿAdawī known as al-Yazīdī. He was called al-Yazīdī because of his association with Yazīd b. Manṣūr, the maternal uncle of al-Mahdī.[7] He died in Khorasan in the year 202 AH.

footnotes.text: The reading of wa-nuʿallimuhū is also disagreed upon, see F.3:48.

statements.heading: U.2.4. Ibn ʿĀmir the Syrian
statements.text: He is ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. ʿĀmir al-Yaḥṣubī, judge of Damascus during the caliphate of al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik. His patronym was ʾAbū ʿImrān. He was among the successors. Out of the seven readers, only he and ʾAbū ʿAmr were Arabs. The rest of them were clients (i.e., non-Arabs). He died in Damascus in the year 118 AH. Ibn Ḏakwān is ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. ʾAḥmad b. Bašīr b. Ḏakwān al-Qurašī the Damascene. His patronym was ʾAbū ʿAmr and he died in [Damascus] in the year 242 AH. Hišām is Hišām b. ʿAmmār b. Nuṣayr b. ʾAbān b. Maysarah al-Sulamī, the Damascene judge. His patronym was ʾAbū al-Walīd. He died in [Damascus] in the year 245 AH. They transmitted the reading from Ibn ʿĀmir through a chain of transmission (i.e., they were not his direct students).

statements.heading: U.2.5. ʿĀṣim the Kufan
statements.text: He is ʿĀṣim b. ʾAbī al-Naǧūd. He is (also) called Ibn Bahdalah, and it is said that ʾAbū al-Naǧūd’s name was ʿAbd and Bahdalah was the name of his mother. He was a client of Naṣr b. Quʿayn al-ʾAsadī. His patronym was ʾAbū Bakr. He was one of the successors affiliated with al-Ḥāriṯ b. al-Ḥassān, an envoy of the Banū Bakr. He died in Kufa in the year 128 AH, though it is also said that it was 127 AH. ʾAbū Bakr is Šuʿbah b. ʿAyyāš b. Sālim al-Kūfī al-ʾAsadī, a client to them (i.e., Banū ʾAsad). It has also been said that his name was Sālim, or that his name was his patronym or that it was something other than that. He died in Kufa in the year 194 AH. Ḥafṣ is Ḥafṣ b. Sulaymān b. al-Muġīrah al-ʾAsadī al-Bazzāz al-Kūfī. His patronym was ʾAbū ʿUmar and he was known as Ḥufayṣ. Wakīʿ said he was trustworthy (in the transmission of hadith). Ibn Maʿīn said that he was a better reader than ʾAbū Bakr [Šuʿbah]. He died close to the year 190 AH.

statements.heading: U.2.6. Ḥamzah the Kufan
statements.text: He is Ḥamzah b. Ḥabīb b. ʿUmārah b. ʾIsmāʿīl al-Zayyāt al-Faraḍī al-Taymī,[8] a client to them (i.e., Taym). His patronym was ʾAbū ʿUmārah. He died in Ḥulwān during the caliphate of ʾAbū Ǧaʿfar al-Manṣūr in the year 156 AH. Ḫalaf is Ḫalaf b. Hišām al-Bazzār. His patronym is ʾAbū Muḥammad. He is from the people of Fam al-Ṣilḥ. He died in Baghdad while in hiding during the time of ǧahmiyyah[9] in the year 229 AH. Ḫallād is Ḫallād b. Ḫālid, and he was called Ibn Ḫulayd, and he was called Ibn ʿĪsā al-Ṣayrafī al-Kūfī. His patronym was ʾAbū ʿĪsā. He died in [Kufa] in the year 220 AH. They transmitted the reading from ʾAbū ʿĪsā Sulaym b. ʿĪsā al-Ḥanafī al-Kūfī from Ḥamzah. Sulaym died in Kufa in the year 188 AH, and it is also said 189 AH.

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

Pretzl has b. al-ʾAḥzam; this is a mistake (al-Dānī 2008a, 33). Note that this ʾisnād is not present in the Taysīr nor in the Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān. It is one of the tilāwah paths for al-Dānī’s teacher ʾAbū al-Ḥasan Ibn Ġalbūn (1991, 27) as well as ʾAbū al-Ṭayyib Ibn Ġalbūn (2015, 185). Both of them indeed explicitly mention this exception (Ibn Ġalbūn 1991, 265; 2015, 436).

statements.heading: U.2.7. Al-Kisāʾī the Kufan
statements.text: He is ʿAlī b. Ḥamzah the grammarian, client to the Banū ʾAsad. His patronym was ʾAbū al-Ḥasan. He was called al-Kisāʾī because he wore a cloak (kisāʾ) as his pilgrimage garb (ʾiḥrām). He died in Ranbūyah, one of the towns of al-Rayy while heading to Ḫurasān with [Hārūn] al-Rašīd in the year 189 AH. ʾAbū ʿUmar is Ḥafṣ b. ʿUmar al-Dūrī the grammarian, [who was also a] student of al-Yazīdī. ʾAbū al-Ḥāriṯ is al-Layṯ b. Ḫālid al-Baġdādī. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: These are the names of the seven readers and the transmitters from them in an abbreviated manner. Success comes from God.

statements.heading: U.3. The Teachers
statements.text: These are the masters who conveyed the recitation to them from the Messenger of God (ṣ).

statements.heading: U.3.1. The Teachers of Nāfiʿ
statements.text: The teachers of Nāfiʿ whom he named are five: ʾAbū Ǧaʿfar Yazīd b. al-Qaʿqāʿ the reader, ʾAbū Dāwūd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Hurmuz al-ʾAʿraǧ, Šaybah b. Niṣāḥ the judge, ʾAbū ʿAbd Aḷḷāh Muslim b. Ǧundab al-Huḏalī the storyteller and ʾAbū Rawḥ Yazīd b. Rūmān. They took the reading from ʾAbū Hurayrah, Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. ʿAyyāš b. ʾAbī Rabīʿah, from ʾUbayy b. Kaʿb, from the Prophet (ṣ).

statements.heading: U.3.2. The Teachers of Ibn Kaṯīr
statements.text: The teachers of Ibn Kaṯīr are three: ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. al-Sāʾib al-Maḫzūmī, companion of the Prophet (ṣ), Muǧāhid b. Ǧabr ʾAbū al-Ḥaǧǧāǧ, client of Qays b. al-Sāʾib, and Dirbās, client of Ibn ʿAbbās. ʿAbd Aḷḷāh [b. al-Sāʾib al-Maḫzūmī] himself took [the reading] from ʾUbayy [b. Kaʿb]. Muǧāhid [b. Ǧabr] and Dirbās took it from Ibn ʿAbbās [who took it] from ʾUbayy and Zayd b. Ṯābit [who both took it] from the Prophet (ṣ).

statements.heading: U.3.3. The Teachers of ʾAbū ʿAmr
statements.text: The teachers of ʾAbū ʿAmr are a group of people from the Hijaz and Basra. So, the people of Mecca are Muǧāhid [b. Ǧabr], Saʿīd b. Ǧubayr, ʿIkrimah b. Ḫālid, ʿAṭāʾ b. ʾAbī Rabāḥ,[10] ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. Kaṯīr, Muḥammad b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Muḥayṣin and Ḥumayd b. Qays al-ʾAʿraǧ. Among the people of Medina are [ʾAbū Ǧaʿfar] Yazīd b. al-Qaʿqāʿ, Yazīd b. Rūmān and Šaybah b. Naṣāḥ. Among the people of Basra are al-Ḥasan b. ʾAbī al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar and others besides those two. They took their recitation from those that have preceded (under Ibn Kaṯīr and Nāfiʿ’s entries) among the companions [of the Prophet] and others.

footnotes.text: On Ḥamzah’s reading in pause, see U.11.6.2.

statements.heading: U.3.4. The Teachers of Ibn ʿĀmir
statements.text: The teachers of Ibn ʿĀmir are ʾAbū al-Dardāʾ ʿUwaymir b. ʿĀmir, companion of the Prophet (ṣ), and al-Muġīrah b. ʾAbī Šihāb al-Maḫzūmī. ʾAbū al-Dardāʾ took [his recitation] from the Prophet (ṣ) and Muġīrah took it from ʿUṯmān b. ʿAffān (r) from the Prophet (ṣ). It was transmitted to us from al-Walīd b. Muslim from Yaḥyā b. al-Ḥāriṯ al-Ḏamārī that Ibn ʿĀmir recited to ʿUṯmān himself. This is incorrect.

statements.heading: U.3.5. The Teachers of ʿĀṣim
statements.text: The teachers of ʿĀṣim are ʾAbū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. Ḥabīb al-Sulamī and ʾAbū Maryam Zirr b. Ḥubayš. ʾAbū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān took [his reading] from ʿUṯmān b. ʿAffān, ʿAlī b. ʾAbī Ṭālib, ʾUbayy b. Kaʿb, Zayd b. Ṯābit and ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. Masʿūd (r), who took it from the Prophet (ṣ). Zirr took [his reading] from ʿUṯmān and Ibn Masʿūd (r) from the Prophet (ṣ).

statements.heading: U.3.6. The Teachers of Ḥamzah
statements.text: The teachers of Ḥamzah are a group of people, among them ʾAbū Muḥammad Sulaymān b. Mihrān al-ʾAʿmaš, Muḥammad b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʾAbī Laylā the judge, Ḥumrān b. ʾAʿyan, ʾAbū ʾIsḥāq al-Sabīʿī, Manṣūr b. al-Muʿtamir, Muġīrah b. Miqsam, Ǧaʿfar b. Muḥammad al-Ṣādiq and others. Al-ʾAʿmaš took (his reading) from Yaḥyā b. Waṯṯāb, and Yaḥyā took it from a group of the companions of Ibn Masʿūd: ʿAlqamah, al-ʾAswad, ʿUbayd b. Nuḍaylah al-Ḫuzāʿī, Zirr b. Ḥubayš, ʾAbū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī from Ibn Masʿūd, from the Prophet (ṣ).

statements.heading: U.3.7. The Teachers of al-Kisāʾī
statements.text: The teachers of al-Kisāʾī are Ḥamzah b. Ḥabīb al-Zayyāt, ʿĪsā b. ʿUmar al-Hamdānī, Muḥammad b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʾAbī Laylā and others from the masters of the Kufans. However, the material of his reading and the foundation of his personal selection comes from Ḥamzah. We have already mentioned the path back to the Prophet of his reading. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: So, these are the appellations of the teachers of the masters of the seven readings in the regional capitals. Success comes from God.

statements.heading: U.4. The ʾisnāds Which Conveyed to Me the Recitation from These Masters along the Described Paths (ṭuruq) in the Modes of Both riwāyah and tilāwah
U.4.1. The ʾisnād of the Reading of Nāfiʿ
U.4.1.1. The Transmission of Qālūn from [Nāfiʿ]
statements.text: ʾAḥmad b. ʿUmar b. Muḥammad al-Ǧīzī narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad b. Munīr narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. ʿĪsā al-Madanī narrated to us, saying: Qālūn narrated it to us from Nāfiʿ. I have recited the full Qurʾān according to [this transmission] to my master ʾAbū al-Fatḥ Fāris b. ʾAḥmad b. Mūsā b. ʿImrān, the teacher of recitation, the blind. He said to me: I recited it to ʾAbū al-Ḥasan ʿAbd al-Bāqī b. al-Ḥasan, the teacher of recitation. He said: I recited it to ʾIbrāhīm b. ʿUmar, the teacher of recitation. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū al-Ḥusayn ʾAḥmad b. ʿUṯmān b. Ǧaʿfar b. Būyān. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū Bakr ʾAḥmad b. Muḥammad b. al-ʾAšʿaṯ. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū Našīṭ Muḥammad b. Hārūn. He said: I recited it to Qālūn. He said: I recited it to Nāfiʿ.

statements.heading: U.4.1.2. The Transmission of Warš
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAbd Aḷḷāh ʾAḥmad b. Maḥfūḏ̣ (= ʾAḥmad b. ʿUmar b. Muḥammad al-Ǧīzī) the judge narrated to us in Egypt, saying: ʾAḥmad b. ʾIbrāhīm b. Ǧāmiʿ narrated to us, saying: ʾAbū Muḥammad Bakr b. Sahl narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Ṣamad b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to us, saying: Warš narrated it to us from Nāfiʿ. I have recited the full Qurʾān according to it (i.e., this transmission) to ʾAbū al-Qāsim Ḫalaf b. ʾIbrāhīm b. Muḥammad b. Ḫāqān, the teacher of recitation in Egypt. He said to me that he recited it to ʾAbū Ǧaʿfar ʾAḥmad b. ʾUsāmah al-Tuǧībī. He said: I recited it to ʾIsmāʿīl b. ʿAbd Aḷḷāh al-Naḥḥās. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf b. ʿAmr b. Yasār al-ʾAzraq. He said: I recited it to Warš. He said: I recited it to Nāfiʿ.

statements.heading: U.4.2. The ʾisnād of the Reading of Ibn Kaṯīr
U.4.2.1. The Transmission of Qunbul
statements.text: ʾAbū Muslim Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad b. ʿAlī al-Baġdādī narrated to us, saying: Ibn Muǧāhid narrated it to us, saying: I recited it to Qunbul. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū al-Ḥasan ʾAḥmad b. Muḥammad b. ʿAwn al-Qawwās. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū al-ʾIḫrīṭ Wahb b. Wāḍiḥ. He said: I recited it to ʾIsmāʿīl b. ʿAbd Aḷḷāh al-Qusṭ. He said: I recited it to Šibl b. ʿAbbād and Maʿrūf b. Muškān. They said: We recited it to Ibn Kaṯīr. I have recited the full Qurʾān to Fāris b. ʾAḥmad al-Ḥimṣī, the teacher of recitation. He said: I recited it to ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. al-Ḥusayn al-Baġdādī. He said: I recited it to Ibn Muǧāhid. He said: I recited it to Qunbul.

statements.heading: U.4.2.2. The Transmission of al-Bazzī
statements.text: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad [b. ʿAlī al-Baġdādī], the scribe narrated it to us, saying: ʾAḥmad b. Mūsā [Ibn Muǧāhid] narrated it to us, saying: Muḍar b. Muḥammad al-Ḍabbī narrated it to us, saying: Ibn ʾAbī Bazzah (= al-Bazzī) narrated to us, saying: I recited it to ʿIkrimah b. Sulaymān b. ʿĀmir and he said: I recited it to ʾIsmāʿīl b. ʿAbd Aḷḷāh al-Qusṭ. He said: I recited it to Ibn Kaṯīr himself. Thus said al-Bazzī.[11] I have recited the whole Qurʾān to ʾAbū al-Qāsim ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ǧaʿfar b. Muḥammad al-Fārisī, the teacher of recitation. He said to me: I recited the Qurʾān to ʾAbū Bakr Muḥammad b. al-Ḥasan al-Naqqāš. He said to me: I recited the Qurʾān from ʾAbū Rabīʿah Muḥammad b. ʾIsḥāq al-Rabaʿī. He said: I recited it to al-Bazzī.

footnotes.text: Pretzl has 216 here; this is a mistake.

statements.heading: U.4.3. The ʾisnād of the Reading of ʾAbū ʿAmr
U.4.3.1. The Transmission of ʾAbū ʿUmar [al-Dūrī]
statements.text: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad b. ʿAlī narrated to us, saying: ʾAbū ʿĪsā Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad b. Qaṭan in the year 318 AH narrated to us, saying: ʾAbū Ḫallād Sulaymān b. Ḫallād narrated to us, saying: al-Yazīdī narrated it to us from ʾAbū ʿAmr.[12] I have recited the whole Qurʾān along the transmission path of ʾAbū ʿUmar to our master ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ǧaʿfar b. Muḥammad b. ʾIsḥāq [al-Fārisī] al-Baġdādī, the teacher of recitation. He said to me: I recited it to ʾAbū Ṭāhir ʿAbd al-Wāḥid b. ʿUmar b. ʾAbī Hāšim, the teacher of recitation, too many times to count. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū Bakr b. Muǧāhid. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū Zaʿrāʾ ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAbdūs. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū ʿUmar [al-Dūrī] and he said: I recited it to al-Yazīdī. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū ʿAmr.

footnotes.text: A different name for Sūrat Muḥammad (Kandil 1992, 52).

statements.heading: U.4.3.2. The Transmission of ʾAbū Šuʿayb [al-Sūsī]
statements.text: Ḫalaf b. ʾIbrāhīm b. Muḥammad, the teacher of recitation, narrated it to us, saying: ʾAbū Muḥammad al-Ḥasan b. Rašīq al-Muʿaddal narrated to us, saying: ʾAbū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ʾAḥmad b. Šuʿayb al-Nasāʾī narrated to us, saying: ʾAbū Šuʿayb [al-Sūsī] narrated to us, saying: al-Yazīdī narrated it to us from ʾAbū ʿAmr. I recited the whole Qurʾān both without assimilation of the first letter of two that are identical or close to each other, and with assimilation[13] from Fāris b. ʾAḥmad, the teacher of recitation. He said to me: I recited it like that to ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. al-Ḥusayn, the teacher of recitation. He said to me: I recited it like that from ʾAbū ʿImrān Mūsā b. Ǧarīr, the grammarian. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū Šuʿayb. He said: I recited it to al-Yazīdī. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū ʿAmr.

footnotes.text: This ʾisnād does not occur in U.4.2.2. nor in the ʾisnād section of Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān.

statements.heading: U.4.3.3. [ʾIsnāds for the Principles of Assimilation]
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad narrated to us the principles of assimilation from Ibn Muǧāhid from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAbdūs from al-Dūrī from al-Yazīdī from ʾAbū ʿAmr. ʾAbū al-Ḥasan [Ibn Ġalbūn], our master, also narrated it to us, saying: ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. al-Mubārak narrated it from Ǧaʿfar b. Sulaymān from ʾAbū Šuʿayb [al-Sūsī] from al-Yazīdī from ʾAbū ʿAmr.

statements.heading: U.4.4. The ʾisnād of the Reading of Ibn ʿĀmir
U.4.4.1. The Transmission of Ibn Ḏakwān
statements.text: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad narrated it to us, saying: ʾAḥmad b. Mūsā [Ibn Muǧāhid] narrated to us, saying: ʾAḥmad b. Yūsuf al-Taġlibī narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. Ḏakwān narrated to us, saying: ʾAyyūb b. Tamīm al-Tamīmī narrated to us, saying: Yaḥyā b. al-Ḥāriṯ al-Ḏamārī narrated to us, saying: I recited it to Ibn ʿĀmir. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: I have recited the full Qurʾān to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ǧaʿfar al-Fārisī, the teacher of recitation. He said to me: I recited it to ʾAbū Bakr Muḥammad b. al-Ḥasan al-Naqqāš. He said: I recited it in Damascus to ʾAbū ʿAbd Aḷḷāh Hārūn b. Mūsā b. Šarīk al-ʾAḫfaš. Al-ʾAḫfaš transmitted it from ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. Ḏakwān.

statements.heading: U.4.4.2. The Transmission of Hišām
statements.text: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad narrated it to us, saying: Ibn Muǧāhid narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥasan b. ʾAbī Mihrān al-Ǧammāl narrated to us, saying: ʾAḥmad b. Yazīd al-Ḥulwānī narrated to us, saying: Hišām b. ʿAmmār narrated to us, saying: ʿIrāk b. Ḫālid al-Murrī narrated to us, saying: I recited it to Yaḥyā b. al-Ḥāriṯ al-Ḏamārī, saying: I recited it to ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. ʿĀmir. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: I have recited the whole Qurʾān to our master ʾAbū al-Fatḥ. He said to me: I recited it to ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. al-Ḥusayn, the teacher of recitation, and he said: I recited it to Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad b. ʿAbdān. He said: I recited it to al-Ḥulwānī. He said: I recited it to Hišām.

statements.heading: U.4.5. The ʾisnād of the Reading of ʿĀṣim
U.4.5.1. The Transmission of ʾAbū Bakr [Šuʿbah]
statements.text: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad b. ʿAlī the scribe narrated it to us, saying: Ibn Muǧāhid narrated to us, saying: ʾIbrāhīm b. ʾAḥmad b. ʿUmar al-Wakīʿī narrated it to us, saying: my father narrated it to us, saying: Yaḥyā b. ʾĀdam narrated to us, saying: ʾAbū Bakr narrated to us from ʿĀṣim. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: I have recited the full Qurʾān to Fāris b. ʾAḥmad the teacher of recitation. He said to me: I recited it to ʾAbū al-Ḥasan ʿAbd al-Bāqī b. al-Ḥasan, the teacher of recitation. He said: I recited it to ʾIbrāhīm b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʾAḥmad al-Baġdādī, the teacher of recitation. He said: I recited it to Yūsuf b. Yaʿqūb al-Wāsiṭī. He said: I recited it to Šuʿayb b. ʾAyyūb al-Ṣarīfīnī. He said: I recited it to Yaḥyā b. ʾĀdam, transmitting from of ʾAbū Bakr from ʿĀṣim. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: Fāris b. ʾAḥmad said to me: I recited it also to ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. al-Ḥusayn. And he informed me that he recited to ʾAḥmad b. Yūsuf al-Qāfulānī. And ʾAḥmad recited to al-Ṣarīfīnī, transmitting from Yaḥyā [b. ʾĀdam] from ʾAbū Bakr from ʿĀṣim.

statements.heading: U.4.5.2. The Transmission of Ḥafṣ
statements.text: ʾAbū al-Ḥasan Ṭāhir b. Ġalbūn, the teacher of recitation, related it to us, saying: ʾAbū Ḥasan ʿAlī b. Muḥammad b. Ṣāliḥ al-Hāšimī the blind, who was a teacher of recitation, related it to us in Basra, saying: ʾAbū ʿAbbās ʾAḥmad b. Sahl al-ʾUšnānī related to us, saying: I recited to ʾAbū Muḥammad ʿUbayd b. al-Ṣabbāḥ. He said: I recited to Ḥafṣ. And he said: I recited to ʿĀṣim. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: I have recited the complete Qurʾān to our master ʾAbū al-Ḥasan [Ibn Ġalbūn]. He said to me: I recited it to al-Hāšimī. He said: I recited it to al-ʾUšnānī, transmitting from ʿUbayd from Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim.

statements.heading: U.4.6. The ʾisnād of the Reading of Ḥamzah
U.4.6.1. The Transmission of Ḫalaf
statements.text: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad related it to us, saying: Ibn Muǧāhid related to us, saying: ʾIdrīs b. ʿAbd al-Karīm related to us, saying: Ḫalaf related to us, transmitting from Sulaym from Ḥamzah. I have recited the complete Qurʾān to our master ʾAbū al-Ḥasan [Ibn Ġalbūn]. He said to me: I recited it to ʾAbū al-Ḥasan Muḥammad b. Yūsuf b. Nahār al-Ḥirtakī in Basra. He said to me: I recited it to ʾAbū al-Ḥusayn ʾAḥmad b. ʿUṯmān b. Ǧaʿfar b. Būyān. He said: I recited to ʾIdrīs b. ʿAbd al-Karīm before he taught according to the personal preference (iḫtiyār) of Ḫalaf (as opposed to the reading of Ḥamzah). He said: I recited to Ḫalaf. He said: I recited to Sulaym. He said: I recited to Ḥamzah.

statements.heading: U.4.6.2. The Transmission of Ḫallād
statements.text: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad related it to us, saying: ʾAḥmad b. Mūsā [Ibn Muǧāhid] related it to us, saying: Yaḥyā b. ʾAḥmad b. Hārūn al-Muzawwiq related it to us from ʾAḥmad b. Yazīd al-Ḥulwānī from Ḫallād from Sulaym from Ḥamzah. I have recited the complete Qurʾān to ʾAbū al-Fatḥ the blind, our master. He said to me: I recited it to ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. al-Ḥusayn, the teacher of recitation. He said: I recited it to Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad b. Šanabūḏ. He said: I recited to ʾAbū Bakr Muḥammad b. Šāḏān al-Ǧawharī, the teacher of recitation. He said: I recited to Ḫallād. He said: I recited to Sulaym, and Sulaym recited to Ḥamzah.

statements.heading: U.4.7. The ʾisnād of the Reading of al-Kisāʾī
U.4.7.1. The Transmission of [ʾAbū ʿUmar] al-Dūrī
statements.text: ʾAbū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿUmar b. Muḥammad al-Muʿaddal narrated it to us, saying: ʿAbd Aḷḷāh b. ʾAḥmad narrated to us, saying: Ǧaʿfar b. Muḥammad b. ʾAsad al-Naṣībī narrated to us, saying: ʾAbū ʿUmar al-Dūrī narrated to us from al-Kisāʾī. I have recited the complete Qurʾān to ʾAbū al-Fatḥ. He said to me: I recited it to ʿAbd al-Bāqī b. al-Ḥasan. He said: I recited it to Muḥammad b. ʿAlī b. al-Ǧulandā al-Mawṣilī. He said: I recited it to Ǧaʿfar b. Muḥammad. He said: I recited it to ʾAbū ʿUmar. He said: I recited it to al-Kisāʾī.

statements.heading: U.4.7.2. The Transmission of ʾAbū al-Ḥāriṯ [al-Layṯ]
statements.text: Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad narrated it to us, saying: Ibn Muǧāhid narrated it to us, saying: Muḥammad b. Yaḥyā narrated it to us from ʾAbū al-Ḥāriṯ from al-Kisāʾī. I have recited the complete Qurʾān to Fāris b. ʾAḥmad. He said to me: I recited it to ʾAbū al-Ḥasan ʿAbd al-Bāqī b. al-Ḥasan. He said: I recited it to Zayd b. ʿAlī. He said: I recited to ʾAḥmad b. al-Ḥasan known as al-Baṭṭī. He said: I recited to Muḥammad b. Yaḥyā al-Kisāʾī.[14] He said: I recited to ʾAbū al-Ḥāriṯ. He said: I recited to al-Kisāʾī. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: So, these are some of the ʾisnāds which convey these transmissions to us, by riwāyah and tilāwah. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: With these two added to the list, the gemination of initial tāʾ is completely regular. It occurs on every single verb which starts with a single tāʾ in the rasm which must be interpreted as a simplification of tata- by haplology rather than assimilation (e.g., Q2:280 تصدقوا taṣṣaddaqū). But these two are only added in this isolated transmission that does not seem to be confirmed by any other transmission (see also the discussion in al-Dānī 2007, 933; Ibn al-Ǧazarī 2018, §2804).

statements.heading: U.5. Al-istiʿāḏah
statements.text: Know that the practice among the experts of the people of the oral tradition[15] regarding its wording is ʾaʿūḏu bi-llāhi min aš-šayṭāni r-raǧīm to the exclusion of any other (wording). That is because of its consistency with the Book and the Sunnah. As for the Book, the words of God Almighty to the Prophet (s) were: fa-ʾiḏā qaraʾta lqurʾāna fa-staʿiḏ bi-llāhi min aš-šayṭāni r-raǧīm “When you recite the Qurʾān, seek refuge with God from Satan the accursed” (Q16:98). As for the Sunnah, what Nāfiʿ b. Ǧubayr b. Muṭʿim transmitted from his father from the Prophet (ṣ) is that he would seek refuge before reciting the Qurʾān with these very same words. And with this (wording) is what I recited (to my teachers) and this is what I adopt. I do not know of any disagreement between the people of the practice in pronouncing it out loud at the start of the Qurʾān or when starting at the beginning of divisions (e.g., a division of the Qurʾān into 30 ʾaǧzāʾ) or anywhere else, according to the tradition of the community, thus following the texts and following the model of the Sunnah. As for the transmission of that (i.e., pronouncing it out loud), it was transmitted from ʾAbū ʿAmr as practice in the path of ʾAbū Ḥamdūn from al-Yazīdī from him (ʾAbū ʿAmr), and in the path of Muḥammad b. Ġālib from Šuǧāʿ from him (ʾAbū ʿAmr). ʾIsḥāq al-Musayyabī transmitted it from Nāfiʿ that he used to say it inaudibly in all of the Qurʾān. Sulaym transmitted from Ḥamzah that he used to pronounce it out loud at the beginning of ʾUmm al-Qurʾān (Q1) only and would say it inaudibly after that in the rest of the Qurʾān. Ḫalaf said it likewise, transmitting from him. Ḫallād, transmitting from him, said that he would allow both saying it out loud and inaudibly for the complete Qurʾān. As for the rest: nothing written has come from them on that topic at all. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This description is more restrictive than it should be. Unlike what the wording might suggest, not just 3sg.m. and 3pl.m. forms, but all forms of the prefix conjugation are meant here, including, e.g., Q25:44 taḥsabu, and Q3:87 li-taḥsa/ibūhū̆.

statements.heading: U.6. The tasmiyah
statements.text: (The readers) disagree in the saying of the tasmiyah[16] between the sūrahs. Ibn Kaṯīr, Qālūn, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī say the tasmiyah between two sūrahs in the whole Qurʾān except between al-ʾAnfāl (Q8) and Barāʾah (= al-Tawbah, Q9). There is no disagreement in the absence of the saying of the tasmiyah between these two. The rest, for what I have recited for them, do not say the tasmiyah between sūrahs. The companions of Ḥamzah connect the end of a sūrah with the beginning of the next (in one breath, without a pause). It is preferred in the tradition of Warš, ʾAbū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir to have a silence between two sūrahs without interruption (i.e., without drawing breath). Ibn Muǧāhid considers it (proper) to connect one sūrah to the next without dropping the ʾiʿrāb. He also considers it (proper) with a silence. Some of our masters, when reading in these traditions (i.e., Warš, ʾAbū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir), used to say the tasmiyah between al-Muddaṯṯir (Q74) and al-Qiyāmah (Q75), between al-Infiṭār (Q82) and al-Muṭaffifīn (Q83), between al-Faǧr (Q89) and al-Balad (Q90) and between al-ʿAṣr (Q103) and al-Humazah (Q104). And when reading in the manner of Ḥamzah, they used to introduce a silence between these pairs of sūrahs (without the tasmiyah). There is no report of that which is transmitted from them (i.e., from Warš, ʾAbū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamzah); it is only a matter of preference of the masters. There is no disagreement in the saying of the tasmiyah at the beginning of the Fātiḥah (Q1) or at the beginning of each sūrah that a reciter begins on and has not connected with what is before it, in the tradition of those who separate (sūrahs with a tasmiyah) and of those who do not. As for beginning at the start of a division of the Qurʾān which is in (the middle of) a sūrah, my teachers allow the reciter to choose between saying the tasmiyah and omitting it. Separation (i.e., drawing breath) after the tasmiyah when one has connected it with the end of the (previous) sūrah is not allowed. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: ‘Removed ones’ refers to word-final yāʾs which, especially in verse-final position, are often unwritten in the Qurʾānic text where classical orthography would expect them. Readers different on whether and when these yāʾs are reconstituted in recitation or not.

statements.heading: U.7. Sūrat ʾUmm al-Qurʾān
statements.text: 4: ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read māliki yawmi d-dīni with an ʾalif. The rest read it without an ʾalif (i.e., maliki). 6, 7: Ḫalaf reads aẓ-ẓirāṭ and ẓirāṭ wherever they occur giving the smell of the zāy to the ṣād. Ḫallād reads with giving the smell of the zāy in the words of the Almighty aẓ-ẓirāṭa l-mustaqīmi here (Q1:6) only. Qunbul reads them with a sīn whenever they occur (i.e., as-sirāṭ, sirāṭ), and the rest read them all with a ṣād (i.e., aṣ-ṣirāṭ, ṣirāṭ).

statements.heading: U.7.1. [The Morphology of the Plural Pronouns]
statements.text: Ḥamzah reads ʿalayhum, ʾilayhum and ladayhum with ḍammah on the hāʾ. The rest read them with kasrah (i.e., ʿalayhim(ū), ʾilayhim(ū), ladayhim(ū)). Ibn Kaṯīr and Qālūn, with some disagreement among his transmitters, place ḍammah on the mīm that marks plurality and attaches to it a wāw (i.e., ʾantumū, -tumū, -kumū, humū, -humū, -himū) whether it is with hamzah (following it) or without it. For example, ʿalayhimū ʾā̆.anḏartahumū ʾam lam tunḏirhumū (Q2:6) and what is like it. Warš only adds the ḍammah and wāw to it when there is hamzah (following it) (i.e., ʿalayhimū ʾānḏartahum), and the rest does not place a vowel on it (the mīm) (i.e., ʿalayhim ʾā̆ʾ/.anḏartahum). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī place ḍammah on the hāʾ and the mīm when there is kasrah or yāʾ before the hāʾ, and a two-consonant cluster (ʾalif waṣl) after the mīm. For example, ʿalayhumu ḏ-ḏillatu (Q2:61) and bihumu l-ʾasbābu (Q2:166) and what is like it. That is in the case of connected speech. When they pause on the mīm, they place kasrah on the hāʾ and no vowel on the mīm (i.e., bihim#). But Ḥamzah, following his principles of the three words mentioned earlier, places ḍammah on the hāʾ in all cases (i.e., ʿalayhum#, ʾilayhum# and ladayhum#). ʾAbū ʿAmr places kasrah on the hāʾ and the mīm in all of those (words) when they occur in connected speech (before a two-consonant cluster) (i.e., ʿalayhimi, ḏ-ḏillatu, bihimi l-ʾasbāb). The rest places kasrah on the hāʾ and ḍammah on the mīm in connected speech (before a two-consonant cluster) (i.e., ʿalayhimu ḏ-ḏillatu, bihimu l-(ʾ)asbāb). There is no disagreement between the community (of readers) that the mīm in all that has preceded does not carry a vowel in pause.

statements.heading: U.8. Explanation of ʾAbū ʿAmr’s Approach to Major Assimilation (al-ʾidġām al-kabīr)
statements.text: Know—may God instruct you—that I have singled out ʾAbū ʿAmr’s approach in this chapter to his assimilation of (pairs of) vowelled letters which are identical in pronunciation or close in place of articulation, and nothing else. These occur in two cases: within a single word and across words. I will explain this according to the way I have received it via riwāyah or tilāwah, if God Almighty wills it. Success comes from God.

statements.heading: U.8.1. Two Identical (Letters) within a Word and between Two Words
statements.text: Know that ʾAbū ʿAmr does not assimilate two identical sounds word-internally except for two instances, and nothing else. The first of these two is in al-Baqarah (Q2:200) manāsikakum (→ manāsik⸗kum). The second is in al-Muddaṯṯir (Q74:42) mā salakakum (→ mā salak⸗kum). He leaves everything other than that unassimilated: for example, ǧibāhuhum (Q9:35), wuǧūhuhum (e.g., Q3:106), bi-širkikum (Q35:14), ʾa-tuḥāǧǧūnanā (Q2:139), ʾa-taʿidāninī (Q46:17), and what is like it. As for two identical sounds when they are in two different words, he assimilates the first to the second of the two, regardless of whether the preceding letter is unvowelled or vowelled, throughout the whole Qurʾān: for example, in His speech fīhi hudan (→ fīh⸗hudan) (Q2:2), ʾinnahū huwa[17] (→ innah⸗huwa) (e.g., Q2:37), li-ʿibādatihī hal (→ li-ʿibādatih⸗hal) (Q19:65), ʾan yaʾtiya yawmun (→ ʾan yātiy⸗yawmun) (e.g., Q2:254), min ḫizyi yawmiʾiḏin (→ min ḫizy⸗yawmiʾiḏin) (Q11:66), lā ʾabraḥu ḥattā (→ lā ʾabraḥ⸗ḥattā) (Q18:60), yašfaʿu ʿindahū (→ yašfaʿ⸗ʿindahū) (Q2:255), ʾiḏā qīla lahum (→ ʾiḏā qīl⸗lahum) (e.g., Q2:11), yastaḥyūna nisāʾakum (yastaḥyūn⸗nisāʾakum) (e.g., Q2:49), nusabbiḥaka kaṯīran (→ nusabbiḥak⸗kaṯīran) (Q20:33), naḏkuraka kaṯīran (→ naḏkurak⸗kaṯīran) (Q20:34), an-nāsa sukārē (→ an-nās⸗sukārē) (Q22:2), aš-šawkati takūnu (→ aš-šawkat⸗takūnu) (Q8:7), šahru ramaḍāna (→ šahr⸗ramaḍāna) (Q2:185), mà ḫtalafa fīhi (→ mà ḫtalaf⸗fīhi) (Q2:213), yaʿlamu mā (→ yaʿlam⸗mā) (e.g., Q2:77), la-ḏahaba bi-samʿihim (→ la-ḏahab⸗bi-samʿihim) (Q2:20) and what is similar to it among the remaining letters of the alphabet whenever they occur, except in the words of the Almighty in Luqmān (Q31:23) fa-lā yaḥzunka kufruhū: he does not assimilate because of the unvowelled nūn before the kāf, as it has undergone partial assimilation (ʾiḫfāʾ)[18] to it. When the first of the two similar letters is geminate or it carries tanwīn or it is the second person suffix -ta/-ti (tāʾ al-ḫiṭāb)[19] or the suffix -tu of the first person (tāʾ al-mutakallim),[20]—for example in His speech wa-ʾuḥilla lakum (e.g., Q2:187), massa saqara (Q54:48), ṣawāffa fa-ʾiḏā (Q22:36), ʾummi mūsǟ (Q28:7, 10), al-yammi mā (Q20:78), min ʾanṣērin // rabbinā (Q3:192-3), ʾa-fa-ʾanta tukrihu (Q10:99), kuntu turāban (Q78:40) and what is like it— he does not assimilate them either. If it is a defective word,[21] for example in the words wa-man yabtaġi ġayra l-ʾislāmi dīnan (Q3:85), yaḫlu lakum (Q12:9), ʾin yaku kāḏiban (Q40:28), and what is like it, the people of the oral tradition disagree on it. So, the approach of Ibn Muǧāhid and his companions is to refrain from assimilation. The approach of ʾAbū Bakr al-Dāǧūnī[22] and others is to apply as-similation. I myself have recited it in both ways. I do not know of any disagreement on the assimilation in the words wa-yā qawmi man yanṣurunī (→ wa-yā qawm⸗man yanṣurunī) (Q11:30), yā qawmi mā liya (→ yā qawm⸗mā liya) (Q40:41), while it belongs to the defective words.[23] As for His speech ʾāla lūṭin (e.g., Q15:59), whenever it occurs, the majority of the Baghdadis (i.e., Baghdadi transmitters of al-Yazīdī) adopt it without assimilation, and this is what Ibn Muǧāhid adopts. It may be defective because of the paucity of letters in the word. Others used to adopt assimilation (in this phrase), and I recite it with assimilation. After all, they agreed on the assimilation of laka kaydan (→ lak⸗kaydan) in Yūsuf (Q12:15) and that word (i.e., laka) has even fewer letters than ʾāla, because it is only two letters, so that shows that it is correct to read it with assimilation (i.e., ʾāl⸗lūṭin). If lack of assimilation is correct, then it is because of the defectiveness of its second root letter. So, the hāʾ (of |ʾahl|, which is taken as the underlying form) is exchanged for the hamzah (to make |ʾaʾl|) and then the hamzah is changed into ʾalif (to make |ʾaAl|), and nothing else. The people of the oral tradition also disagree on the (assimilation) of the wāw of huwa when there is ḍammah on the hāʾ before it, and it meets with the same letter (another wāw): for example, in the words of the Almighty ʾillā huwa wa-malāʾikatu (Q3:18), and kaʾannah⸗huwa wa-ʾūtīnà l-ʿilma (Q27:42), and what is like it. Ibn Muǧāhid adopts it without as-similation, and the others adopt it with assimilation (i.e., ʾillā huw⸗wa-malāʾikatu, ka-ʾannah⸗huw⸗wa-ʾūtīnà l-ʿilma). I recite it with assimilation, and it is by force of analogy because Ibn Muǧāhid and others are in agreement on the assimilation of a yāʾ to another yāʾ in His speech ʾan yaʾtiya yawmun (→ ʾan yātiy⸗yawmun)[24] (e.g., Q2:254) and nūdiya yā mūsǟ (→ nūdiy⸗yā mūsǟ) (Q20:11). There is a kasrah before the yāʾ and there is no (relevant) difference between the two categories.[25] If the hāʾ of huwa does not carry a vowel (hwa),[26] or if there is another unvowelled letter other than the hāʾ before the wāw, there is no disagreement on the assimilation, and that is, for example, in His speech wa-hwa waliyyuhum (→ wa-hw⸗waliyyuhum) (Q6:127), wa-hwa wāqiʿun bihim (→ wa-hw⸗wāqiʿun bihim) (Q42:22), ḫuḏi l-ʿafwa wa-ʾmur (→ ḫuḏi l-ʿafw⸗wāmur) (Q7:199), min al-lahwi wa-min at-tiǧārati (→ min al-lahw⸗wa-min at-tiǧārati) (Q62:11) and what is similar to it. As for His speech wa-llāʾi yaʾisna in al-Ṭalāq (Q65:4), ʾAbū ʿAmr’s practice is to replace the hamzah with a vowelless yāʾ (wa-llāy), and it is not permissible to assimilate it, because the replacing letter (the yāʾ in place of the hamzah) is accidental (i.e., it is not part of the underlying form).[27] That is reinforced by the defectiveness of this word, as the yāʾ has been removed at the end[28] and the hamzah has been replaced with the yāʾ. If it was assimilated there would be a meeting of those three defects (i.e., 1. the dropping of yāʾ, 2. the replacement of hamzah and 3. assimilation). Success comes from God.

Pretzl has ୚ඤن (al-Dānī 2008a, 35). Subḥān is an alternative name for Sūrat al-ʾIsrāʾ (Kandil 1992, 50).

The words hā ʾantumū are seen as having a word-boundary between them. As Ibn Kaṯīr does not have an overlong vowel with long vowels before hamzah between two words, this is not lengthened (see U.11.2.).
This refers to a recognised possibility by grammarians to replace the hamzah of the interrogative particle ʾa- with a hāʾ (Saeed 2023, 83).

Note that al-Dānī refers to a hamzah followed by another hamzah pronounced bayna bayn as madd ‘length’. This is ambiguous because he also calls a hamzah followed by ā madd. The wording therefore also allows the reading ʾān. Al-Dānī is explicit that the intended reading is ʾa-.an in his Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān (al-Dānī 2007, 970).
