Iḫtilās normally means ‘ultrashort’, but it is technically a relative term, i.e., shorter than its ʾaṣl ‘base’. As the base is yuʾaddihī, iḫtilās should be simply understood here to mean a normal-length kasrah, -hi. See I.4.2.
The Taysīr only has ʾisnāds for Hišām that go through al-Ḥulwānī. The Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān has other paths, but few seem to have explicit information on this topic (al-Dānī 2007, 980–81).

statements.heading: U.8.2. Two Letters that Are Close to One Another within a Word and Two Words
statements.text: Know that he (ʾAbū ʿAmr) also does not assimilate two sounds that are close to one another (in place of articulation) when they occur within a word, except the qāf to the kāf that is part of the masculine plural pronoun (-kum) when the letter before the qāf is vowelled, and nothing else. That is, for example, in the words ḫalaqakum (→ ḫalak⸗kum) (e.g., Q2:21), razaqakum (→ razak⸗kum) (e.g., Q5:88), yaḫluqukum (→ yaḫluk⸗kum) (Q39:6), yarzuqukum ( → yarzuk⸗kum) (e.g., Q10:31), wāṯaqakum (→ wāṯak⸗kum) (Q5:7), and what is like it. For the remainder, he leaves (the qāf) unassimilated when the letter before the qāf is unvowelled, and when there is no mīm that follows the kāf, for example in the words mīṯāqakum (Q2:63, etc.),[29] bi-warqikum (Q18:19), ḫalaqaka (Q18:37; Q82:7), narzuquka (Q20:132) and what is like it. The people of the oral tradition disagree about His speech ʾin ṭallaqakunna in al-Taḥrīm (Q66:5). Ibn Muǧāhid adopts it without assimilation, and that is what most of his companions adopt. But al-Yazīdī wanted ʾAbū ʿAmr (to allow for) assimilation, and this indicates that he (al-Yazīdī) transmitted it from him (ʾAbū ʿAmr) without assimilation. I myself read it with assimilation and this is analogy on the basis of the heaviness of the feminine plural. As for what is among the letters that are close to one another (in place of articulation) between two words, he assimilated them for 16 letters, and no others; they are ḥāʾ, qāf, kāf, ǧīm, šīn, ḍād, sīn, dāl, tāʾ, ḏāl, ṯāʾ, rāʾ, lām, nūn, mīm and bāʾ. These are collected in a mnemonic sentence for the letters and it is sanašuddu ḥuǧǧataka biḏulli raḍḍi quṯama. It also does not occur if the first letter has tanwīn or it is a geminate letter or it is the second person suffix -ta or -ti or it is followed by a vowel of a weak stem, for example, wa-lā naṣīrin // laqad (Q9:116–7), al-ḥaqqu ka-man (Q13:19), li-man ḫalaqta ṭīnan (Q17:61), lam yuʾta saʿatan (Q2:247) and what is like it. So as for the ḥāʾ, he assimilates it to the ʿayn in His speech in ʾĀl ʿImrān (Q3:185) fa-man zuḥziḥa ʿani n-nēri (→ fa-man zuḥziʿ⸗ʿani n-nēri) and nothing else. This was transmitted in written form by ʾAbū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. al-Yazīdī from his father from him (ʾAbū ʿAmr). He does not assimilate it in any other case, for example fa-lā ǧunāḥa ʿalayhimā (e.g., Q2:229), al-masīḥv̆ ʿīsǟ (e.g., Q3:45), wa-mā ḏubiḥa ʿalà n-nuṣubi (Q5:3), lā yuṣliḥu ʿamala (Q10:81) and what is like it. As for the qāf, he assimilates it to the kāf if there is a vowelled letter before it; for example, ḫāliqu kulli šayʾin (→ ḫālik⸗kulli šayʾin) (e.g., Q6:102), ḫalaqa kulla šayʾin (→ ḫalak⸗kulla šayʾin) (e.g., Q6:101), ḫalaqa kulla dābbatin (→ ḫalak⸗kulla dābbatin) (Q24:45) and what is like it. If there is an unvowelled letter before the qāf, it is not assimilated; for example, wa-fawqa kulli ḏī ʿilmin (Q12:76) and what is like it. As for the kāf, he also assimilates it to the qāf when there is a vowelled letter before it, for example, in the words nuqaddisu laka qāla (→ nuqaddisu laq⸗qāla) (Q2:30), kāna rabbuka qadīran (→ kāna rabbuq⸗qadīran) (Q25:54) and what is like it. If there is no vowel before the kāf, it does not assimilate; for example, ʾilayka qāla (e.g., Q7:143), lā yaḥzunka qawluhum (e.g., Q10:65) and what is like it. As for the ǧīm, he assimilates it to the šīn in His speech ʾaḫraǧa šaṭʾahū (→ ʾaḫraš⸗ šaṭʾahū) (Q48:29) and to the tāʾ in His speech ḏì l-maʿāriǧi // taʿruǧu (→ ḏì l-maʿārit⸗taʿruǧu) (Q70:3–4) and nothing else. As for the šīn, he assimilates it to the sīn in His speech ʾilā ḏì l-ʿarši sabīlan (→ ʾilā ḏì l-ʿars⸗sabīlan) (Q17:44) and nothing else. Ibn al-Yazīdī transmitted this in written form from his father from him (ʾAbū ʿAmr). As for the ḍād, he assimilates it to the šīn in the words of the Almighty li-baʿḍi šaʾnihim (→ li-baʿš⸗šānihim) (Q24:62) and nothing else. Al-Sūsī transmits it in written form from al-Yazīdī from him (ʾAbū ʿAmr). As for the sīn, he assimilates it to the zāy in His speech wa-ʾiḏà n-nufūsu zuwwiǧat (→ wa-ʾiḏà n-nufūz⸗zuwwiǧat) (Q81:7), and nothing else; and to the šīn with disagreement among his transmitters in His speech ar-raʾsu šayban (→ ar-rāš⸗šayban) (Q19:4), and I read it with assimilation. As for the dāl, he assimilates it if there is a vowelled letter before it, with five letters following it. 1. With the tāʾ in His speech fì l-masāǧidi tilka (→ fì l-masāǧit⸗tilka) (Q2:187) and nothing else. 2. With the ḏāl in His speech al-qalāʾida ḏālika (→ al-qalāʾiḏ⸗ḏālika) (Q5:97) and nothing else. 3. With the sīn in His speech ʿadada sinīna (→ ʿadas⸗sinīna) (Q23:112) and nothing else. 4. With the šīn in His speech wa-šahida šāhidun (→ wa-šahiš⸗šāhidun) in Yūsuf (Q12:26) and al-Aḥqāf (Q46:10) and nothing else. 5. With the ṣād in His speech nafqidu ṣuwāʿa l-maliki (→ nafqiṣ⸗ṣuwāʿa l-maliki) (Q12:72) and fī maqʿadi ṣidqin (→ fī maqʿaṣ⸗ṣidqin) (Q54:55) and nothing else. If there is no vowel in front of it and it (the dāl) carries kasra or ḍamma, he assimilates it with nine letters.[30] 1. With the tāʾ in His speech min aṣ-ṣaydi tanāluhū (→ min aṣ-ṣayt⸗tanāluhū) (Q5:94), takādu tamayyazu (→ takāt⸗tamayyazu) (Q67:8) and nothing else. 2. With the ḏāl, for example, in His speech min baʿdi ḏālika (→ min baʿḏ⸗ḏālika) (e.g., Q2:52), al-marfūdu // ḏālika (→ al-marfūḏ⸗ḏālika) (Q11:99–100) and what is like it. 3. With the ṯāʾ in His speech yurīdu ṯawāba d-dunyǟ (→ yurīṯ⸗ṯawāba d-dunyǟ) (Q4:134), li-man nurīdu ṯumma (→ nurīṯ⸗ṯumma) (Q17:18) and nothing else. 4. With the ḏ̣āʾ in His speech yurīdu ḏ̣ulman (→ yurīḏ̣⸗ḏ̣ulman) in ʾĀl ʿImrān (Q3:108) and Ġāfir (Q40:31) and min baʿdi ḏ̣ulmihī (→ min baʿḏ̣⸗ḏ̣ulmihī) in al-Māʾidah (Q5:39) and nothing else. 5. With the zāy in His speech turīdu zīnata (→ turīz⸗zīnata) (Q18:28), yakādu zaytuhā (→ yakāz⸗zaytuhā) (Q24:35) and nothing else. 6. With the sīn in His speech al-ʾaṣfādi // sarābīluhum ( → al-ʾaṣfās⸗sarābīluhum) (Q14:49–50), yakādu sanā barqihī (→ yakās⸗sanā barqihī) (Q24:43) and nothing else.[31] 7. With the ṣād in His speech fì l-mahdi ṣabiyyan (→ fì l-mahṣ⸗ṣabiyyan) (Q19:29), wa-min baʿdi ṣalāti l-ʿišāʾi (→ wa-min baʿṣ⸗ṣalāti l-ʿišāʾi) (Q24:58) and nothing else. 8. With the ḍād in His speech min baʿdi ḍarrāʾi (→ min baʿḍ⸗ḍarrāʾi) in Yūnus (Q10:21) and Fuṣṣilat (Q41:50) and min baʿdi ḍuʿfin (→ min baʿḍ⸗ḍuʿfin) in al-Rūm (Q30:54) and nothing else. 9. With the ǧīm in His speech dāwūdu ǧālūta (→ dāwūǧ⸗ǧālūta) (Q2:251), al-ḫuldi ǧazāʾan ( → al-ḫulǧ⸗ǧazāʾan) (Q41:28) and nothing else. Ibn Muǧāhid does not admit assimilation of the second phrase (i.e., al-ḫuldi ǧazāʾan) because the unvowelled letter was not a weak letter (i.e., not y, w or ā). In this and what is like it,[32] the grammarians and skilled teachers of recitations apply ʾiḫfāʾ (to be understood as iḫtilās, i.e., al-ḫuldĭ ǧazāʾan, min baʿdĭ ḏālika, etc.). This is what has been adopted by me. If the dāl follows an unvowelled letter and carries a fatḥah, he did not assimilate it (to any letter) except tāʾ, since the two of them (dāl and tāʾ) have the same place of articulation. This is in His speech: mā kāda tazīġu (→ mā kāt⸗tazīġu) (Q9:117) and baʿda tawkīdihā (→ baʿt⸗tawkīdihā) (Q16:91) and nothing else. As for the tāʾ, he assimilates it—when it is not a second person pronoun—to ten letters. 1. With the ṭāʾ, for example, aṣ-ṣalāta ṭarafayi n-nahēri (→ aṣ-ṣalāṭ⸗ṭarafayi n-nahēri) (Q11:114), aṣ-ṣāliḥāti ṭūbǟ lahum (→ aṣ-ṣāliḥāṭ⸗ṭūbǟ lahum) (Q13:29) and what is like it. As for His speech wa-l-taʾti ṭāʾifatun (Q4:102), I read it in both ways (wa-ltāṭ⸗ṭaʾifatun and wa-l-tāti ṭāʾifatun), and Ibn Muǧāhid considered it to be without assimilation, because it is defective. Others favour it with assimilation due to the strength of the kasrah. 2. With the ḏāl, for example, in ʿaḏāba l-ʾāḫirati ḏālika (→ ʿaḏāba l-ʾāḫiraḏ⸗ḏālika) (Q11:103), wa-ḏ-ḏāriyāti ḏarwan (→ wa-ḏ-ḏāriyāḏ⸗ḏarwan) (Q51:1) and what is like it. As for His speech wa-ʾāti ḏà l-qurbǟ (Q17:26), Ibn Muǧāhid considered it to be without assimilation. I read it in both ways (wa-ʾāḏ⸗ḏà l-qurbǟ and wa-ʾāti ḏà l-qurbǟ). 3. With the ṯāʾ, for example, in His speech bi-l-bayyināti ṯumma (→ bi-l-bayyināṯ⸗ṯumma) (e.g., Q2:92), an-nubuwwata ṯumma ( → an-nubuwwaṯ⸗ṯumma) (Q3:79), al-mawti ṯumma (→ al-mawṯ⸗ṯumma) (Q29:57) and what is like it. As for His speech wa-ʾātù zzakāta ṯūmma (Q2:83) and ḥummilù t-tawrāta ṯumma (Q26:5), Ibn Muǧāhid did not consider these to assimilate, because of the lightness of the fatḥah. I read it in both ways (az-zakāṯ⸗ṯumma and az-zakāta ṯumma; at-tawrāṯ⸗ṯumma and at-tawrāta ṯumma). 4. With the ḏ̣āʾ in His speech al-malāʾikatu ḏ̣ālimī (→ al-malāʾikaḏ̣⸗ḏ̣ālimī) in al-Nisāʾ (Q4:97) and al-Naḥl (16:28) and nothing else. 5. With the ḍād in His speech wa-l-ʿādiyāti ḍabḥan (→ wa-l-ʿādiyāḍ⸗ḍabḥan) (Q100:1) and nothing else. 6. With the šīn in His speech ʾinna zalzalata s-sāʿati šayʾun (→ as-sāʿaš⸗šayʾun) (Q22:1) and in His speech bi-ʾarbaʿati šuhadāʾa (→ bi-ʾarbaʿaš⸗šuhadāʾa) in two locations (Q24:4, 13) and nothing else. ʾAbū al-Fatḥ taught me to read la-qaǧ⸗ǧīti šayʾan fariyyan (Q19:27) with assimilation (ǧīš⸗šayʾan) because of the strength of the kasrah. I also read it without assimilation because of the reduction of the second root letter (from |ǧayiʾti| to ǧiʾti). 7. With the ǧīm, for example, in His speech aṣ-ṣāliḥāti ǧunāḥun (→ aṣ-ṣāliḥāǧ⸗ǧunāḥun) (Q5:93), miʾata ǧaldatin (→ miʾaǧ⸗ǧaldatin) (Q24:2), taṣliyatu ǧaḥīmin (→ taṣliyaǧ⸗ ǧaḥīmin) (Q56:94) and what is like it. 8. With the sīn, for example, in His speech bi-s-sāʿati saʿīran (→ bi-s-sāʿas⸗saʿīran) (Q25:11), aṣ-ṣāliḥāti sa-nudḫiluhum (→ aṣ-ṣāliḥās⸗sa-nudḫiluhum) (Q4:57), as-saḥaratu sāǧidīna (→ as-saḥaras⸗sāǧidīna) (Q7:120), and what is like it. 9. With the ṣād in His speech wa-ṣ-ṣāffāti ṣaffan (→ wa-ṣ-ṣāffāṣ⸗ṣaffan) (Q37:1), wa-lmalāʾikatu ṣaffan (→ wa-l-malāʾikaṣ⸗ṣaffan) (Q78:38), fa-l-muġīrāti ṣubḥan (→ fa-lmuġīraṣ⸗ṣubḥan) (Q100:3) and nothing else. 10. With the zāy in His speech bi-l-ʾāḫirati zayyannā (→ bi-l-ʾāḫiraz⸗zayyannā) (Q27:4), fa-z-zāǧirāti zaǧran (→ fa-z-zāǧirāz⸗zaǧran) (Q37:2), ʾilà l-ǧannati zumaran (→ ʾilà lǧannaz⸗zumaran) (Q39:84) and nothing else. As for the ḏāl, he assimilates it to the sīn in His speech fa-ttaḫaḏa sabīlahū (→ fa-ttaḫas⸗sabīlahū) in two locations (Q18:61, 63), and to the ṣād in His speech mà ttaḫaḏa ṣāḥibatan (→ mà ttaḫaṣ⸗ṣāḥibatan) (Q82:3) and nothing else. As for the ṯāʾ, he assimilates it to five letters. 1. To the ḏāl in His speech wa-l-ḥarṯi ḏālika (→ wa-l-ḥarḏ⸗ḏālika) (Q3:14) and nothing else. 2. To the tāʾ in His speech ḥayṯu tuʾmarūna (→ ḥayt⸗tūmarūna) (Q15:65), al-ḥadīṯi taʿǧabūna (→ al-ḥadīt⸗taʿǧabūna) (Q53:59) and nothing else. 3. To the šīn in His speech ḥayṯu šiʾtum (→ ḥayš⸗šītum), ḥayṯu šiʾtumā (→ ḥayš⸗šītumā) whenever it occurs, and in His speech ṯalāṯi šuʿabin (ṯalāš⸗šuʿabin) (Q77:30) and nothing else. 4. To the sīn, for example, in His speech wa-wariṯa sulaymānu (→ wa-waris⸗sulaymānu) (Q27:16), min ḥayṯu sakantum (→ min ḥays⸗sakantum) (Q65:6), bi-hāḏà l-ḥadīṯi sanastadriǧuhum (→ bi-hāḏà l-ḥadīs⸗sa-nastadriǧuhum (Q68:44) and what is like it. 5. To the ḍād in His speech ḥadīṯu ḍayfi ʾibrāhīma (→ ḥadīḍ⸗ḍayfi) (Q51:24) and nothing else. As for the rāʾ, he assimilates it to the lām if a vowelled letter occurred before it; for example, saḫḫara lanā (→ saḫḫal⸗lanā) (Q43:13), li-yaġfira laka (→ li-yaġfil⸗laka) (Q48:2) and what is like it. If there is an unvowelled letter (including long vowels) before it, and it is followed by kasrah or ḍammah, it is also assimilated; for example, al-maṣīru // lā yukallifu (→ al-maṣīl⸗lā yukallifu) (Q2:285–6), kitāba l-fuǧǧēri la-fī (→ kitāba l-fuǧǧēl⸗la-fī) (Q83:7) and what is like it. But when the following vowel is fatḥah, it is not assimilated; for example, wa-l-ḥamīra li-tarkabūhā (Q16:8) and wa-ʾinna l-fuǧǧāra la-fī (Q82:14). The ʾimālah[33] remains when the assimilation takes place, for example, in ʾinna kitāba l-ʾabrēri la-fī (→ ʾinna kitāba l-ʾabrēl⸗la-fī) (Q83:18), ʿaḏāba n-nēri // rabbanā (→ ʿaḏāba nnēr⸗rabbanā) (Q3:191-2) and what is like it, because it (the assimilation) is accidental (i.e., the ʾidġām is more superficial or later in derivation than ʾimālah[34]). As for the lām, he assimilates it to the rāʾ when there was a vowelled letter before it; also, for example, subula rabbiki (→ subur⸗rabbiki) (Q16:69), qaǧ⸗ǧaʿala rabbuki (→ qaǧ⸗ǧaʿar⸗ rabbuki) (Q19:24) and what is like it. If there is an unvowelled letter (including a long vowel) before it and it is followed by kasrah or dammah, he also assimilates it: ʾilā sabīli rabbika (→ sabīr⸗rabbika) (Q16:125), man yaqūlu rabbanā (→ yaqūr⸗rabbanā) (Q2:200, 201) and what is like it. But if it is followed by fatḥah, he does not assimilate it; for example, fa-yaqūla rabbi (Q63:10), rasūla rabbihim (Q69:10) and what is like it, except for qāla rabbi (e.g., Q2:38), qāla rabbukum (e.g., Q26:26) and qāla rabbunā (Q20:50), followed by a pronominal suffix or not. In that case he does assimilate it (i.e., qār⸗rabb-), as has been transmitted textually and orally, because of the power of the length of the ʾalif. Analogous to these are qāla raǧulāni (→ qār⸗raǧulāni) (Q5:23) and qāla raǧulun (→ qār⸗raǧulun) (Q40:28). There is no disagreement among the people of the oral tradition in their assimilation. As for the nūn, if there is a vowelled letter before it, he assimilates it to the lām and the rāʾ: for example, in His speech zuyyina li-n-nāsi (→ zuyyil⸗li-n-nāsi) (Q3:14), lan nuʾmina laka (→ lan nūmil⸗laka) (e.g., Q2:55), ʾit⸗taʾaḏḏana rabbuka (→ ʾit⸗taʾaḏḏar⸗rabbuka) (Q7:167), ḫazāʾina raḥmati rabbī (→ ḫazāʾir⸗raḥmati) (Q17:100) and what is like it. If there is an unvowelled letter (including long vowels) before it, it is not assimilated regardless of the vowel that is on it (the nūn); for example, muslimayni laka (Q2:128), bi-ʾiḏni rabbihim (e.g., Q14:1) and what is like it, except for His speech wa-naḥnu lahū (→ wa-naḥl⸗lahū) (e.g., Q2:133), mā naḥnu lakumā (→ naḥl⸗lakumā) (Q10:78) and naḥnu laka (→ naḥl⸗laka) (e.g., Q11:54), whenever they occur; he assimilates that because of the invariance of the ḍammah of the nūn. As for the mīm, he gave it ʾiḫfāʾ[35] next to a bāʾ when there is a vowelled letter before it; for example, bi-ʾaʿlama bi-š-šākirīna (→ bi-ʾaʿlam⸗bi-š-šākirīna) (Q6:53), yaḥkumu bihī (→ yaḥkum⸗bihī) (Q5:95) and what is like it. The readers call it ʾidġām (‘assimilation’), but that is not the case (i.e., not the appropriate term), as change of the first letter (to the next letter) is prevented. Instead, the vowel drops, and the mīm undergoes ʾiḫfāʾ. If there is an unvowelled letter (including long vowels) before it, he does not give it ʾiḫfāʾ, for example, in His speech ʾibrāhīmu banīhi (Q2:132), aš-šahru l-ḥarāmu bi-š-šahri l-ḥarāmi (Q2:194) and what is like it. As for the bāʾ, it is assimilated to the mīm in His speech wa-yuʿaḏḏibu man yašāʾu (→ wa-yuʿaḏḏim⸗man) (e.g., Q2:284) whenever it occurs and nothing else. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: So, these are the abridged principles of assimilation, and it will be possible to derive analogically from it (the treatment of) identical and similar occurrences, if God Almighty wills it. We have collected all the cases where ʾAbū ʿAmr assimilates the letters that carry a vowel and have found that in the tradition of Ibn Muǧāhid and his companions they are 1,273 letters, and that according to what we were taught they are 1,305 letters. So, all of what has disagreement in it among the people of the oral tradition are 32 words in total.

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

Hišām is only transmitted through tilāwah by ʾAbū al-Fatḥ in the Taysīr (see U.4.4.2.), but the specific mention of ʾAbū al-Fatḥ implies that al-Dānī knows other tilāwah transmission from Hišām that has taḥsabanna. This is indeed the case, as he points it out in the Ǧamiʿ al-bayān (al-Dānī 2007, 994).

This is an addition in one of the manuscripts that Pretzl consulted. Al-Ḍāmin includes it without making mention of manuscripts that lack it. I have found it in both the Berlin and Paris manuscripts, and in one of the four Princeton manuscripts (Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett no. 213Y). It is unlikely to be an addition of later copyists; it has either been dropped out, or it points to a later recension of al-Taysīr with this added by al-Dānī. Hišām indeed appears to have had a book describing Ibn ʿĀmir’s reading, and al-Dānī had access to it, as he cites it several times in his Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān as well (Hamdan 2018, 55, fn. 4).
This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).
The word hunā is missing in Pretzl (al-Dānī 2008a, 36).

statements.heading: U.8.2.1. Subsection: [Option to Do rawm or ʾišmām]
statements.text: Know that al-Yazīdī related from ʾAbū ʿAmr that he, when he assimilates the first of two letters that are identical or close (in terms of place of articulation), regardless of whether there was an unvowelled letter before it or a vowelled letter, if it carried ḫafḍ or rafʿ, it would hint towards its vowel, as an indication of it. This hinting at it may be rawm or ʾišmām. Rawm is firmer due to what is in it in terms of clarity of the quality of the vowel. However, proper assimilation is blocked because of it (i.e., ḫāliqu kulli šayʾin → ḫāliqŭ kulli šayʾin, ʾilā ḏì l-ʿarši sabīlan → ʾilā ḏì l-ʿaršĭ sabīlan, etc.), whereas (assimilation) is proper with ʾišmām (i.e., ḫāliqu kulli šayʾin → ḫālikʷ⸗kulli šayʾin, etc.). ʾIšmām is prevented for a letter with ḫafḍ. If the first letter carries naṣb, its vowel is not hinted towards because of its weakness. Likewise, the vowel of the mīm cannot be hinted towards when it encounters its equal (an-other mīm) or a bāʾ, nor (towards the vowel of) the bāʾ when it encounters its equal (another bāʾ) or a mīm, regardless of the vowel it carries. That is because hinting towards it is difficult in that case because of the closure of the lips. Success comes from God. SŪRAT AL-BAQARAH (GENERAL PRINCIPLES)

statements.heading: U.9. The hāʾ al-kināyah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr adds ṣilah to the hāʾ al-kināyah that is singular and masculine, when it is ḍammah and there is an unvowelled letter before it, with wāw. When it is kasrah (it receives the ṣilah) of yāʾ. When he pauses, he drops this ṣilah because it is extra. It is the same regardless of whether the unvowelled letter is a regular letter or a weak letter (wāw, yāʾ or ʾalif). So, the ones with ḍammah, for example, are ʿaqalūhū (Q2:75), šarawhū (Q12:20), fa-ǧtabāhū (Q68:50), fa-l-yaṣumhū (Q2:185), fa-bašširhū (e.g., Q31:7), minhū (e.g., Q2:217), ʿanhū (e.g., Q4:31), and what is like it. The ones with kasrah are, for example, li-ʾaḫīhī (Q7:142), [li-]ʾabīhī (e.g.Q6:74), tuʾwīhī (Q70:13), fīhī (e.g., Q2:2), and ʾabawayhī (e.g., Q12:99), and ʾilayhī (Q2:28) and what is like it. This is only the case when the hāʾ does not encounter a (following) unvowelled letter; for example, yaʿlamhu ḷḷāhu (Q2:197; Q3:29), ʿanhu s-sūʾa (Q12:24), fa-ʾarāhu l-ʾāyata (Q79:20), ʾātāhu ḷḷāhu (e.g., Q2:251), ʿalayhi llāha (Q48:10) and what is like it except for His speech ʿanhû ttalahhā (Q80:10) in the manner of al-Bazzī, as he lengthens the hāʾ with a wāw despite the gemination of the tāʾ after it, because the geminate is accidental (i.e., the underlying form, from which the rule is derived, lacks the geminate, |tatalahhaA|, and thus does not trigger shortening of ʿanhū).[1] The rest pronounces it with a short vowel (as opposed to long) for the ḍammah and the kasrah in connected speech in what has preceded (i.e., ʿaqalūhu, šarawhu, fa-ǧtabāhu, fa-lyaṣumhu, fīhi, ʾilayhi, etc.). All of them add ṣilah of the (hāʾ al-kināyah) that has kasrah with yāʾ and the (hāʾ al-kināyah) that has ḍammah with wāw when the preceding letter is vowelled whenever it occurs (e.g., Q2:17 ḥawlahū, Q2:64 wa-raḥmatuhū, Q2:22 bihī).[2] Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This is a reference to Sībawayh (1988, IV:202) who explicitly tells us that ʾAbū ʿAmr reads it with an ultrashort vowel, not with no vowel.

statements.heading: U.10. The Lengthening and Shortening[3]
statements.text: Know that the hamzah, when it is with a letter of length or weakness (i.e., ā, ī or ū) within a single word, whether it is in the middle or at the end, there is no disagreement between them (the readers) in the additional lengthening of the long vowel (i.e., making it overlong). That is found, for example, in the words of the Almighty ʾulâʾika (e.g., Q2:5), šâʾa ḷḷāhu (e.g., Q2:20), al-malâʾikatu (e.g., Q2:210), yuḍîʾu (Q24:35), hâʾumu qraʾū (Q69:19) and what is like it. When the hamzah is the beginning of a word and a long vowel is the end of another word (the one before it), they disagree on the additional lengthening of the long vowel there. Ibn Kaṯīr and Qālūn, with some disagreement, ʾAbū Šuʿayb [al-Sūsī] and others, transmitting from al-Yazīdī, keep the long vowel short (in comparison to the overlong vowel). So, they do not add to it lengthening, except what length it has (intrinsically) which it receives (automatically) in connected speech. These are, for example, the words of the Almighty: bi-mā ʾunzila ʾilayka wa-mā ʾunzila min qablika (e.g., Q2:4), fī ʾāyātinā (e.g., Q6:68), yā ʾayyuhà n-nāsu (e.g., Q2:21), hā ʾulāʾi (e.g., Q2:31),[4] qālū ʾāmannā (e.g., Q2:14) and what is like it— they are the shortest in lengthening in the first type (i.e., word-internal lengthening) that is agreed upon. The rest lengthen the long vowel additionally in these cases (i.e., bi-mâ ʾunzila etc.). The longest articulation of overlength among them, in both types together (i.e., wordinternal and in between words), are Warš and Ḥamzah, and after those two (the longest) is ʿĀṣim, and after him are Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾī, and after them are ʾAbū ʿAmr in the transmission of the People of Iraq and Qālūn in the transmission of ʾAbū Našīṭ, with some disagreement. All of this is done in moderation, without excessiveness (in lengthening). Rather, it is proportionate to their slow and rapid ways of recitation. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This is one of the alternative names of Sūrat al-Šūrā (Kandil 1992, 51).

statements.heading: U.10.1. Subsection: [Overlength Typical of Warš]
statements.text: If there comes a hamzah before a long vowel, regardless of whether it is fully articulated or its vowel is thrown onto a preceding vowelless letter[5] or it is replaced (by a semi-vowel),[6]— for example, in the words ʾādam (e.g., Q2:31), ʾāzara (Q6:74), ʾāmana (Q2:13), wa-laqad ʾātaynā (e.g., Q2:87), man ʾūtiya (e.g., Q69:19), li-ʾīlāfi qurayšin (Q106:1), li-l-ʾīmāni (e.g., Q3:167), yastahziʾūna (e.g., Q6:5), hā ʾulāʾi ʾālihatan (Q21:99) and what is like it—the people of the oral tradition among the Egyptian experts adopting it in the transmission of ʾAbū Yaʿqūb [al-ʾAzraq] from Warš apply moderate additional lengthening to the long vowel, according to the slowest pace of recitation (i.e., ʾâdam, ʾâzara, ʾâmana, wa-laqad‿âtaynā, man‿ûtiya, li-ʾîlāfi qurayšin, li-l‿îmāni, yastahziʾûna, hâ ʾulâʾi yâlihatan). They make an exception from that in the word ʾisrâʾīl (i.e., not ʾisrâʾîl) (e.g., Q2:40) whenever it occurs. They do not want to lengthen the yāʾ in it. They agree on the removing of the additional lengthening when there was an unvowelled letter before the hamzah and that vowelless letter was not a letter of length or weakness (ʾalif, wāw, yāʾ) (when it is inside a single word); for example, masʾūlan (e.g., Q17:34), maḏʾūman (e.g., Q7:18), al-qurʾān (e.g., Q2:185), aḏ̣-ḏ̣amʾān (Q24:39) and what is like that. Likewise (they agreed on removing the additional lengthening) when the hamzah is prosthetic[7] due to starting (after a pause), as in uʾtumina (→ #ʾūtumina) (Q2:283), iʾti bi-qurʾānin (→ #ʾīti) (Q10:15), iʾḏan lī (→ #ʾīḏan) (Q9:49), and what is like it. The rest does not add anything to the length of the long vowels in what has preceded. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).
The reading of wa-nuʿallimuhū is also disagreed upon, see F.3:48.

statements.heading: U.11.1. The Two Consecutive hamzahs within a Word
statements.text: Know that when (two hamzahs within a word) both carry fatḥah—for example, in ʾa-ʾanḏartahum(ū) (Q2:6; Q36:10), ʾa-ʾantum(ū) ʾaʿlamu (Q2:140), ʾa-ʾasǧudu (Q17:61) and what is like it—the two of the holy cities (Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kaṯīr), ʾAbū ʿAmr and Hišām soften the second (hamzah) of the two (i.e., ʾa-.anḏartahum(ū), etc.). Warš (according to other paths from him) replaces it with an ʾalif (ʾānḏartahum, etc.), but the regular outcome (qiyās) would be that it is pronounced in between (i.e., ʾa-.anḏarathum(ū)). Ibn Kaṯīr does not insert an ʾalif before it (the weakened hamzah), but Qālūn, Hišām and ʾAbū ʿAmr do insert one (i.e., ʾā-.anḏartahum etc.). The rest fully pronounce the two hamzahs. When the (two hamzahs) differ (in vocalisation) by a fatḥah and a kasrah, as for example in the words ʾa-ʾiḏā kunnā (e.g., Q13:5), ʾa-ʾilāhun maʿa ḷḷāhi (Q27:60–64), ʾa-ʾinna lanā (Q26:41) and what is like it, the two of the holy cities and ʾAbū ʿAmr soften the second (hamzah) (i.e., ʾa-.iḏā). Qālūn and ʾAbū ʿAmr insert an ʾalif before it (the second hamzah) (i.e., ʾā-.iḏā kunnā, etc.). The rest pronounces the two hamzahs fully. Hišām, in what I recited to ʾAbū al-Fatḥ, (always) inserts an ʾalif between the two (hamzahs), and in what I recited to ʾAbū al-Ḥasan [Ibn Ġalbūn],[8] he inserts it in seven places (only): 1. In al-Aʿrāf ʾā-ʾinnakum (Q7:81) 2. and ʾā-ʾinna lanā la-ʾaǧran (Q7:113). 3. In Maryam ʾā-ʾiḏā mā muttu (Q19:66). 4. In al-Šuʿarāʾ ʾā-ʾinna lanā la-ʾaǧran (Q26:41). 5. In al-Ṣāffāt ʾā-ʾinnaka (Q37:52) 6. and ʾā-ʾifkan (Q37:87). 7. In Fuṣṣilat ʾā-.innakum (Q41:9), and he softens the second (hamzah) here only. When the (two hamzahs) differ (in vocalisation) by a fatḥah and a ḍammah—and this occurs in (only) three places: (1) in ʾĀl ʿImrān qul ʾa-ʾunabbiʾukum (Q3:15), (2) in Ṣād ʾa-ʾunzila ʿalayhi (Q38:8) and (3) in al-Qamar ʾa-ʾulqiya ḏ-ḏikru (Q54:25)—the two of the holy cities and ʾAbū ʿAmr soften the second (hamzah) (ʾa-.unabbiʾukum(ū), etc.). Qālūn inserts an ʾalif between the two (ʾā-.unabbiʾukum). Hišām, in what I recited to ʾAbū al-Ḥasan [Ibn Ġalbūn], pronounces both hamzahs fully without an ʾalif between them in ʾĀl ʿImrān (i.e., ʾa-ʾunabbiʾukum), softens the second (hamzah) and inserts an ʾalif before it in the remaining two (i.e., ʾā-.unzila, ʾā-.ulqiya).[9] The rest pronounce the two hamzahs fully for all of these (ʾa-ʾunabbiʾukum, ʾa-ʾunzila ʿalayhi, ʾa-ʾulqiya ḏ-ḏikru). Hišām, in what I recited to ʾAbū al-Fatḥ, is like that (in the full pronunciation of the two hamzahs), and he inserts an ʾalif between them (i.e., ʾā-ʾunabbiʾukum, ʾā-ʾunzila, ʾā-ʾulqiya). Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

Pretzl has b. al-ʾAḥzam; this is a mistake (al-Dānī 2008a, 33). Note that this ʾisnād is not present in the Taysīr nor in the Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān. It is one of the tilāwah paths for al-Dānī’s teacher ʾAbū al-Ḥasan Ibn Ġalbūn (1991, 27) as well as ʾAbū al-Ṭayyib Ibn Ġalbūn (2015, 185). Both of them indeed explicitly mention this exception (Ibn Ġalbūn 1991, 265; 2015, 436).

statements.heading: U.11.2. The Two hamzahs from Two Words
statements.text: Know that when (two hamzahs of two different words) correspond in carrying a kasrah—for example, in hā ʾulāʾi ʾin kuntum (Q2:31), min an-nisāʾi ʾillā (Q4:22, 24) and what is like it— Qunbul and Warš pronounce the second as if it were a vowelless yāʾ (i.e., not identical to it but in between yāʾ and hamzah: hā ʾulāʾi .in kuntum, min an-nisāʾi .illā). [Ḫalaf b. ʾIbrāhīm] Ibn Ḫāqān taught me to recite it for Warš by making this second hamzah a yāʾ carrying a kasrah in al-Baqarah in the words of the Almighty hā ʾulāʾi yin kuntum (Q2:31) and in al-Nūr ʿalà l-biġāʾi yin‿aradna (Q24:33) only. That (practice) is well-known for Warš in the oral transmission without basis in textual transmission. Qālūn and al-Bazzī make the first (of the two hamzahs) like a yāʾ followed by a kasrah (i.e., not identical to it but in between yāʾ and hamzah: hāʾulā.i ʾin kuntum, min an-nisā.i ʾillā), and ʾAbū ʿAmr drops it (the first kasrah with the hamzah) (i.e., hāʾulā ʾin kuntum, min an-nisā ʾillā). The rest fully pronounce both hamzahs. If (two hamzahs in two different words) correspond in carrying a fatḥah—for example, in ǧāʾa ʾaǧaluhum (e.g., Q7:34), šāʾa ʾanšarahū (Q80:22) and what is like it—Warš and Qunbul make the second (hamzah) like a long vowel (i.e., not exactly like length, but in between: ǧāʾa .aǧaluhum, šāʾa .anšarahū). Qālūn, al-Bazzī and ʾAbū ʿAmr drop the first (hamzah) (i.e., ǧā ʾaǧaluhum, šā ʾanšarahū). The rest fully pronounce both hamzahs. If (two hamzahs in two different words) correspond in carrying a ḍammah—(this occurs) in one location, (namely) al-ʾAḥqāf (Q46:32) in the words of the Almighty ʾawliyāʾu ʾulāʾika (Q46:32) and nowhere else—Warš and Qunbul make the second (hamzah) to be like a wāw not carrying a vowel (i.e., ʾawliyāʾu .ulāʾika). Qālūn and al-Bazzī make the first (hamzah) like a wāw carrying a ḍammah (i.e., ʾawliyā.u ʾulāʾika) and ʾAbū ʿAmr drops it (i.e., ʾawliyā ʾulāʾika). The rest fully pronounce both hamzahs. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: When the first hamzah of the two corresponding ones is softened or it is dropped, the ʾalif that is before it (will still be) made overlong, as if it were in the state of being pronounced fully, relying on it (i.e., its virtual presence). It is also permissible to shorten the ʾalif because of the absence of the hamzah of a word, but the first (option) is preferable. So when (the two hamzahs) differ in vocalisation, whatever the state (of the vowel carried by either hamzah)—as, for example, in His speech as-sufahāʾu ʾa-lā (Q2:13), min al-māʾi ʾaw mimmā (Q7:50), šuhadāʾa ʾiḏ ḥaḍara (Q2:133), man yašāʾu ʾilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīmin (e.g., Q2:142), ǧāʾa ʾummatan (Q23:44) and what is like it—the two of the holy cities and ʾAbū ʿAmr soften the second hamzah (i.e., as-sufahāʾu wa-lā etc.). The rest pronounce both of them fully. As for the softening of one of the two hamzahs in this category, it only takes place in connected speech and nowhere else (i.e., not in pause), because contact of (the two words) is required for it. The rule of the softening of the hamzah in both categories is that (the sound) is in between the hamzah and the letter that its vowel is derived from (i.e., u from wāw, i from yāʾ and a from ʾalif), so long as the hamzah does not carry a fatḥah and there is a kasrah or a ḍammah before it. In that situation (i.e., when a kasrah or a ḍammah is followed by a hamzah carrying a fatḥah) (the hamzah) is replaced. In the case of kasrah (before it), it is replaced with yāʾ (e.g., an-nisāʾi yaw), in the case of ḍammah (before it), it is replaced with wāw (e.g., as-sufahāʾu wa-lā) and both (the yāʾ and wāw) carry fatḥah. As for a (hamzah) that carries a kasrah and there is ḍammah before it, it is softened in two ways: (1) the (hamzah) carrying the kasrah is replaced with wāw (i.e., yašāʾu wilā) or (2) the sound is made in between the hamzah and the yāʾ for its vowel (i.e., yašāʾu .ilā). The first is the manner of the readers and it is preferred. The second is the manner of the grammarians and it is stronger in terms of regularity. Success comes from God.

statements.heading: U.11.3. The Single hamzah
statements.text: Know that Warš softens the single hamzah, whether it is unvowelled or vowelled, when it is in the place of the first root letter. As for the unvowelled (hamzah), examples are His speech yāḫuḏu (Q9:104; Q18:79), yākulu (e.g., Q10:24), yālamūna (Q4:104), liqāʾanāti (← liqāʾanà ʾti) (Q10:15), yūminu (e.g., Q2:232), al-mūminūna (e.g., Q2:285), yūṯirūna (Q59:9), yūtūna (e.g., Q4:53), al-mūtafikātv̆ (Q9:70; Q69:9), al-mūtafikata (Q53:53), allaḏītumina (← allādì ʾtumina) (Q2:283), al-malikūtūnī (← al-maliku ʾtūnī) (Q12:50, 54) and what is like it. As for the vowelled (hamzah), examples are His speech yuwaddihī ʾilayka (← yuʾaddihī) (Q3:75), muwaǧǧalan (← muʾaǧǧalan) (Q3:145), muwallafati (← muʾallafati) (Q9:60), muwaḏḏinun (← muʾaḏḏinun) (Q7:44; Q12:70), yuwaḫḫiruhum (← yuʾaḫḫiruhum) (e.g., Q14:42), lā tuwāḫiḏnā (tuʾāḫiḏnā) (Q2:286) and what is like it. Excepted from the unvowelled ones are wa-tuʾwī ʾilayka (Q33:51), ʾallatī tuʾwīhi (Q70:13), and all other derivations of the verb ʾīwāʾ ‘to seek refuge’, for example, al-maʾwǟ (Q32:19), maʾwǟhum (e.g., Q2:151), maʾwǟkum (e.g., Q29:25), fa-ʾwū ʾila l-kahfi (Q18:16) and what is like it. From the vowelled ones (are excepted) wa-lā yaʾūduhū (Q2:255), taʾuzzuhum (Q19:83)[10] and also maʾāban (Q78:22, 39), maʾābin (e.g., Q13:29), maʾāribu (Q20:18), wa-mā taʾaḫḫara (e.g., Q2:203), faʾaḏḏana (Q7:44) and what is like it, (that is) whenever the spelling[11] is with an ʿalif, apply the hamzah to all of them. The rest pronounced the hamzah fully in all of these. ʾAbū ʿAmr,[12] Ḥamzah and Hišām[13] have specific manners which I will mention later if God Almighty wishes it.

footnotes.text: On Ḥamzah’s reading in pause, see U.11.6.2.
Pretzl has 216 here; this is a mistake.
A different name for Sūrat Muḥammad (Kandil 1992, 52).
This ʾisnād does not occur in U.4.2.2. nor in the ʾisnād section of Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān.

statements.heading: U.11.3.1. Subsection
statements.text: Warš also softens the hamzah of bīsa (← biʾsa) (e.g., Q2:126), bīsa-mā (← biʾsa-mā) (e.g., Q2:90), al-bīr (← al-biʾr),[14] aḏ-ḏīb (aḏ-ḏiʾb) (e.g., Q12:13) and liyallā (← li-ʾallā) (Q2:150) in all of the Qurʾān. Al-Kisāʾī follows him with aḏ-ḏīb only, so he removes its hamzah. The rest pronounce the hamzah fully in all of these whenever it occurs. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: With these two added to the list, the gemination of initial tāʾ is completely regular. It occurs on every single verb which starts with a single tāʾ in the rasm which must be interpreted as a simplification of tata- by haplology rather than assimilation (e.g., Q2:280 تصدقوا taṣṣaddaqū). But these two are only added in this isolated transmission that does not seem to be confirmed by any other transmission (see also the discussion in al-Dānī 2007, 933; Ibn al-Ǧazarī 2018, §2804).

statements.heading: U.11.4. The Transposition of the Vowel of the hamzah to the Letter before It
statements.text: Know that Warš casts the vowel of the following hamzah onto the unvowelled letter before it, so that it becomes vowelled with its (the hamzah’s) vowel and it (the hamzah) is dropped from pronunciation. That is the case whenever the unvowelled letter is not a long vowel (ḥarf madd wa-līn, i.e., ā, ī, ū), it occurs at the end of a word and the hamzah is the beginning of a following word. This preceding unvowelled letter comes in three kinds: The first kind is (the n of) tanwīn, as for example in His speech min nabīʾin‿illā (← min nabīʾin ʾillā) (Q7:94; Q43:7), min šayʾin‿iḏ kānū (← min šayʾin ʾiḏ kānū) (Q46:26), kufuʾan‿ aḥadun (← kufuʾan ʾaḥadun) (Q112:4), mubīnun‿anu ʿbudù ḷḷāha (← mubīnun // ʾanu ʿbudù ḷḷāha) (Q71:3–4) and what is like it. The second kind is (the l of) the definite article, for example al‿arḍ (← al-ʾarḍ) (e.g., Q2:11), al‿āḫirah (← al-ʾāḫirah) (e.g., Q2:4), al‿āzifah (← al-ʾāzifah) (Q40:18; Q53:57), al‿ūlǟ (← al-ʾūlǟ) (e.g., Q20:21), al‿āna (← al-ʾāna) (e.g., Q2:71), wa-l‿uḏna (← wa-l-ʾuḏna) (Q5:45) and what is like it. This is the case even though the hamzah is connected to the previous word in writing; (the definite article) is treated by the readers as a separate word. The third kind are all the remaining letters (that do not carry a vowel); for example, the words man‿āmana (← man ʾāmana) (e.g., Q2:62), min‿istabraqin (← min ʾistabraqin) (Q55:54), wa-ḏkur‿ismāʿīla (← wa-ḏkur ʾismāʿīla) (Q38:48), ʾalif lām mīm‿a-ḥasiba n-nāsu (← ʾalif lām mīm // ʾa-ḥasiba n-nāsu) (Q29:1–2), qālat‿ūlǟhum (← qālat ʾulǟhum) (Q7:39), qālat‿ uḫrǟhum (← qālat ʾuḫrǟhum) (Q7:38), ḫalaw‿ilā (← ḫalaw ʾilā) (Q2:14), taʿālaw‿atlu (← taʿālaw ʾatlu) (Q6:151), nabaʾa bnay‿ādama (← ibnay ʾādama) (Q5:27), ḏawātay‿uklin (← ḏawātay ʾuklin) (Q34:16) and what is like it. The companions of ʾAbū Yaʿqūb [al-ʾAzraq], transmitting from Warš, make an exception from this (rule) in one word in al-Ḥāqqah, and it is His speech kitābiyah // ʾinnī ḏ̣anantu (Q69:19–20). They leave the hāʾ unvowelled and fully pronounce the hamzah after it as if intending to cut off (the sentence) and restart (there). I have recited it like this (i.e., without naql) to the Egyptian experts and this is what I adopt. The other readers read with full pronunciation of the hamzah in all that preceded with the clear pronunciation of the vowelless letters before it. They (the other readers) disagree on (applying the transposition) to the words ʾāl-ʾāna wa-qad kuntum (Q10:51) and ʾāl-ʾāna wa-qad ʿaṣayta (Q10:91) in Yūnus and in the word ʿādani l-ʾūlā/ǟ/ē (Q53:50) in al-Naǧm. (The discussion) of the disagreement on that will come in its place (in the specific variants section)[15] if God Almighty wills it. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This description is more restrictive than it should be. Unlike what the wording might suggest, not just 3sg.m. and 3pl.m. forms, but all forms of the prefix conjugation are meant here, including, e.g., Q25:44 taḥsabu, and Q3:87 li-taḥsa/ibūhū̆.

statements.heading: U.11.5. The Manner of ʾAbū ʿAmr in the Removal of the hamzah
statements.text: Know that ʾAbū ʿAmr, when he recites in prayer, or recites at a fast pace, or recites with assimilation, does not apply the hamzah for each unvowelled hamzah, whether it is the first, the second or the third root letter. For example the words yūminūna (← yuʾminūna) (e.g., Q2:3), yūlūna ( ← yuʾlūna) (Q2:226), al-mūtafikātu ( ← al-muʾtafikātu) (Q69:9), bīsa (← biʾsa) (e.g., Q2:126), bīsamā (← biʾsamā) (e.g., Q2:90), aḏ-ḏību ( ← aḏ-ḏiʾbu) (e.g., Q12:13), al-bīr (← al-biʾr),[16] ar-rūyā (← ar-ruʾyā) (e.g., Q17:60), rūyāka (← ruʾyāka) (Q12:5), ka-dābi (← ka-daʾbi) (e.g., Q3:11), ǧīta (← ǧiʾta) (e.g., Q2:71), ǧītum (← ǧiʾtum) (Q10:81; Q19:89), šītum (← šiʾtum) (Q2:58), šīnā ( ← šiʾnā) (Q76:28), fa-ddārātum (Q2:72), iṭmānantum (← iṭmaʾnantum) (Q4:103) and what is like it. Excepted are cases where (the hamzah) is unvowelled to mark the ǧazm, for example, ʾaw nansaʾhā (Q2:106), tasuʾhum (Q3:120; Q9:50), ʾin našaʾ (Q26:4; Q34:9; Q36:43), yuhayyiʾ lakum (Q18:16) and what is like it. This occurs in 19 places.[17] (Another excepted case is) when it marks the stem formation (of the imperative), for example, ʾanbiʾhum (Q2:33), iqraʾ (Q17:14; Q96:1, 3), ʾarǧiʾhu (Q7:111; Q26:36), hayyiʾ (Q18:10) and what is like it. This occurs in 11 places.[18] (A third excepted case is) when the removal of the hamz would be more burdensome than pronouncing it; that is in the words of the Almighty tuʾwī (Q33:51) and tuʾwīhi (Q70:13). (A fourth excepted case is) when ambiguity would occur if it was not given a hamzah; that is the case in the word wa-riʾyan (Q19:74).[19] (A fifth excepted case is) when it would turn a linguistic variant into another linguistic variant and that is (the case) in the word muʾṣadah (Q90:20; Q104:8).[20] Ibn Muǧāhid prefers the clear pronunciation of the hamz in all of these because of these meanings, and I have recited like this [and I adopt it].[21] When the hamzah carries a vowel—for example, in His speech yuʾallifu (Q24:43), muʾaḏḏinun (Q7:44; Q12:70), yuʾaḫḫiru and what is like it—there is no disagreement in transmission from him (ʾAbū ʿAmr) about the full pronunciation of the hamzah in any of these. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: ‘Removed ones’ refers to word-final yāʾs which, especially in verse-final position, are often unwritten in the Qurʾānic text where classical orthography would expect them. Readers different on whether and when these yāʾs are reconstituted in recitation or not.
The details of this softening of the hamzah have already been discussed in U.11.2.

The words hā ʾantumū are seen as having a word-boundary between them. As Ibn Kaṯīr does not have an overlong vowel with long vowels before hamzah between two words, this is not lengthened (see U.11.2.).

statements.heading: U.11.6. The Manner of Ḥamzah and Hišām in Pausing on the hamzah
statements.text: Know that Ḥamzah and Hišām, when they pause on an unvowelled or vowelled hamzah soften it whenever it occurs at the end of a word. In connected speech they pronounce it fully. When they soften (a hamzah) with ḍammah before it, they replaced it with a wāw, whether it is vowelled or unvowelled; for example, in the word lūlū# (Ḥamzah)[22]/luʾlū# (Hišām) (← luʾluʾu/in) (Q22:23; Q35:33; Q52:24), ʾin imrū# (← ʾin imruʾun) (Q4:176) and what is like it. There is no instance in the Qurʾān where it is unvowelled. When they soften (a hamzah) with kasrah before it, they replace it in both cases (followed by a vowel or not) with a yāʾ; for example, in the words of the Almighty wa-hayyī# lanā (← wa-hayyiʾ lanā) (Q18:10), nabbī# ʿibādī (← nabbiʾ ʿibādī) (Q15:49), tubawwī# (← tubawwiʾu) (Q3:121), min šāṭī# (← min šāṭiʾi) (Q28:30) and what is like it. When they soften (a hamzah) with fatḥah before it, they replaced it in both cases (followed by a vowel or not) with an ʾalif; for example, in the words of the Almighty ʾin yašā# (← ʾin yašaʾ) (e.g., Q4:133), ḏarā# (← ḏaraʾa) (Q6:136; Q16:13), badā# (← badaʾa) (e.g., Q12:76), yustahzā# (← yustahzaʾu) (Q4:140), al-malā# (← al-malaʾu) (e.g., Q7:60) and what is like it. It is not allowed to add an ultrashort vowel (rawm) or labialisation (ʾišmām) to the letter which replaces the hamzah because it is a pure unvowelled letter. If the hamzah is preceded by an unvowelled letter and they soften the hamzah, they place (the hamzah’s) vowel on the preceding letter[23] and then drop (the hamzah), if that is a root letter other than an ʾalif; for example, in the words of the Almighty al-mar# (← al-marʾv̆) (e.g., Q2:102), dif# (← difʾun) (Q16:6), al-ḫab# (← al-ḫabʾa) (Q27:250), šay# (← šayʾu/in) (e.g., Q2:20), saw# (← sawʾin) (e.g., Q19:28), ʿan sū# (← sūʾin) (Q4:149), sī# (← sīʾa) (Q11:77; Q29:33), ǧī# (← ǧīʾa) (Q39:69; Q89:23), al-musī# (← al-musīʾu) (Q40:58), yuḍī# (← yuḍīʾu) (Q24:35) and what is like it. If the unvowelled letter is a long vowel as an extra letter and it is a yāʾ or wāw, the hamzah is replaced by a yāʾ (when before it is a) yāʾ, and wāw (when before it is a) wāw, and it assimilated to what is before it in both cases, for example, in His speech bariyy# (← barīʾun) (e.g., Q6:19), an-nasiyy# (← an-nasīʾu) (Q9:37), ṯalāṯata quruww# (← qurūʾin) (Q2:228) and what is like it. Rawm and ʾišmām are permitted with the letter that is vowelled with the vowel of the (now dropped) hamzah or the letter that replaced it (the hamzah)—except the ʾalif—if they carry a ḍammah. Rawm (but not ʾišmām) is allowed if they carry a kasrah. Only dropping the vowel (not rawm or ʾišmām) is allowed if it carries a fatḥah (in connected speech). This is just like with the hamzah (if it were retained). If the unvowelled letter is an ʾalif—regardless of whether (the ʾalif) is replacing a root letter (e.g., ǧāʾa) or is an extra letter (e.g., as-samāʾ)—the hamzah after it is replaced with an ʾalif irrespective of the vowel it was carrying. Then, one of the two ʾalifs is elided due to the presence of two (subsequent) vowelless letters (i.e., |as-samaAʾ| = as-samāʾ → |as-samaAA| → |as-samaA| = as-samā). If you wish, you may add to the length and strengthen it (i.e., make it overlong),[24] so as to place a separation between the two (ʾalifs) (|samaAA| → |samaAaA|= samâ) without dropping (one of the two ʾalifs). That is more proper, and it is reported in texts transmitting from Ḥamzah in the transmission path of Ḫalaf and others. That is like the words of the Almighty wa-s-samâ# (← wa-s-samāʾv̆) (e.g., Q2:22), ʾiḏā ǧâ# (← ʾiḏā ǧāʾa) (e.g., Q4:83), min mâ# (← min māʾin) (e.g., Q2:164), ʿalā sawâ# (← ʿalā sawāʾin) (Q8:58), minhu l-mâ# (← minhu l-māʾu) (Q2:74), as-sufahâ# (← as-sufahāʾv̆) (e.g., Q2:13), ʾabnâ# (← ʾabnāʾv̆) (e.g., Q24:31), šuhadâ# (← šuhadāʾv̆) (e.g., Q2:133) and what is like it wherever it occurs. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This refers to a recognised possibility by grammarians to replace the hamzah of the interrogative particle ʾa- with a hāʾ (Saeed 2023, 83).
See U.11.1. for the insertion of an ʾalif with the question particle ʾa- before hamz.

statements.heading: U.11.6.1. Subsection: [Ḥamzah’s Dropping of hamzah inside the Word in Pause]
statements.text: Ḥamzah is unique in the softening of the hamzah that is in the middle of a word. There are rules for that which I will now explain, if God wills it. Know that the hamzah, when it is in the middle of a word and is unvowelled, is replaced with a pure letter (i.e., not bayna bayn), in the case of softening, as has preceded. That is the case, for example, in the words of the Almighty al-mūminūn# (← al-muʾminūna) (Q2:285), yūfakūn# (← al-yuʾfakūna) (Q5:75), ar-rūyā# (← ar-ruʾyā) (e.g., Q17:16), tasūkum# (← tasuʾkum) (Q5:101), yākulūn# (← yaʾkulūna) (Q2:174), ka-dāb# (← ka-daʾbi) (e.g., Q3:11), aḏ-ḏīb# (← aḏ-ḏiʾbu) (e.g., Q12:13), al-bīr# (← al-biʾru),[25] bīs (← biʾsa) (e.g., Q2:126) and what is like it. It is likewise for allaḏītumin# (← allaḏì ʾtumina) (Q2:283), liqāʾanāt# (← liqāʾanà ʾti) (Q10:15), firʿawnūtūnī# (← firʿawnu ʾtūnī) (Q10:79) and what is like it. Our teachers disagreed on the assimilation of the replacing letter for the hamzah and (alternatively) its clear pronunciation in the words wa-riyyā/wa-rīyā# (← wa-riʾyan) (Q19:74), tuwwī/tūwī# (← tuʾwī) (Q33:51) and tuwwīh/tūwīh# (←tuʾwīhi) (Q70:13). So, there are those who assimilate (wa-riyyā#, wa-tuwwī#, tuwwīh#), following what is written (وريا وتوى تويه), and those who do not assimilate (wa-rīyā#, wa-tūwī#, tūwīh#), because the replacement is (merely) accidental. Both options are acceptable. The people of the oral tradition also disagree on the changing of the vowel (due to vowel harmony) of the hāʾ with the replacement of the hamzah with a yāʾ before it in the words ʾanbīhum/him# (← ʾanbiʾhum) (Q2:33) and nabbīhum/him# (← nabbiʾhum) (Q54:28). So, some of them favour giving it a kasrah, because of the yāʾ, and others retain the ḍammah on the hāʾ because the yāʾ is accidental. They are both correct. When the hamzah carries a vowel and it is in the middle of a word, then what is before it is either unvowelled or vowelled. If it is unvowelled and it is a root letter, then when you soften it (the hamzah), you transfer its vowel onto that unvowelled letter, giving it the vowel (of the hamzah), as long as it is not an ʾalif. That is, for example, in the words šayā# (← šayʾan) (e.g., Q2:48), ḫiṭā# (← ḫiṭʾan) (Q17:31), al-mašamah# (← al-mašʾamati) (Q56:9; Q90:19), ka-hayah# (← ka-hayʾati) (Q3:49; Q5:110), taǧarūn# (← taǧʾarūna) (Q16:53), yasalūn# (← yasʾalūna) (e.g., Q2:273), wa-sal# (← wa-sʾal) (Q12:82; Q43:45), al-qurān# (← al-qurʾānv̆) (e.g., Q2:185), maḏūmā# (← maḏʾūman) (Q7:18), masūlā# (← masʾūlan) (e.g., Q17:34), siyat# (← sīʾat) (Q67:27), mawilā# (← mawʾilan) (Q18:58), al-mawūdah# (← mawʾūdatu) (Q81:8) and what is like it. If it is an extra letter (i.e., a letter of the stem formation, not of the root), then you replace (the hamzah with a respective glide) and assimilate it (to the previous glide), when it is a yāʾ or a wāw, for example, in the words hanīʾan mariyyā# (← marīʾan) (Q4:4), bariyyā# (← barīʾan) (Q4:112), bariyyūn# (← barīʾūna) (Q10:41), ḫaṭiyyah# (← ḫaṭīʾatan) (Q4:112), ḫaṭiyyātikum# (← ḫaṭīʾātikum) (Q7:161) and what is like it. There is no such case with the wāw in the Qurʾān (word-internally). If the unvowelled letter is an ʾalif—regardless of whether it is a replacement (of a root letter) or is an extra letter—you make the hamzah after it in between (the hamzah and a glide). If you want you can make the ʾalif overlong before it, or if you want you can keep it short (i.e., regular long vowel length). Making it overlong is more regular. That is, for example, in the words nisâ.ukum# (← nisāʾukum) (Q2:223), ʾabnâ.ukum# (← ʾabnāʾukum) (Q4:11; Q9:24), mâ.ā# (← māʾan) (e.g., Q2:22), ġuṯâ.ā# (← ġuṯāʾan) (Q23:41; Q87:5), sawâ.ā# (← sawāʾan) (e.g., Q3:113), wa-ʾ/.ābâ.ukum# (← wa-ʾābāʾukum) (e.g., Q4:11), hâ.um# (← hāʾum) (Q69:19), min ʾābâ.ihim#[26] (← min ʾābāʾihim) (Q6:87), malâ.ikatuh (← malāʾikatuhū) (Q33:43) and what is like it. If before the hamzah there is a letter that carries a vowel, and (the hamzah) carries a fatḥah and the letter before it carries a kasrah or a ḍammah, when you soften it in pause, you replace (the hamzah) with yāʾ in case of (a preceding) kasrah and with wāw in case of (a preceding) ḍammah. That is, for example, the words wa-nunšiyakum# (← wa-nunšiʾakum) (Q56:61), ʾinna šāniyak# (← ʾinna šāniʾaka) (Q108:3), muliyat# (← muliʾat) (Q72:8), al-ḫāṭiyah# (← al-ḫāṭiʾati) (Q69:9), li-yallā# (← li-ʾallā) (e.g., Q2:150),[27] lūluwā# (← luʾluʾan) (Q76:19), yuwaddih# (← yuʾaddih) (Q3:75), yuwallif# (← yuʾallifu) (Q24:43) and what is like it. Besides this, you make (the hamzah) in between (bayna bayn) in all the remaining cases where it carries a vowel and (the consonant) that precedes it also carries a vowel. If the hamzah carries a ḍammah, you make it between the hamzah and the wāw, for example, in the words of the Almighty qul fa-dra.ū# (← qul fa-draʾū, ( )قل فادرواQ3:168), ya.ūsā# (← yaʾūsan, ( )يوسQ17:83), ra.uf# (← raʾufun, ( )روفe.g., Q2:207), bi-ru.ūsikum# (← bi-ruʾūsikum, અ੷( )ޙ޻وسQ5:6), lā ya.ūduh# (← lā yaʾūduhū, গজ يوده) (Q2:255),[28] mustahzi.ūn# (← mustahziʾūna, ( )مسኑኟزونQ2:14),[29] li-yuwāṭi.ū# (← li-yuwāṭiʾū, ( )ليواطواQ9:37), ya-bna-.umm# (← ya-bna-ʾummi ( )يبنومQ20:94)[30] and what is like it. (You do this) as long as it does not have the shape of a yāʾ (in the rasm), for example, ʾunabbiyukum# (← ʾunabbiʾukum, અ੷( )انبيQ3:49), sa-nuqriyuk# (← sa-nuqriʾuka, ( )سنقريكQ87:6), kāna sayyiyuh# (← kāna sayyiʾuhū, كၨن سييه) (Q17:38)[31] and what is like it. (In that case) you replace (the hamzah) with a yāʾ carrying a ḍammah. This is according to Ḥamzah’s practice to pronounce the word how it is written when he pauses when it comes to the hamzah. This is the opinion of al-ʾAḫfaš; by that I mean the softening in that (context) by replacement (of the hamzah with a yāʾ).[32] If (the hamzah) carries a fatḥah, you make it between the hamzah and the ʿalif; for example, in the words of the Almighty sa.altahum# (← saʾaltahum) (e.g., Q9:65), wayka.ann# ʾaḷḷāha (← waykaʾanna ḷḷāha) (Q28:82), wayka.annah# (← waykaʾannahū) (Q28:82), ḫaṭa.ā# (← ḫaṭaʾan) (Q4:92), malǧa.ā# (← malǧaʾan) (Q9:57), muttaka.ā# (← muttakaʾan) (Q12:31) and what is like it. If (the hamzah) carries a kasrah, you make it between the hamzah and the yāʾ; for example, in the words ǧabra.īl# (ǧabraʾīlu) (e.g., Q66:4), ya.is# ʾallaḏīna (← yaʾisa llaḏīna) (Q5:3), su.il# (← suʾila) (Q2:108), yawma.iḏ# (← yawmaʾiḏin) (e.g., Q3:167), ḥīna.iḏ# (← ḥīnaʾiḏin) (Q56:84) and what is like it.

footnotes.text: Note that al-Dānī refers to a hamzah followed by another hamzah pronounced bayna bayn as madd ‘length’. This is ambiguous because he also calls a hamzah followed by ā madd. The wording therefore also allows the reading ʾān. Al-Dānī is explicit that the intended reading is ʾa-.an in his Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān (al-Dānī 2007, 970).
An alternate name for Sūrat al-Šūrā (Kandil 1992, 51).

Iḫtilās normally means ‘ultrashort’, but it is technically a relative term, i.e., shorter than its ʾaṣl ‘base’. As the base is yuʾaddihī, iḫtilās should be simply understood here to mean a normal-length kasrah, -hi. See I.4.2.
The Taysīr only has ʾisnāds for Hišām that go through al-Ḥulwānī. The Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān has other paths, but few seem to have explicit information on this topic (al-Dānī 2007, 980–81).
This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

Hišām is only transmitted through tilāwah by ʾAbū al-Fatḥ in the Taysīr (see U.4.4.2.), but the specific mention of ʾAbū al-Fatḥ implies that al-Dānī knows other tilāwah transmission from Hišām that has taḥsabanna. This is indeed the case, as he points it out in the Ǧamiʿ al-bayān (al-Dānī 2007, 994).

This is an addition in one of the manuscripts that Pretzl consulted. Al-Ḍāmin includes it without making mention of manuscripts that lack it. I have found it in both the Berlin and Paris manuscripts, and in one of the four Princeton manuscripts (Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett no. 213Y). It is unlikely to be an addition of later copyists; it has either been dropped out, or it points to a later recension of al-Taysīr with this added by al-Dānī. Hišām indeed appears to have had a book describing Ibn ʿĀmir’s reading, and al-Dānī had access to it, as he cites it several times in his Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān as well (Hamdan 2018, 55, fn. 4).

statements.heading: U.11.6.2. Subsection: Ḥamzah’s Pausal hamzah Softening on Word Boundaries
statements.text: Know that in everything that Ḥamzah softens among the hamzahs, he adheres to the writing of the muṣḥaf, rather than (reasoning by) analogy, like what we have presented before. Our teachers disagree on the softening of an (initial) hamzah rendered word-medial by the addition of a clitic before it (i.e., some apply softening and other do not); for example, in the words ʾa-fa-ʾant/ʾa-fa-.ant# (← ʾa-fa-ʾanta) (e.g., Q10:42), fa-bi-ʾayy/fa-bi-yayy# ʾālāʾi (← fa-bi-ʾayyi ʾalāʾi) (Q53:55), bi-ʾayyikum/bi-yayyikum# (← bi-ʾayyikum) (Q68:6), ka-ʾayyin/ka-.ayyin# (← ka-ʾayyin) (e.g., Q3:146), ka-ʾannah/ka-.annah# (← ka-ʾannahū) (Q7:171), fa-la-ʾuqaṭṭiʿann/fa-la-.uqaṭṭʿann# (← fa-la-ʾuqaṭṭiʿanna) (Q20:71), la-bi-ʾimām/la-bi-.imām# (← la-bi-ʾimāmin) (Q15:79), al-ʾarḍ/alarḍ# (← al-ʾarḍv̆) (e.g., Q2:11), al-ʾāḫirah/alāḫirah# (← al-ʾāḫirah) (e.g., Q2:94) and what is like it. Likewise (there is disagreement), when two words are joined in writing, and so they are made into a single word; for example, in the words of the Almighty hā.ulā(ā)#/hā ʾulā(ā)# (← hā ʾulāʾi জগ( )هوe.g., Q2:31), hā.antum#/hā ʾantum# ( ← hā ʾantum ࠸ࠪ( )هانe.g., Q3:66), yā.ayyuhā#/yā ʾayyuhā# (← yā ʾayyuhā ( )ياቛኟاe.g., Q2:21), yā.uḫt#/yā ʾuḫt# (← yā ʾuḫta ( )ياختQ19:28), yā.ādam#/yā ʾādam# (← yā ʾādamu ( )يادمe.g., Q2:33), yā.ulī/yā ʾulī (← yā ʾulī ياوᇃى) (e.g., Q2:179) and what is like it.[33] So, some of them favour softening in these, relying on what happens word-medially (to words where it does affect the rasm). Others do not favour anything but full pronunciation of the hamzah, relying on their status as word-initial hamzahs. Both practices are good, and they have been transmitted in texts of transmitters. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

statements.heading: U.12. The Lack of Assimilation and the Assimilation of Unvowelled Letters
U.12.1. [The Assimilation of ʾiḏ]
statements.text: They disagree on the (assimilation of the) ḏāl of ʾiḏ with six letters: with ǧīm, zāy, sīn, ṣād, tāʾ and dāl, as for example in the words of the Almighty wa-ʾiḏ ǧaʿalnā (Q2:125), wa-ʾiḏ zayyana (Q8:48), ʾiḏ samiʿtumūhu (Q24:12, 16), ʾiḏ ṣarafnā (Q46:29), ʾiḏ tabarraʾa (Q2:166), ʾiḏ daḫalū (e.g., Q15:52). The two of the holy cities and ʿĀṣim pronounce the ḏāl unassimilated with all of these letters. Ibn Ḏakwān assimilates it to the dāl only (i.e., ʾid⸗daḫalū but wa-ʾiḏ ǧaʿalnā, etc.). Ḫalaf assimilates it to the tāʾ and the dāl (i.e., ʾit⸗tabarraʾa, ʾid⸗daḫalū but wa-ʾiḏ ǧaʿalnā, etc.) Ḫallād and al-Kisāʾī leave it unassimilated with the ǧīm only (and assimilated it to all others) (i.e., wa-ʾiḏ ǧaʿalnā but wa-ʾiz⸗zayyana, etc.). ʾAbū ʿAmr and Hišām assimilate it to all six letters (i.e., wa-ʾiǧ⸗ǧaʿalnā, wa-ʾiz⸗zayyana, ʾis⸗samiʿtumūhu, ʾiṣ⸗ṣarafnā, ʾit⸗tabarraʾa, ʾid⸗daḫalū).

statements.heading: U.12.2. [The Assimilation of qad]
statements.text: They disagree on the (assimilation of the) dāl of qad with eight letters: with ǧīm, sīn, šīn, ṣād, zāy, ḏāl, ḏ̣āʾ, ḍād; for example, in the words of the Almighty la-qad ǧāʾakum (e.g., Q2:92), la-qad samiʿa (Q3:181), qad šaġafahā (Q12:30), la-qad ṣarrafnā (e.g., Q17:41), la-qad ḏaraʾnā (Q7:179), la-qad zayyannā (Q67:5), fa-qad ḍalla (Q2:108) and fa-qad ḏ̣alama (Q2:231). Ibn Katīr, Qālūn and ʿĀṣim pronounce the dāl unassimilated with all of these letters. Warš assimilates it to the ḍād and ḏ̣āʾ only (i.e., fa-qaḍ⸗ḍalla, fa-qaḏ̣⸗ḏ̣alama, but la-qad ǧāʾakum, etc.). Ibn Ḏakwān assimilates it to the zāy, ḏāl, ḍād and ḏ̣āʾ, those four and nothing else (i.e., la-qaz⸗zayyannā, la-qaḏ⸗ḏaraʾnā, fa-qaḍ⸗ḍalla, fa-qaḏ̣⸗ḏ̣alama, but la-qad ǧāʾakum, etc.). Al-Naqqāš transmits from al-ʾAḫfaš [from Ibn Ḏakwān] no assimilation with the zāy (i.e., la-qad zayyannā). Hišām keeps la-qad ḏ̣alamaka unassimilated in Ṣād (Q38:24) only (and assimilated qad to all eight letters everywhere else). The rest assimilate the dāl to (all) eight letters (i.e., la-qaǧ⸗ǧāʾakum, la-qas⸗samiʿa, qaš⸗šaġafahạ̄, la-qaṣ⸗ṣarrafnā, la-qaḏ⸗ḏaraʾnā, la-qaz⸗zayyannā, fa-qaḍ⸗ḍalla, fa-qaḏ̣⸗ḏ̣alama).

statements.heading: U.12.3. [The Assimilation of the Third Person Singular Feminine Verbal Suffix -at]
statements.text: They disagree on the (assimilation of) the feminine verbal suffix -at with six letters, with ǧīm, sīn, ṣād, zāy, ṯāʾ, ḏ̣āʾ, as for example in the words of the Almighty naḍiǧat ǧulūduhum (Q4:56), kaḏḏabat ṯamūdu (e.g., Q26:141), nuzzilat sūratun (Q47:20), ḥaṣirat ṣudūruhum (Q4:90), ḫabat zidnāhum (Q17:97), kānat ḏ̣ālimatan (Q21:11) and what is like it. So, Ibn Kaṯīr, Qālūn and ʿĀsim keep the tāʾ unassimilated with all of these letters. Warš assimilates it to the ḏ̣āʾ only (i.e., kānaḏ̣⸗ḏ̣ālimatan, but naḍiǧat ǧulūduhum, etc.). Ibn ʿĀmir pronounces it unassimilated with the ǧīm, sīn and zāy (i.e., naḍiǧat ǧulūduhum, nuzzilat sūratun, ḫabat zidnāhum, but ḥaṣiraṣ⸗ṣudūruhum, etc.). There is disagreement between Ibn Ḏakwān and Hišām on the word la-huddimat ṣawāmiʿu (Q22:40): Ibn Ḏakwān assimilates it (i.e., la-huddimaṣ⸗ṣawāmiʿu), and Hišām does not (i.e., la-huddimat ṣawāmiʿu). The rest assimilate the tāʾ in the six cases (i.e., naḍiǧaǧ⸗ǧulūduhum, kaḏḏabaṯ⸗ṯamūdu, nuzzilas⸗sūratun, ḥaṣiraṣ⸗ṣudūruhum, ḫabaz⸗zidnāhum, kānaḏ̣⸗ḏ̣ālimatan).

statements.heading: U.12.4. [The Assimilation of hal and bal]
statements.text: They disagree on the (assimilation of the) lām of hal and bal with eight letters, with tāʾ, ṯāʾ, sīn, zāy, ṭāʾ, ḏ̣āʾ, ḍād, nūn; for example, in the words of the Almighty hal taʿlamu (Q19:65), hal ṯuwwiba (Q83:36), bal sawwalat (Q12:18, 83), bal zuyyina (Q13:33), bal ṭabaʿa (Q4:155), bal ḏ̣anantum (Q48:12), bal ḍallū (Q46:28), hal nadullukum (Q34:7), hal nunabbiʾukum (Q18:103), hal naḥnu (Q26:203) and what is like it. Al-Kisāʾī assimilates the lām to (all) eight letters (hat⸗taʿlamu, haṯ⸗ṯuwwiba, bas⸗sawwalat, baz⸗zuyyina, baṭ⸗ṭabaʿa, baḏ̣⸗ḏ̣anantum, baḍ⸗ḍallū, han⸗nadullukum). Ḥamzah assimilates it only to the tāʾ, ṯāʾ, and sīn (hat⸗taʿlamu, haṯ⸗ṯuwwiba, bas⸗sawwalat, but bal zuyyina, etc.). There are divergent transmissions from Ḫallād regarding the ṭāʾ in the word bal ṭabaʿa ḷḷāhu (Q4:155). I have recited it in both ways (baṭ⸗ṭabaʿa ḷḷāhu/bal ṭabaʿa ḷḷāhu), but with assimilation is what I adopt for his (reading). Hišām leaves it unassimilated with the nūn and the ḍād, and with the tāʾ in the word in al-Raʿd (Q13:16) ʾam hal tastawī and nothing else (i.e., hat⸗taʿlamu, haṯ⸗ṯuwwiba, bas⸗sawwalat, baz⸗zuyyina, baṭ⸗ṭabaʿa, baḏ̣⸗anantum, but bal ḍallū, hal nadullukum, etc.). ʾAbū ʿAmr assimilates hat⸗tarē min fuṭūrin, fa-hat⸗tarē lahum in al-Mulk (Q67:3) and al-Ḥāqqah (Q69:8) and nothing else. The rest leave the lām unassimilated with (all) eight letters.

statements.heading: U.12.5. Subsection: [Various Assimilations]
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr, Ḫallād and al-Kisāʾī assimilate the bāʾ to the fāʾ wherever it occurs; for example, in the words of the Almighty ʾaw yaġlif⸗fa-sawfa (← yaġlib fa-sawfa) (Q4:74), wa-man lam yatuf⸗faʾulāʾika (← yatub fa-ʾulāʾika) (Q49:11) and what is like it. Ḫallād gives (the reciter) a choice in wa-man lam yatub fa-ʾulāʾika (both assimilated and unassimilated). Al-Kisāʾī assimilates the fāʾ to the bāʾ; for example, in the words of the Almighty ʾin našaʾ naḫsib⸗bihumu l-ʾarḍ (← naḫsif bihim) in Sabaʾ (Q34:9). The others leave these unassimilated. ʾAbū al-Ḥāriṯ assimilates the lām of wa-man yafʿal—if it was unvowelled to mark the ǧazm—to the ḏāl; for example, in the words of the Almighty wa-man yafʿaḏ⸗ḏālika (← yafʿal ḏālika) (e.g., Q2:231) and the others leave it unassimilated. The two of the holy cities and ʿĀṣim leave unassimilated labiṯta (e.g., Q2:259), labiṯtu (Q2:259, Q10:16), labiṯtum (e.g., Q17:52) and man yurid ṯawāba (Q3:145) whenever they occur. The rest assimilate those (i.e., labitta, labittu, labittum, man yuriṯ⸗ṯawāba). Ḥišām, ʾAbū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī assimilate ʾurittumūhā (← ʾuriṯtumūhā) in both places (Q7:43; Q43:72). ʾAbū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī assimilate fa-nabattuhā (← fa-nabaḏtuhā) (Q20:96) and wa-ʾinnī ʿuttu bi-rabbī (← wa-ʾinnī ʿuḏtu bi-rabbi) (Q40:37; Q44:30). The others leave it unassimilated. Ibn Kaṯīr and Ḥafṣ leave ittaḫaḏtum (e.g., Q29:25), ʾaḫaḏtum (Q3:81; Q8:68), la-ttaḫaḏta/la-taḫiḏta (Q18:77) and what is similar to them unassimilated, but the others assimilate them (i.e., ittaḫattum, ʿaḫattum, la-ttaḫatta/la-taḫitta). Ibn Kaṯīr, Warš and Hišām leave yalhaṯ ḏālika (Q7:176) unassimilated, and there is disagreement in transmission from Qālūn (with and without assimilation). The others assimilate it (i.e., yalhaḏ⸗ḏālika). ʾAbū ʿAmr assimilates an unvowelled rāʾ to a lām, such as in the words of the Almighty naġfil⸗lakum (← naġfir lakum) (Q2:58; Q7:161), iṣbil⸗li-ḥukmi rabbika (← iṣbir li-ḥukmi) (e.g., Q52:48) and what is like it, with disagreement among the people of Iraq on this matter. Muḥammad b. ʾAḥmad b. ʿAlī related to us, saying that Ibn Muǧāhid related to us from his teachers, from al-Yazīdī, from ʾAbū ʿAmr that it was with assimilation, and he did not mention disagreement nor another option.[34] The others leave it unassimilated. Warš, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamzah leave yā bunayyi rkab maʿanā (Q11:42) unassimilated, and there was disagreement in transmission from Qālūn, al-Bazzī and Ḫallād (to assimilate it, i.e., irkam⸗maʿanā/irkab maʿanā). Warš leaves wa-yuʿaḏḏib man yašāʾu in al-Baqarah (Q2:284) unassimilated, and there is also disagreement in transmission from Qunbul and al-Bazzī (to assimilate it, i.e., wa-yuʿaḏḏim⸗man/wa-yuʿaḏḏib man). The rest assimilate it (i.e., irkam⸗maʿanā, wa-yuʿaḏḏim⸗man).[35] Among what is discussed in this chapter (i.e., on the topic of assimilation) concerning the beginnings of the sūrahs (i.e., the disconnected letters), we will mention it there (under the relevant chapter on the sūrah with disconnected letters) if God wills it.

footnotes.text: The word hunā is missing in Pretzl (al-Dānī 2008a, 36).

statements.heading: U.12.6. Subsection: [Assimilation of the nūn and tanwīn]
statements.text: (The readers) agree on the assimilation of the unvowelled nūn and the tanwīn with the rāʾ and lām without nasalisation (e.g., Q2:5 mir⸗rabbihim(ū) ← min rabbihim(ū); Q2:25 ṯamaratir⸗rizqan ← ṯamaratin rizqan; Q2:12 wa-lākil⸗lā ← wa-lākin lā; Q2:17 ẓulumātil⸗lā ← ẓulumātin lā). They agree on the assimilation of the two of them to the mīm and nūn with nasalisation (e.g. Q2:23 bi-sūratim⸗mim⸗miṯlihī ← bi-sūratin min miṯlihī; Q2:48 ʿan⸗nafsin ← ʿan nafsin; Q2:58 ḥiṭṭatun⸗naġfir ← ḥiṭṭatun naġfir). They disagree with regard to the yāʾ and the wāw. So Ḫalaf reads with assimilation without nasalisation, as for example the words wa-may⸗yaqul (← wa-man yaqul) (Q21:29), yawmaʾiḏiy⸗yaṣṣaddaʿūna (← yawmaʾiḏin yaṣṣaddaʿūna) (Q30:43), miw⸗wālin (← min wālin) (Q13:11), yawmaʾiḏiw⸗wāhiyah (← yawmaʾiḏin wāhiyah) (Q69:16) and what is like it, and the rest assimilate them while retaining the nasalisation (i.e., maỹ⸗yaqul, yawmaʾiḏiỹ⸗ yaṣṣadaʿūna, miw̃⸗wālin, yawmaʾiḏiw̃⸗wāhiyah), so true replacement (of the n) is prevented by it. They also agree on the lack of assimilation of the two (nūn and tanwīn) to the six guttural letters, and those are: hamzah, hāʾ, ḥāʾ, ʿayn, ḫāʾ and ġayn, except when it comes to the manner of Warš with the hamzah as he places the vowel that is on the hamzah on them (the nūn or tanwīn), and this has already been mentioned.[36] Likewise, they agree on the changing of both (nūn and tanwīn) into a mīm next to a bāʾ only, and on the ʾiḫfāʾ with the remaining letters of the alphabet. ʾIḫfāʾ is a state between clear pronunciation and assimilation, and it is devoid of gemination, so know it! Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: See U.11.6.1. The phrase ‘in pause’ is missing in the Pretzl edition. This must be a mistake (al-Dānī 2008a, 263).

statements.heading: U.13. The fatḥ and the ʾimālah and What Is in between the Two Sounds
statements.text: Know that Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī pronounce with ʾimālah all the nouns and verbs that have a stem-final yāʾ; for example, nouns in the words of the Almighty mūsē (e.g., Q2:51), ʿīsē (e.g., Q2:87), yaḥyē (e.g., Q6:85), al-mawtē (Q2:73), ṭūbē (Q13:29), ʾiḥdē (e.g., Q8:7), kusālē (Q4:142; Q9:54), ʾasrē (Q8:67), yatāmē (Q4:127), furādē (Q6:94; Q34:46), an-naṣarē (Q2:62), al-ʾayāmē (Q24:32), al-ḥawāyē (Q6:146), bušrē (Q2:97), ḏikrē (Q6:69), sīmē,[37] ḍīzē (Q53:22) and what is like it among those (nouns) whose ʾalif marks the feminine. It is likewise for al-hudē (Q2:120), al-ʿamē (Q41:17), aḍ-ḍuḥē (Q93:1), az-zinē (Q17:32), maʾwēhu (e.g., Q3:162), maʾwēkum (e.g., Q29:25), maṯwēhu (Q12:21), maṯwēkum (Q6:128; Q47:19) and what is like it among those that end in ʾalif maqṣūrah. Likewise, for al-ʾadnē (Q7:169; Q32:21), ʾazkē (e.g., Q2:232), ʾawlē (e.g., Q3:68), al-ʾaʿlē (Q16:60) and what is like it among the (elative) adjectives. As for the verbs, examples are in the words of the Almighty: ʾabē (Q2:34), saʿē (Q2:114), zakkē,[38] fa-sawwē (Q75:38; Q87:2), yaḫfē (e.g., Q3:5), tahwē (e.g., Q2:87), yarḍē (e.g., Q4:108) and what is like it of those (verbs) whose ʾalif replaces a (final radical) yāʾ. Likewise, both apply ʾimālah to ʾannē when it has the meaning ‘how’, for example, in His speech ʾannē šiʾtum (Q2:223) and ʾannē laki (Q3:37) and what is like it. Likewise, matē (e.g., Q2:214), balē (e.g., Q2:81) and ʿasē (Q2:216), whenever they occur, and everything else similar to it from among those written in the rasm of the muṣḥafs with yāʾ, with the exception of five words, and they are ḥattā, ladā, ʿalā, ʾilā and mā zakā (Q24:21). Those are unanimously pronounced with ā.[39] The same is true (that they are pronounced with ā) for all those among the nouns and verbs that have a stem-final wāw. So, the nouns are, for example, aṣ-ṣafā (Q2:158), sanā barqihī (Q24:43), ʿaṣāhu (e.g., Q7:107), šafā ǧurufin (Q9:109), ʾabā ʾaḥadin (Q33:40) and what is like it. The verbs are, for example ḫalā (Q2:76; Q35:24), daʿā (e.g., Q3:38), badā (e.g., Q6:28), danā (Q53:8), ʿafā (e.g., Q2:187), ʿalā (Q28:4) and what is like it, so long as they do not occur among the words with stem-final yāʾ in sūrahs that end in yāʾ (i.e., Q93:2 saǧē/ā)[40] or if they are derived stems, for example in the words of the Almighty yudʿē (Q61:7), tutlē (e.g., Q3:101), fa-man iʿtadē (Q2:178), man istaʿlē (Q20:64), ʾanǧēkum (Q14:6), and like that naǧǧēnā (e.g., Q7:89), naǧǧēkum (Q17:67), zakkēhā (Q91:9) and what is like it. ʾImālah in these is fitting as derivation has changed them into stems with final yāʾ. You can find out which of the nouns have root-final wāw through the dual, when you say ṣafawāni, ʿaṣawāni, sanawāni, šafawāni and what is like it. You find this out for the verbs by inflecting it for the first person, when you say: ḫalawtu, badawtu, danawtu, ʿalawtu and what is like it. So, the wāw becomes apparent to you in all of these cases, and ʾimālah is prevented due to that. Likewise, you can find out which nouns and verbs are among the ḏawāt al-yāʾ through the dual and by conjugating the verb in the first person. When you say hudayāni, ʿamayāni, hawayāni, saʿaytu, hadaytu and what is like it, the yāʾ becomes apparent to you in all these cases, so you apply ʾimālah. ʾAbū ʿAmr reads from all that preceded (only) those that have a rāʾ and a yāʾ after it with ʾimālah (e.g., yarē Q53:12). (He read) in between the two sounds those (words) which are verse-final in the sūrahs whose verses end in yāʾ or (yāʾ with) hāʾ and ʾalif (i.e., the pronoun -hā) (e.g. Q92:1 yaġšǟ, Q91:1 wa-ḍuḥǟhā). (He also reads it in between the two sounds) when the pattern is faʿlǟ, fiʿlǟ or fuʿlǟ with fatḥah, kasrah or ḍammah as the vowel of the first root letter and do not also have a rāʾ in it (before the final yāʾ) (e.g., al-qurbǟ, al-mawtǟ, ʾiḥdǟ). (He reads) everything else with fatḥ (i.e., with ā). Warš reads all of these in between the two sounds except what is among those in the sūrah that ends with verses that have (yāʾ) with hāʾ and ʾalif. So, he pronounces those with pure fatḥ (i.e., with ā) in it (i.e., Q79:27–32, 42–46; Q91, e.g. banāhā, fa-sawwāhā, etc.). There is disagreement among the people of oral tradition on that detail (i.e., some do read banǟhā, fa-sawwǟhā, etc.), but this is only the case when there is no rāʾ in it. There is not a single text that reports disagreement on this (in the case of rāʾ, all agree it is ḏikrǟhā).[41] ʾAbū Bakr applies ʾimālah to ramē in al-ʾAnfāl (Q8:17) and ʾaʿmē in both places in Subḥān (Q17:72). ʾAbū ʿAmr agrees with him in applying ʾimālah to ʾaʿmē (in Q17:72) in its first occurrence only; and he applies the fatḥ to all besides that one. Ḥafṣ applies ʾimālah in maǧrēhā in Hūd (Q11:41) and nothing else. Among the path of the People of Iraq transmitting from ʾAbū ʿAmr I have recited yā waylatǟ (Q5:31; Q11:72; Q25:82), yā ḥasratǟ (Q39:56) and ʾannǟ (e.g., Q2:223) when it is an interrogative (i.e., ‘ أᆇ ّىhow?’, not أྚّا ‘that we’) between the two sounds and yā ʾasafā (Q12:84) with fatḥ (i.e., ā). I have recited (all of) these with fatḥ along the path of the people of Raqqa (i.e., the transmitters of al-Sūsī). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī apply ʾimālah to these according to their principle (i.e., yā waylatē, etc.). The rest read with pure fatḥ in all that preceded.

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

statements.heading: U.13.1. Subsection: [ʾImālah of Some Words Unique to al-Kisāʾī]
statements.text: Al-Kisāʾī diverges from Ḥamzah in applying ʾimālah to ʾaḥyēkum (Q22:66), fa-ʾaḥyē bihī (Q2:164) and ʾaḥyēhā (Q5:32) whenever it occurs, when it is prefixed by fāʾ or not prefixed, but nothing else (i.e., not when prefixed by wa-, for which al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamzah agree, see below). (He also diverges from Ḥamzah) with the words ḫaṭāyēkum (Q2:58; Q29:12), ḫaṭāyēhum (Q29:12), ḫaṭāyēnā (Q20:73; Q26:51), ar-ruʾyē (e.g., Q17:60), ruʾyēya (Q12:43; Q12:100), marḍēti llāhi (e.g., Q2:207), marḍētī (Q60:1) whenever they occur, and with the words of the Almighty in ʾĀl ʿImrān (Q3:102) ḥaqqa tuqētihī, in al-ʾAnʿām (Q6:80) wa-qad hadēni, in ʾIbrāhīm (Q14:36) wa-man ʿaṣēnī, in al-Kahf (Q18:63) wa-mā ʾansēnīhi, in Maryam (Q19:30) ʾātēniya l-kitāba, wa-ʾawṣēnī bi-ṣ-ṣālāti (Q19:31), in al-Naml (Q27:36) fa-mā ʾātēni llāhu, in al-Ǧāṯiyah (Q45:21) maḥyēhum, in al-Nāziʿāt (Q79:30) daḥēhā, in al-Šams talēhā (Q91:2), ṭaḥēhā (Q91:6) and in al-Ḍuḥā (Q93:2) saǧē. He agrees with Ḥamzah on the ʾimālah in the words of the Almighty wa-yaḥyē (Q8:42), wa-lā yaḥyē (Q20:74; Q87:13), ʾamāta wa-ʾaḥyē (Q53:44) when it is prefixed by wāw, and likewise ad-dunyē (e.g., Q2:85), al-ʿulyē (Q9:40), al-ḥawāyē (Q6:146), aḍ-ḍuḥē (Q93:1), ḍuḥēhā (Q91:1), ar-ribē (e.g., Q2:275), ʾinnanī hadēnī (Q6:161), ʾātēnī in Hūd (Q11:28, 63), wa-law ʾanna ḷḷāha hadēnī (Q39:57), minhum tuqētan (Q3:28), muzǧētin (Q12:88), ʾaw kilēhumā (Q17:23) and ʾinēhu wa-lākin (Q33:35). Hišām follows the two of them in the ʾimālah of ʾinēhu only, and the rest read all of this with fatḥ. The manner of ʾAbū ʿAmr with fvʿlā (nouns) and the manner of Warš with words that have a root final yāʾ have already been mentioned.[42]

footnotes.text: Pretzl has يصْ دقون. This does not occur in the Qurʾān (al-Dānī 2008a, 36).

statements.heading: U.13.2. Subsection: [ʾImālah that Is Unique to al-Dūrī from al-Kisāʾī]
statements.text: Al-Kisāʾī is also unique in the transmission of al-Dūrī with ʾimālah in the words ʾāḏēnihim (Q2:19, etc.), ʾāḏēninā (Q41:5), ṭuġyēnihim (Q2:15, etc.) whenever they occur and hudēya (Q2:38; Q20:123), maṯwēya (Q12:23), maḥyēya (Q6:162), ruʾyēka at the beginning of Sūrat Yūsuf (Q12:5) specifically, bēriʾikum in both occurrences (both in Q2:54), bēriʾu l-muṣawwir (Q59:24), sēriʿū (Q3:133), yusēriʿūna (e.g., Q3:114) and nusēriʿu (Q23:56), whenever they occur, and al-ǧēri in both places (Q4:36), ǧabbērīna in both places (Q5:22; Q26:130), al-ǧawēri in al-Šūrā (Q42:32), al-Raḥmān (Q55:24) and Kuwwirat (Q81:16), man ʾanṣērī ʾilà ḷḷāhi in both places (Q3:52; Q61:41) and ka-miškētin in al-Nūr (Q24:35). The rest apply fatḥ in all of these words except the word ruʾ/ūyǟka: ʾAbū ʿAmr and Warš read it (with the sound) in between as per their principle. As for His words al-ǧǟri (e.g., Q4:36) and ǧabbǟrīna (Q5:22; Q26:130), Warš reads those two also in between (fatḥah and ʾimālah) with disagreement in transmission from him between the people of the oral tradition. The foremost way (i.e., with ǟ) is how I have recited it and what I adopt. [ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ǧaʿfar] al-Fārisī transmitted to me from ʾAbū Ṭāhir from ʾAbū ʿUṯmān Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān the blind from ʾAbū ʿUmar [al-Dūrī] from al-Kisāʾī[43] that he applies ʾimālah to yuwērī and fa-ʾuwērī in the two occurrences in al-Māʾidah (Q5:31); no one else transmitted that from him. I adopt that (ʾimālah) for this path, and I have read them both (the two words) in the path of Ibn Muǧāhid with fatḥ.

footnotes.text: Qālūn had a book that described his recitation of Nāfiʿ (Hamdan 2018, 37). It appears that this early work lacked the sophistication to express the concept of an epenthetic ultrashort vowel, and thus he described it as bi-ʾiskān ‘without a vowel’. However, the oral tradition apparently places an epenthetic vowel here. See also the discussion in the Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān (al-Dānī 2007, 1020–21) where al-Dānī seems to explicitly prefer the taʿddū reading calling it ʾāṯar ‘better supported by sources’.

statements.heading: U.13.3. Subsection: [Hollow Root ʾimālah and Some Others]
statements.text: Ḥamzah is unique in applying the ʾimālah to ten verbs. These are ǧēʾa (e.g., Q4:43), šēʾa (Q2:20), zēda,[44] rēna (Q83:14), ḫēfa (e.g., Q2:182), ṭēba (Q4:3), ḫēba (e.g., Q14:15), ḥēqa (e.g., Q6:10), ḍēqa (e.g., Q11:77), zēġa in al-Naǧm (Q53:17) and zēġū in al-Ṣaff (Q61:5) and nothing else;[45] it is the same whether these verbs were followed by a pronominal suffix or not, when it is of three letters (i.e., stem I) and in the perfect. Al-Kisāʾī and ʾAbū Bakr follow him in the ʾimālah in bar⸗rēna (Q83:14) and nothing else. Ibn Ḏakwān follows him in the ʾimālah of ǧēʾa and šēʾa whenever they occur and fa-zēdahum at the beginning of al-Baqarah (Q2:10); this is the transmission of Muḥammad b. al-ʾAḫram[46] from al-ʾAḫfaš from him (i.e., Ibn Ḏakwān). Others transmit it from him with ʾimālah (of zēda not just in al-Baqarah, but) in all of the Qurʾān. Ḥamzah is also unique in applying the ʾimālah of the fatḥah of the hamzah, through ʾišmām,[47] in the words of the Almighty ʾana ʾētīka bihī in the two occurrences in al-Naml (Q27:39, 40). (He is also unique in applying of) ʾimālah of the fatḥah of the ʿayn in the word ḍiʿēfan in al-Nisāʾ (Q4:9). There is disagreement in transmission from Ḫallād in these three places and I adopt fatḥ for him (i.e., ʾātīka and ḍiʿāfan).

footnotes.text: Again, Pretzl has ୚ඤن for Subḥān (al-Dānī 2008a, 267). Subḥān is an alternative name for Sūrat al-ʾIsrāʾ (Kandil 1992, 50).

statements.heading: U.13.4. Subsection: [The āri → ēri ʾimālah of ʾAbū ʿAmr and al-Dūrī ← al-Kisāʾī]
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī, in the transmission of al-Dūrī, apply ʾimālah to each ʾalif which has after it a rāʾ with ǧarr on it when it is the third root letter of the word; for example, ʿalā ʾabṣērihim (Q2:7),[48] ʾāṯērihim (e.g., Q5:46), an-nēri (Q2:39), al-qahhēri (Q14:48; Q40:16), al-ġēri (Q9:40), bi-qinṭērin (Q3:75), bi-dīnērin (Q3:75), al-ʾabrēri (Q3:193; Q83:18) and what is like it.[49] ʾAbū al-Ḥāriṯ follows them in applying the ʾimālah (only) when the root contains a double rāʾ in it; for example, qarērin (Q14:26), al-ʾašrēri (Q38:62), al-ʾabrēri (Q3:193; Q83:18) and pronounces the rest (of these words) with pure fatḥ. The disagreement (among the readers) in His speech ǧurufin hērin (Q9:109) will be discussed in its place.[50] Warš reads all of these words in between the two sounds (i.e., ʾabṣǟrihim, etc.), and Ḥamzah agrees with him in whatever is among them with a repeated rāʾ (i.e., qarǟrin, etc.), and in the word al-qahhǟri (Q14:48; Q40:16) wherever it occurs, and dāra l-bawǟri (Q14:28) and nothing else. He pronounces with pure fatḥ what remains. According to the way I recited to [ʾAbū al-Fatḥ] Fāris b. ʾAḥmad and ʾAbū al-Qāsim al-Fārisī, Ibn Ḏakwān pronounces (only) ʾilā ḥimērika and al-ḥimēri in al-Baqarah (Q2:259) and al-Ǧumuʿah (Q62:5) with ʾimālah and nothing else.[51] The rest read with pure fatḥ in all (words mentioned in) this category.

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).
This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).
Unlike F.2:184. and F.34:15., where the miskīn/masākīn is disagreed upon.

statements.heading: U.13.5. Subsection: [More ʾimālah of ʾAbū ʿAmr and al-Dūrī ← al-Kisāʾī]
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr, as well as al-Kisāʾī in the transmission of al-Dūrī, apply ʾimālah to the fatḥah of the kāf of al-kēfirīna (e.g., Q2:19) and kēfirīna (Q3:100) (that is) when after the rāʾ there is a yāʾ (as opposed to a wāw of the rafʿ), whenever it occurs. Warš reads these with the sound in between (the two sounds) (i.e., (al-)kǟfirīna). The rest read it with pure fatḥ (i.e., (al-)kāfirīna). [ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ǧaʿfar] al-Fārisī taught me to recite according to his recitation to ʾAbū Ṭāhir in the reading of ʾAbū ʿAmr (via al-Dūrī) with ʾimālah of the fatḥah of the nūn of an-nēsi (e.g., Q2:8) with ǧarr, wherever it occurs. of this rule, they are exempt from it in the transmission of ʾAbū ʿAmr. This is mentioned rather This is also the transmission of ʾAbū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān [Ibn al-Yazīdī], ʾAbū Ḥamdūn and Ibn Saʿdān from al-Yazīdī.[52] The other one (i.e., ʾAbū al-Fatḥ) taught me to recite with fatḥ; this is the transmission of ʾAḥmad b. Ǧubayr from al-Yazīdī,[53] and it is what Ibn Muǧāhid observes. The rest read it with that (with fatḥ).

statements.heading: U.13.6. Subsection: [ʾImālah Unique to Hišām and Ibn Ḏakwān]
statements.text: Hišām is alone in applying ʾimālah in the words of the Almighty wa-mašēribu in Yā-Sīn (Q36:73), min ʿaynin ʾēniyatin in al-Ġāšiyah (Q88:5) and ʿēbidūna (Q109:3), ʿēbidun (Q109:4), ʿēbidūna (Q109:5) in the three (occurrences) in al-Kāfirūna and nothing else. Ibn Ḏakwān is unique, according to the way I recited to ʾAbū al-Fatḥ, in applying ʾimālah to the words ʿimrēn and al-miḥrēb whenever they occur, min baʿdi ikrēhihinna in al-Nūr (Q24:33) and al-ʾikrēm in two instances in al-Raḥmān (Q55:27, 78). But I recited to al-Fārisī transmitting from al-Naqqāš with ʾimālah of the rāʾ for al-miḥrēb only, whenever it occurs. I recited to ʾAbū al-Ḥasan [Ibn Ġalbūn][54] with ʾimālah of the rāʾ in al-miḥrēbi when it occurs with ḫafḍ, and that is in two places: in ʾĀl ʿImrān (Q3:39) and Maryam (Q19:11).
