The rest read with pure fatḥ in all of these places except for what is in the manner of Warš for the rāʾs. This will come later,[55] if God wills it. So, these are the principles of ʾimālah from which (the particular instances) can be derived analogically. As for those that remain among those that occur dispersed among the sūrahs, we will mention them in their respective places, if God Almighty wills it.

footnotes.text: The Pretzl edition renders it incorrectly with two lāms. It should read وუჸار اগᔃজൡൿة. Corrected by al-Ḍāmin (al-Dānī 2008a, 274).
This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

statements.heading: U.13.7. Subsection: [Treatment of ʾimālah in Pause and Connected Speech]
statements.text: Whatever is given ʾimālah in connected speech due to a trigger that is absent in pause, or if it is read in between the two sounds (due to such a trigger)—for example bi-miqdēr# (Q13:8), bi-dīnēr# (Q3:75), al-ʾabrēr# (Q3:193), min an-nēs# (Q2:204), bi-rabbi n-nēs# (Q114:1) and what is similar to it, among what occurs with a rāʾ and a ǧarrah on the word-end—these are also given ʾimālah or are pronounced in between in pause, because the pausal forms are accidental. As for all those whose ʾimālah is prevented in connected speech because of an unvowelled letter which follows it, whether tanwīn or something else—as for example in the words of the Almighty hudan/hudē# (e.g., Q2:2), muṣaffan/muṣaffē# (Q47:15), musamman/musammē# (e.g., Q2:282), ḍuḥan/ḍuḥē# (e.g., Q7:98; Q20:59), muṣallan/muṣallē# (Q2:125), ġuzzan/ġuzzē# (Q3:156), mawlan/mawlē# (Q44:41), riban/ribē# (Q30:39), muftaran/muftarē (Q28:36; Q34:43), al-ʾaqṣà llaḏī/al-ʾaqṣē# (Q17:1), ṭaġà l-māʾu/ṭaġē# (Q69:11), an-naṣārà lmasīḥu/an-naṣārē# (Q9:30), mūsà l-kitāba/mūsē# (e.g., Q2:53), ʿīsà bnu maryama/ʿīsē (e.g., Q3:45), ǧanà l-ǧannatayni/ǧanē# (Q55:54) and what is like it—ʾimālah is appropriate in pause in these cases, because that following unvowelled letter is absent there. However, ʾAbū Šuʿayb [al-Sūsī] transmits from al-Yazīdī the ʾimālah of the rāʾ even with a following unvowelled letter in connected speech, for example, in the words of the Almighty narè ḷḷāha (Q2:55),[56] yarè llaḏīna (Q2:165; Q34:6), kubrè ḏhab (Q20:23–24), qurè llatī (Q36:18), an-naṣārè l-masīḥu (Q9:30) and what is like it from those which have a rāʾ. That is what I recited for his (ʾAbū Šuʿayb’s) manner and what I adopt. So learn that well. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This is different from the modern practice of Warš in the path of al-ʾAzraq, which allows this option, but seems to prefer replacing the hamzah with ā, thus creating overlong vowels like ʾa-râytum because the ā stands before a two-consonant cluster (Ibn al-Ǧazarī 2018, §1501–2).

statements.heading: U.14. The Tradition of al-Kisāʾī When He Pauses on the hāʾ of the Feminine Ending
statements.text: Know that al-Kisāʾī pauses on the hāʾ of the feminine and what is similar to it in sound,[57] with the ʾimālah, for example, in His words ǧanneh# (← ǧannatv̆n) (e.g., Q2:265), rabweh# (← rabwatin) (Q2:265; Q23:50), niʿmeh# (← niʿmatv̆n) (e.g., Q8:53), al-qiyāmeh# (← al-qiyāmatv̆) (e.g., Q2:85), la-ʿibreh# (← la-ʿibratvan) (e.g., Q3:13), al-ʾāḫireh# ( ← al-ʾāḫiratv̆) (e.g., Q2:4), ḫāṭiʾeh# (← ḫāṭiʾaṭin) (Q96:16), wiǧheh# (← wiǧhatun) (Q2:148), ḫaṭīʾeh# (← ḫaṭīʾatun) (Q4:112), al-malāʾikeh# (← al-malāʾikatv̆) (e.g., Q2:31), mušrikeh# (← mušrikatv̆n) (Q2:221; Q25:3), al-ʾaykeh# (← al-ʾaykati) (e.g., Q15:78), fākiheh# (← fākihatv̆n) (e.g., Q36:57), ʾāliheh# (← ʾālihatv̆n) (e.g., Q6:19), humazeh# (← humazatin) (Q104:1), lumazeh# (← lumazatin) (Q104:1), baṣīreh (← baṣīratv̆n) (Q12:108; Q75:14) and what is like it. However, (some transmitters transmit an absence of ʾimālah) if there occurs before the hāʾ one of the ten letters ṭāʾ, ḏ̣āʾ, ṣād, ḍād, ḫāʾ, ġayn, qāf, ʾalif, ʿayn, ḥāʾ, for example, basṭah# (← basṭatan) (Q2:247), mawʿiḏ̣ah# ( ← mawʿiḏ̣atv̆n) (e.g., Q2:66), ḫaṣāṣah# (← ḫaṣāṣatun) (Q59:9), qabḍah# (← qabḍatan) (Q20:96), aṣ-ṣāḫḫah# (← aṣ-ṣāḫḫatu) (Q80:33), al-bāliġah# (← al-bāliġatu) (Q6:149), al-ḥāqqah# (← al-ḥāqqatu) (Q69:1, 2, 3), aṣ-ṣalāh# (← aṣ-ṣalātv̆) (e.g., Q2:3), az-zakāh# (← az-zakātv̆) (e.g., Q2:43), al-ḥayāh# (← al-ḥayātv̆) (e.g., Q2:85), an-naǧāh# (← an-naǧāti) (Q40:41), manāh# (← manāta) (Q53:20), hayhāh# (← hayhāta)[58] (Q23:36), an-naṭīḥah# (← an-naṭīḥatu) (Q5:3), al-qāriʿah# (← al-qāriʿatu) (Q101:1, 2, 3) and what is like it, and if the hāʾ is preceded by 1. a rāʾ and (the letter) before the rāʾ carries a fatḥah or a ḍammah, 2. or a hamzah and (the letter) before it carries a fatḥah or is an ʾalif, 3. or a hāʾ and (the letter) before it is an ʾalif, 4. or a kāf and (the letter) before it carries a ḍammah or a fatḥah. So, for the rāʾ, examples are the words ġamrah# (← ġamratin) (Q23:63; Q51:11), ḥufrah# (← ḥufratin) (Q3:103), sūrah (← sūratv̆n) (e.g., Q9:64), maḥšūrah# (← maḥšūratan) (Q38:19), bararah# (← bararatin) (Q80:16), ʿimārah# (← ʿimārata) (Q9:20) and what is like it. As for the hamzah, examples are the words imraʾah# (← imraʾatv̆n) (e.g., Q4:12), barāʾah# (← barāʾatun) (Q9:1; Q54:43), an-našʾah# (← an-našʾata) (e.g., Q29:20), sawʾah# (← sawʾata) (Q5:31) and what is like it. For the hāʾ, in the word safāhah# (← safāhatv̆n) (Q7:66, 67) and nothing else. As for the kāf, for example, at-tahlukah# (← at-tahlukati) (Q2:195), aš-šawkah (← aš-šawkati) (Q8:7) and what is like it. In these excepted cases, Ibn Muǧāhid and his companions do not apply ʾimālah of the hāʾ and what precedes (i.e., ṭāʾ, ḏ̣āʾ, ṣād, ḍād, ḫāʾ, ġayn, qāf, ʾalif, ʿayn, ḥāʾ, rāʾ, hamzah, hāʾ, kāf). However, written transmission of these exceptions from al-Kisāʾī is missing. I recited it with full generalisation (i.e., even applying ʾimālah where the exceptions listed above are in place, e.g., basṭeh#, aṣ-ṣāḫḫeh#) to ʾAbū al-Fatḥ from his recitation to ʿAbd al-Bāqī. The same was narrated to us by Muḥammad [b. ʾAḥmad] b. ʿAlī, who said that it was narrated to him by Ibn al-ʾAnbārī who said that it was narrated to him by ʾIdrīs from Ḫalaf from al-Kisāʾī.[59] The first way (i.e., a generalised ʾimālah without exceptions) is what I prefer, except that, when the hāʾ is preceded by an ʾalif, ʾimālah is not allowed. The rest pause (on these words) with fatḥ. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).
This transmission path is not present in U.4.4.1. but it is mentioned in al-Dānī’s Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān (al-Dānī 2007, 334).

statements.heading: U.15. The Manner of Warš for the rāʾs, Summarised[60]
statements.text: Know that Warš applies ʾimālah to the fatḥah of the rāʾ a little bit in between the two sounds[61] whenever it is immediately preceded by a kasrah that is essential (i.e., part of the word), or an unvowelled letter with kasrah before it, or an unvowelled yāʾ. This is the case regardless of whether the rāʾ carries tanwīn or not. So, as for those in which the kasrah comes right before the rāʾ, examples are the words of the Almighty al-āḫiŕatv̆ (e.g., Q2:4), bāsiŕatun (Q75:24), nāḍiŕatun (Q75:22), fāqiŕatun (Q75:25), tabṣiŕatan (Q50:8), mudabbiŕāti (Q79:5), al-muʿṣiŕāti (Q78:14), ṭahhiŕā (Q2:125), sāḥiŕāni (Q20:63), mudbiŕan (Q27:10; Q28:31), ṣābiŕan (Q18:69; Q38:44) and what is like it. As for the case where between the rāʾ and the kasrah there is an unvowelled letter, examples are the words of the Almighty aš-šiʿŕa (Q36:69), as-siḥŕa (e.g., Q2:102), aḏ-ḏikŕa (e.g., Q15:9), sidŕatv̆ (Q53:14, 16), ḏū miŕŕatin (Q53:6), la-ʿibŕatan (e.g., Q3:13), and what is like it. As for those where there is a yāʾ adjacent to the rāʾ regardless of whether the letter before (the yāʾ) carries a fatḥah or a kasrah, these are for example His words al-ḫayŕāti (e.g., Q2:148), ḥayŕāna (Q6:71), al-ḫayŕa (Q22:77), ġayŕakum (e.g., Q9:39), al-muġīŕāti (Q100:3), al-faqīŕa (Q22:28), ḫabīŕan (e.g., Q4:35), baṣīŕan (e.g., Q4:58), naḏīŕan (e.g., Q2:119), ḫayŕan (e.g., Q2:158), ṭayŕan (Q105:3), sayŕan (Q52:10) and what is like it. He violates his manner with the kasrah in both cases (i.e., with an intervening letter or without), in the words aṣ-ṣiṛāṭv̆ (e.g., Q1:6) and ṣiṛāṭv̆n (e.g., Q2:142), whenever they occur, and al-fiṛāqu (Q75:28), fiṛāqu baynī (Q18:78), al-išṛāqi (Q38:18), ʾiʿṛāḍan (Q4:128), ʾiʿṛāḍuhum (Q6:35), midṛāṛan (e.g., Q6:6), ʾisṛāṛan (Q71:9), ḍiṛāṛan (Q2:231; Q9:107), fiṛāṛan (e.g., Q18:18), ʾibṛāhīmv̆ (e.g., Q2:124), ʾisṛāʾīlv̆ (Q2:40), ʿimṛāna (e.g., Q3:33), ʾiṛama ḏāti (Q89:7), ʾimṛan (Q18:71), ḏikṛan (Q2:200), sitṛan (Q18:90), wizṛan (Q20:100), ṣihṛan (Q25:54), ḥiǧṛan (Q25:22), ʾiṣṛahum (Q7:157), ʾiṣṛan (Q2:286), miṣṛa (Q10:87), miṣṛan (Q2:61), qiṭṛan (Q18:96), fiṭṛata ḷḷāhi (Q30:30), wiqṛan (Q51:2) and what is similar to these examples. So, the fatḥah is fully pronounced on the rāʾ for all of these because of the presence of an emphatic or uvular letter (ḥarf al-istiʿlāʾ) (i.e., ṣ, ṭ, ḍ, ḏ̣, q, ḫ, ġ), or because they are foreign words or because of the repeated rāʾ that carries a fatḥah or ḍammah.[62] The rule for the rāʾ carrying a ḍammah with a kasrah (before it) that is part of the word formation or an unvowelled yāʾ—for his (Warš’s) manner—is identical to the rule for (a rāʾ) carrying a fatḥah, for example, yusiŕŕūna (e.g., Q2:77), munḏiŕun (e.g., Q13:7), qadīŕun (e.g., Q2:20), baṣīŕun (e.g., Q2:96), ḫabīŕun (Q2:234), ḫayŕun (Q2:54), ḏikŕun (e.g., Q7:63), bikŕun (Q2:68) and what is like it. There is no disagreement in transmission from him on the pure pronunciation of the fatḥah of the rāʾ when the kasrah is not part of the word formation; for example, bi-ṛasūlin (Q61:6), li-ṛasūlin (e.g., Q3:183), bi-ṛašīdin (Q11:97), li-ṛabbika (e.g., Q37:149), bi-ṛuʾūsikum (Q5:6), li-ṛuqiyyika (Q17:93), and what is like it. He also applies ʾimālah to the fatḥah of the rāʾ in His speech in al-Mursalāt (Q77:32) bi-šaŕaŕin because of the ǧarrah on the second rāʾ that comes after it. But he pronounced it with pure fatḥ in His speech ʾulì ḍ-ḍaṛaŕi in al-Nisāʾ (Q4:95) because of the ḍād before it. The rest read with pure fatḥ (i.e., with emphatic ṛ) in all that has preceded.

footnotes.text: This ʾisnād for Šuʿbah is not present in U.4.5.1., but it is mentioned in the Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān (al-Dānī 2007, 345). This same transmission is also reported by Ibn Muǧāhid, where the ʾisnād is likewise not present in the ʾisnād section (Ibn Muǧāhid 1972, 261).

statements.heading: U.15.1. Subsection: [The Emphatic ṛāʾ Is Preceded by u or a]
statements.text: Every rāʾ which has fatḥah or ḍammah before it—whether an unvowelled letter intervenes between or not—(and the rāʾ itself) carries a fatḥah or a ḍammah or is unvowelled, it is emphatic (mufaḫḫam) with agreement (among all the readers); for example, ḥaḏaṛa l-mawtu (Q2:19), tuṛaddūna (Q9:94), yaṛuddūkum (Q3:149), al-ʿusṛati (Q9:117), al-yusṛa (Q2:185), maṛǧiʿukum (e.g., Q3:55), kuṛsiyyihī (Q38:34) and what is like it. Likewise, this occurs with an unvowelled rāʾ if it is preceded by an accidental kasrah (i.e., a vowel that connects the two words, epenthetic or otherwise, which is not part of the same word) or if an emphatic or uvular letter (ḥarf istiʿlāʾ, i.e., ḫ, ġ, q, ṭ, ṣ, ḏ̣, ḍ) occurs after it; for example, ʾam iṛtābū (Q24:50), yā bunayyi ṛkab maʿanā (Q11:42), ʾiṛṣādan (Q9:107), miṛṣādan (Q78:21), fiṛqatin (Q9:122), qiṛṭāsin (Q6:7), and what is like it. But if the kasrah that is before it is essential (i.e., part of the word), and there is no emphatic or uvular letter after it, then it is pronounced without emphasis, for example, miŕyatin (e.g., Q11:17), šiŕʿatan (Q5:48), fiŕʿawnv̆ (e.g., Q2:49), al-ʾiŕbati (Q24:31) and what is like it. It is like that (that it is not pronounced emphatically) for each rāʾ that carries a kasrah, whether the kasrah is essential (i.e., a case vowel as in al-musaḫḫaŕi, Q2:164) or accidental (i.e., epenthetic as in lam yuḏkaŕ ismu, Q6:121). There is no disagreement in that case on the lack of emphasis in connected speech. There is a rule for when (the rāʾ) comes at the end of a word and (its kasrah) is essential, in pause that I will present next, if God Almighty wills it.

statements.heading: U.15.2. Subsection: [Emphasis of ṛāʾ in Pause]
statements.text: As for pausing on the rāʾ that carries a fatḥah or a ḍammah or no vowel, when it occurs on the end of a word, it is as if it were pronounced in connected speech. So, if you pronounce it (in connected speech) as unemphatic, it will be unemphatic (in pause) and if you pronounced it (in connected speech) as emphatic, it will be emphatic (in pause), regardless of whether you hint at the final vowel ḍammah with rawm or ʾišmām[63] or do not hint at it, as long as it is not preceded by kasrah or yāʾ. In that case (i.e., when kasrah or yāʾ precedes), if you pause on it with rawm specifically (and not ʾišmām), in the manner of (all the readers) other than Warš, it is emphatic; without it (rawm) it is unemphatic (e.g., Q3:129 yaġfiṛᵘ# but with regular pause it is fa-yaġfiŕ# and with ʾišmām it is fa-yaġfiŕʷ#). As for the rāʾ that carries a kasrah, there are two options: if you apply rawm of the vowel, you pronounce it unemphatic, like in connected speech (e.g., Q2:164 al-musaḫḫaŕⁱ#); if you pause on it with no vowel, you make it emphatic (e.g., al-musaḫḫaṛ#) as long as there is no kasrah or unvowelled yāʾ before it, for example, in His speech munhamiŕ# (Q54:11), naḏīŕ# (e.g., Q5:19), nor a faṭhah that has undergone ʾimālah (e.g., an-nēŕ#, Q2:39),[64] or, for example, words like bi-šaŕaŕ# (Q77:32) according to the reading of Warš.[65] (In those cases) you pronounce it without emphasis in both connected speech and pause. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

The unusual use of the term wāqifah for no vowel, where al-Dānī usually uses the term ʾiskān, suggests that he is citing an older source with different vocabulary here. Indeed, ʾAbū al-ʾAzhar ʿAbd al-Ṣamad b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān wrote a book dedicated to the reading of Nāfiʿ as contrasted with that of Ḥamzah; these quotes probably come from this book (Hamdan 2018, 48, fn. 5). The riwāyah transmission of Warš in the Taysīr in fact comes through this cited ʾisnād, and probably took the form of the transmission of this book. See U.4.1.2. and the discussion in Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān (al-Dānī 2007, 1072).

statements.heading: U.16. The lāms
statements.text: Know that Warš makes the lām thick (i.e., emphatic) when it carries a fatḥah and before it was ṣād, ḏ̣āʾ or ṭāʾ and those three letters either carry a fatḥah or are unvowelled, and nothing else.[66] As for the ṣād, there are, for example, His words aṣ-ṣaḷātv̆ (e.g., Q2:3), muṣaḷḷan (Q2:125), fa-yuṣḷabu (Q12:41), fa-ṣaḷḷā (Q87:15) and what is like it. As for the ḏ̣āʾ, for example, wa-ʾiḏā ʾaḏ̣ḷama (Q2:20), yuḏ̣ḷamūna (e.g., Q2:281), bi-ḏ̣aḷḷāmin (e.g., Q3:182) and what is like it. As for the ṭāʾ, for example, aṭ-ṭaḷāqv̆ (Q2:227, 229), muʿaṭṭaḷatin (Q22:45), baṭaḷa (Q7:118) and what is like it. If a lām occurs with a ṣād in a word and it is the last word of a verse in a sūrah that ends its verses in yāʾ—for example, wa-lā ṣaḷḷā (Q75:31), fa-ṣaḷḷā (Q87:15)—both the thickening and thin pronunciation (tarqīq) are allowed (i.e., ṣaḷḷā, fa-ṣaḷḷā, or ṣallǟ, fa-ṣallǟ to agree with the rhyme). But the thin pronunciation is more regular so that the verses have the same sound.[67] Likewise, if the lām occurs at the end of a word and (one of) the three letters (i.e., ṣ, ḏ̣ and ṭ) comes before it, it is possible to pause on it with either thick or thin pronunciation (for example in a word like Q2:249 where both faṣaḷ# and faṣal# would be allowed); thickening is more regular, in accordance with (the pronunciation in) connected speech. The rest read it with fatḥ of this lām without full pronunciation (ʾišbāʿ),[68] whenever it occurs. They all agree on the thickening of the lām from the name of Aḷḷāh Almighty with fatḥah or ḍammah (before it), for example in His speech qāla ḷḷāhu (e.g., Q3:55), rusulu ḷḷāhi (Q6:125), qālù ḷḷāhumma (Q8:32) and what is like it, and on the thin pronunciation (of the lām), if a kasrah precedes it in connected speech, such as in the words of the Almighty bi-smi llāhi (e.g., Q1:1), al-ḥamdu li-llāhi (e.g., Q1:2), qul illāhumma (Q3:26; Q39:46) and what is like it. The remainder of the lāms are like this (i.e., unemphatic); there is no disagreement in their light pronunciation, whether they carry a vowel or not. Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: This ʾisnād is not in the Taysīr but it is mentioned in the Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān (al-Dānī 2007, 299).
See F.6:152. This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).
This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

statements.heading: U.17. The Pause at the Endings of Words
statements.text: Know that it is the custom of the readers to pause on the end of words that carry vowels in connected speech with no vowel and nothing else because that is the default. There is the transmission from the Kufans (ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥamzah) and ʾAbū ʿAmr in pause, where there is an allusion to the final vowel, regardless of whether it is a case vowel or part of the stem formation. This allusion is rawm or ʾišmām. As for the rest, no such an account comes from them at all. Most of our teachers from among the people of oral tradition prefer to pause in their manners with this allusion (to the case vowel), because of the clarity it gives. As for the meaning of rawm, it is when you weaken the sound of the vowel until it has gone almost completely, so that you will hear it as a concealed sound. A blind person can perceive it with his sense of hearing. As for the meaning of ʾišmām, you bunch up your lips after pronouncing the letter as vowelless according to the default (of pausing). A blind person cannot perceive that information, because it is seen with the eye and nothing else. For it is only a gesture with the articulator towards the vowel. So as for the rawm, according to the reciters,[69] it is applied to rafʿ, ḍamm, ḫafḍ or kasr, and they do not employ it for naṣb or fatḥ because of their lightness. As for ʾišmām, it only occurs for the rafʿ and ḍamm, and nothing else. By our word pairs, ‘the rafʿ, ḍamm, ḫafḍ, kasr, naṣb and fatḥ’, we intend the vowel of ʾiʿrāb that is changeable and the essential vowel of the word-formation, respectively.

statements.heading: U.17.1. Subsection: [Pause on Plural Pronouns, Epenthetic Vowels and the Feminine Ending]
statements.text: As for accidental vowels (i.e., epenthetic vowels) and the vowel of the mīm of plurality (i.e., -humū/-himū, -kumū, -tumū, humū, ʾantumū) in the manner of those who place a ḍammah on it as part of their principle,[70] it is incorrect to allude to them with rawm or ʾišmām, because they go away in pause by default. The same is true for the hāʾ of the feminine ending, which is not given rawm nor ʾišmām because it is not followed by a vowel. There is no part of it that has a vowel. Success comes from God.

statements.heading: U.18. The Pause on What Is Written in the rasm
statements.text: Know that the transmission we have from Nāfiʿ, ʾAbū ʿAmr and the Kufans, in terms of how they pause on what is written in the rasm, is well-established. We do not have such transmission at all from Ibn Kaṯīr or Ibn ʿĀmir. The choice of our imams is that they pause in their manner on the rasm in the way that it was transmitted from them (i.e., Nāfiʿ, ʾAbū ʿAmr and the Kufans). Disagreement has come down to us from them in certain places; I will mention them briefly, if God wills it. So for all those feminine endings that are written in the muṣḥafs originally with a tāʾ— for example, ابنت ,ايت ,ا৫৹أت ,غيبت ,ك္௛ت ,جنت ,ୋୗرت ,ଢ଼ඤرت ,رᄹᅋت ,نعمت and what is like it—al-Kisāʾī and ʾAbū ʿAmr pause on them with a hāʾ (i.e., niʿma/eh#, etc.). It is by analogy that it is taken to be the manner of Ibn Kaṯīr because al-Ḥasan b. al-Ḥubāb[71] asked al-Bazzī about the pause of His speech ṯamaratin min ʾakmāmihā (Q41:47) and he said it was with a hāʾ. Al-Kisāʾī pauses with a hāʾ for ( ৫৹ضاتi.e., marḍēh#) (e.g., Q2:207) whenever it occurs, and on ( اللت والعزىi.e., allāh#) (Q53:19), ( ذات ቢኟ໺ةi.e., ḏāh#) (Q27:60),[72] ( গজت ໥ഽنi.e., lāh#) (Q38:3), ( هኄኟات هኄኟاتi.e., hayhāh#) (Q23:36). Al-Bazzī follows him in this only for هኄኟات هኄኟات, so he pauses on both of them with a hāʾ. Ibn Kaṯīr and Ibn ʿĀmir pause on يابت with a hāʾ (i.e., yā ʾabah#) (e.g., Q12:4) whenever it occurs. The rest pause in these cases with a tāʾ for all of them, following the writing of the muṣḥaf. ʾAbū ʿAmr, along the transmission of Ibn al-Yazīdī from his father [al-Yazīdī] from him [ʾAbū ʿAmr] paused on His speech كၨ੎ن (ka-ʾayyin) in the whole Qurʾān with a yāʾ (i.e., ka-ʾayy#) (e.g., Q3:146). The rest pause on the nūn (i.e., ka-ʾayyin# or kāʾin#).[73] Al-Kisāʾī in the transmission of al-Dūrī and the other one (i.e., al-Layṯ) for His speech ԵឝԳ( ويكၨن اwaykaʾanna llāha) (Q28:82) and ويكၨنه (waykaʾannahū) (Q28:82) pauses separating at the yāʾ (i.e., way# kaʾanna). It was transmitted from ʾAbū ʿAmr that he pauses on the kāf (i.e., wayk# ʾanna). The rest pause on the word, connecting the elements together (i.e., waykaʾann# and waykaʾannah#). ʾAbū ʿAmr, in the transmission of ʾAbū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān [Ibn al-Yazīdī] from his father from him [ʾAbū ʿAmr] pauses in His speech জগ( ᄯᅋال هوfa-mā li-hā ʾulāʾi) (Q4:78), مال هذا الـكتب (mā li-hāḏà l-kitābi) (Q18:49), ( مال هذا اආ඗سولmā li-hāḏà r-rasūli) (Q25:7), ᄯᅋال اუჷ੎ن كفروا (fa-mā li-llaḏīna kafarū) (Q70:36) on the mā# without the lām in these four (places). There is disagreement on that point in transmission from al-Kisāʾī. It has been transmitted from him with pause on mā# and on the lām (i.e., māl#). The rest pause on the lām connecting the elements together (i.e., māl#). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī pause with His speech ا଻ୗا ࢇ࢜عوا (ʾayyan mā tadʿū) (Q17:110) on the ʾayyan without the mā and they substitute the tanwīn with an ʾalif (i.e., ʾayyā#). The rest pause on mā (i.e., ʾayyam⸗mā#).[74] ʾAbū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī pause with His speech ايه اঐঔومنഽنin al-Nūr (Q24:31), ൿൢ يايه الساin al-Zuḫruf (Q43:49), ايه الثقேௌن in al-Raḥmān (Q55:31) with an ʾalif for the three of them (i.e., ʾayyuhā#). The rest pause without an ʾalif (i.e., ʾayyuh#). Al-Kisāʾī is the only one who pauses on واد اࡀ࡛࡬ل (Q27:18) with a yāʾ (i.e., wādī#); the rest pause without the yāʾ (i.e., wād#). As for the remaining words in this topic, they will come in their place (in the part on the Farš al-ḥurūf, F.2.‒114.), if God Almighty wills it.

footnotes.text: As opposed to the same phrase in Q7:88 in the story of Šuʿayb.
This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

statements.heading: U.18.1. Subsection
statements.text: Al-Bazzī is alone in adding a hāʾ of silence while pausing on mā (i.e., mah#) when it is a question word and when it is next to a preposition; for example, in His speech fa-li-ma taqtulūna (Q2:91), li-ma taqūlūna (Q61:2), fī-ma ʾanta (Q79:43), mim-ma ḫuliqa (Q86:5), fa-bima tubašširūna (Q15:54), bi-ma yarǧiʿu (Q27:35), ʿam-ma yatasāʾalūna (Q78:1) and what is like it, so he pauses (them as) fa-li-mah#, fī-mah#, mim-mah#, fa-bi-mah#, bi-mah# and ʿammah#. The rest pause with a mīm not followed by a vowel (i.e., lim#, fīm#, mim#, fabim#, bim#, ʿamm#). Success comes from God.

statements.heading: U.19. The Manner of Ḥamzah on the Silence on the Vowellessness before the hamzah
statements.text: Know that Ḥamzah, in the transmission of Ḫalaf, is silent after an unvowelled letter at the end of a word, if it is not a long vowel, and a hamzah comes after it (in the next word), with a brief silence without a strong break (i.e., taking a breath) in order to articulate the hamzah clearly. This is the case for example in His speech man <silence> ʾāmana (Q2:62), hal <silence> ʾatēka (Q20:9), ʿalayhum <silence> ʾa-ʾanḏartahum <silence> ʾam (Q2:6; Q36:10), nabaʾa bnay <silence> ʾādama (Q5:27), ḫalaw <silence> ʾilā šayāṭīnahum (Q2:14), qad <silence> ʾaflaḥa (e.g., Q20:64), min šay<silence>ʾin[75] <silence> ʾiḏ (Q46:26), ḥāmiyatun <silence> // ʾalhēkum (Q101:11–Q102:1)[76] and what is like it. Like that is al-<silence>ʾāḫiratv̆ (e.g., Q2:4), al-<silence>ʾarḍv̆ (Q2:11), al-<silence>ʾāzifatv̆ (Q40:18; Q53:57), al-<silence>ʾāna (e.g., Q2:71) and what is like it, because it behaves as if it is in between two words. If there is a vowelless letter with a hamzah within a word, then you do not introduce a silence on the vowelless letter except for one general rule, and it is for what belongs to the word šayʾ<silence>u/in and šayʾ<silence>an and nothing else. ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: I recited it to ʾAbū al-Ḥasan [Ibn Ġalbūn] in both (i.e., Ḥamzah’s) transmissions with a silence on the lām of the definite article and šayʾ and šayʾan whenever they occur and nothing else.[77] The rest read in context the sākin followed by hamzah without a silence. The manner of Warš has already been mentioned before. Success comes from God.

statements.heading: U.20. Their Manners in the fatḥ and the ʾiskān of the yāʾs of Annexation
statements.text: Know that there is a group (of words with the 1sg. suffix) which are disagreed upon. There are 214 yāʾs (like that): 1. In the case of a (following) hamzah that carries the fatḥah there are 99; 2. In the case of a (following hamzah) that carries a kasrah there are 52; 3. In the case of a (following hamzah) that carries a ḍammah there are ten; 4. In the case of a (following) ʾalif al-waṣl which has a lām after it there are 16; 5. In the case (of a following ʾalif al-waṣl that) does not have a lām after it there are seven. 6. And with those words that remain, altogether, there are 30. We will mention it in what is to come in each sūrah in this group with the disagreements that are in it, explained for each yāʾ. We will collect here their general principles and point out exceptions to them, so that (these exceptions) can be remembered together and (otherwise) analogy can be applied to what is transmitted, if God wills it.

statements.heading: U.20.1. Subsection: [The yāʾ Followed by a hamzah Carrying a fatḥah]
statements.text: Know that to every yāʾ after which there is a hamzah that carries a fatḥah—for example in His speech ʾinnī ʾaʿlamu (e.g., Q2:30), ʾannī ʾaḫluqu (Q3:49), lī ʾan ʾaqūla (Q5:116), and what is like it—the two of the holy cities (Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kaṯīr) and ʾAbū ʿAmr apply a fatḥah whenever it occurs (i.e., ʾinniya ʾaʿlamu, ʾanniya ʾaḫluqu, liya ʾan ʾaqūla). Ibn Kaṯīr is alone in applying the fatḥah to three yāʾs: in al-Baqarah (Q2:152) fa-ḏkurūniya ʾaḏkurkumū, in Ġāfir ḏarūniya ʾaqtul (Q40:26) and udʿūniya ʾastaǧib lakumū (Q40:60). He violates his principle in both of his transmissions after this (condition) in ten places, so he does not place a vowel on the yāʾ on it (even though the principle predicts it): 1. in ʾĀl ʿImrān (Q3:41) and 2. Maryam (Q19:10) iǧʿal lī ʾāyatan, 3. in Hūd (Q11:78) fī ḍayfī ʾalyasa, 4. in Yūsuf (Q12:36) ʾinnī ʾarāniya 5. in two places (in this verse); I mean the yāʾ of ʾinnī, without the one of ʾarāniya (which does receive a fatḥah), 6. and ḥattā yaʾḏunu lī ʾabiya (Q12:80), I mean the yāʾ of lī, 7. and sabīlī ʾadʿū (Q12:108), 8. in Kahf (Q18:102) min dūnī ʾawliyāʾa, 9. in Ṭāhā (Q20:26) yassir lī ʾamrī, and 10. in al-Naml (Q27:40) li-yabluwanī ʾāškuru. Qunbul transmitting from him (Ibn Kaṯīr) adds seven locations where he does not place a vowel on the yāʾ: 1. in Hūd (Q11:29) 2. and al-ʾAḥqāf (Q46:23) wa-lākinnī ʾarānī, 3. in faṭaranī ʾa-fa-lā (Q11:51) 4. and ʾinnī ʾarākumū (Q11:84), 5. in al-Naml (Q27:19) ʾawziʿnī ʾan, and 6. in al-Zuḫruf (Q43:51) min taḥtī ʾa-fa-lā. 7. ʾAbū Rabīʿah transmits from Qunbul and from al-Bazzī in al-Qaṣaṣ (Q28:78) ʿindī ʾa-wa-lam with no vowel (on the yāʾ). He is alone (in doing so).[78] Nāfiʿ is alone in applying the fatḥah on two yāʾs: 1. in Yūsuf (Q12:108) hāḏihī sabīliya ʾadʿū 2. and in al-Naml (Q27:40) li-yabluwaniya ʾā(.a)škuru. Warš transmits from him ʾawziʿniya (Q27:19; Q46:15) in two sūrahs with a fatḥah. Qālūn transmits from him the two words with no vowel (on the yāʾ) (i.e., ʾawziʿnī). ʾAbū ʿAmr violates his principle in nine places. So, he does not apply a vowel to the yāʾ: 1. in Hūd (Q11:51) faṭaranī ʾa-fa-lā, 2. in Yūsuf la-yaḥzununī ʾan (Q12:31) 3. and sabīlī ʾadʿū (Q12:108), 4. in Ṭāhā (Q20:125) lima ḥašartanī ʾaʿmā, 5. in al-Naml ʾawziʿnī ʾan (Q27:19) 6. and li-yabluwanī ʾā-.aškuru (Q27:40), 7. in al-Zumar (Q39:64) taʾ/āmurunnī ʾaʿbudu, 8. in al-ʾAḥqāf ʾawziʿnī ʾan (Q46:15) 9. and ʾataʿidāninī ʾan (Q46:17). Ibn ʿĀmir applied the fatḥah in both of his transmissions to eight yāʾs: 1. laʿalliya whenever it occurs (Q12:46; 2. Q20:10; 3. Q23:100; 4. Q28:29, 5. 38; 6. Q40:36), 7. in al-Tawbah (Q9:83) maʿiya ʾabadan, 8. in al-Mulk (Q67:28) wa-man maʿiya ʾaw raḥimanā and nothing else. Ibn Ḏakwān, transmitting from him, adds to it in Hūd (Q11:92) ʾa-rahṭiya ʾaʿazzu. Hišām, transmitting from him, adds to it mā liya ʾadʿūkum in Ġāfir (Q40:41). Ḥafṣ applies a fatḥah to two yāʾs in al-Tawbah (Q9:83) and al-Mulk (67:28) maʿiya and nothing else. The rest does not apply a vowel to the yāʾ (in this context) in all of the Qurʾān.

footnotes.text: This is according to the general principle of Ibn Kaṯīr that ʾa-ʾā is pronounced with the softening of the second hamzah (see section U.11.1.).

statements.heading: U.20.2. Subsection: [The yāʾ Followed by a hamzah Carrying a kasrah]
statements.text: For each yāʾ with a hamzah that carries a kasrah after it—for example, in the words of the Almighty minniya ʾillā (Q2:249), minniya ʾinnaka (Q3:35), yadiya ʾilayka (Q5:28), rabbiya ʾilā ṣirāṭin (Q6:161) and what is like it—Nāfiʿ and ʾAbū ʿAmr add a fatḥah to it in all of the Qurʾān. Nāfiʿ is alone, excluding him (ʾAbū ʿAmr), in applying the fatḥah in eight places: 1. in ʾĀl ʿImrān (Q3:52), and 2. al-Ṣaff (Q61:41) min ʾanṣāriya ʾilà ḷḷāhi, 3. in al-Ḥiǧr (Q15:71) banātiya ʾin kuntum, 4. in al-Kahf (Q18:69), 5. al-Qaṣaṣ (Q28:27) and 6. al-Ṣāffāt (Q37:102) sa-taǧiduniya ʾin šāʾa ḷḷāhu, 7. in al-Šuʿarāʾ (Q26:52) bi-ʿibādiya ʾinnakum, and 8. in Ṣād (Q38:78) laʿnatiya ʾilā. Warš transmitting from him adds to it in Yūsuf (Q12:100) wa-biya ʾiḫwatiya ʾinna. Ibn Kaṯīr applies the fatḥah from among these on two yāʾs: 1. in Yūsuf (Q12:38) ʾābāʾiya ʾibrāhīma 2. and in Nūḥ (Q71:6) duʿāʾiya ʾillā and nothing else. Ibn ʿĀmir applies the fatḥah to 15 yāʾs: 1. ʾaǧriya ʾillā whenever it occurs (Q10:72; 2. Q11:29, 3. 51; 4. Q26:109, 5. 127, 6. 145, 7. 164, 8. 180; 9. Q34:47), 10. in Māʾidah (Q5:116) wa-ʾummiya ʾilāhayni, 11. in Hūd (Q11:88) wa-mā tawfīqiya ʾillā, 12. in Yūsuf wa-ḥuzniya ʾilā ḷḷāhi (Q12:86) 13. and ʾābāʾiya ʾibrāhīma (Q12:38), 14. in al-Muǧādilah (Q58:21) wa-rusuliya ʾinna ḷḷāha, 15. in Nūḥ (Q71:6) duʿāʾiya ʾillā and nothing else. Ḥafṣ applies the fatḥah to the yāʾ of ʾaǧriya ʾillā (e.g., Q10:72) whenever it occurs. In Māʾidah yadiya ʾilayka (Q5:28) and wa-ʾummiya ʾilāhayni (Q5:116) and nothing else. The rest does not apply a vowel to the yāʾ (in this context) in all the Qurʾān.

statements.heading: U.20.3. Subsection: [The yāʾ with a hamzah Carrying a ḍammah after It]
statements.text: For each yāʾ with a hamzah that carries a ḍammah after it—for example, in the words of the Almighty wa-ʾinniya ʾuʿīḍuhā bika (Q3:36), ʾinniya ʾumirtu (Q6:14; Q39:11) and what is like it—Nāfiʿ applies a fatḥah to it whenever it occurs. The rest does not apply a vowel to the yāʾ (in this context) in all the Qurʾān.

statements.heading: U.20.4. Subsection: [The yāʾ with a Definite Article after It]
statements.text: For each yāʾ with an ʾalif and a lām after it—for example in the words of the Almighty rabbì llaḏī (Q2:258), ʾātānì l-kitāba (Q19:30), ʿibādì ṣ-ṣāliḥūna (Q21:105) and what is like it—Ḥamzah does not place a vowel on it whenever it occurs. Al-Kisāʾī follows him in not placing a vowel (on the yāʾ) in three places: 1. in ʾIbrāhīm (Q14:31) qul li-ʿibādì llaḏīna, 2. in ʿAnkabūt (Q29:56) 3. and in al-Zumar (Q39:53) yāʿ ibādì llaḏīna. ʾAbū ʿAmr follows him in two places: 1. in ʿAnkabūt (Q29:56), 2. in al-Zumar (Q39:53) and nothing else. Ibn ʿĀmir follows him in also two places: 1. in al-ʾAʿrāf (Q7:146) ʿan ʾāyātì llaḏīna 2. and in ʾIbrāhīm (Q14:31) qul li-ʿibādì llaḏīna only. Ḥafṣ follows him for His words in al-Baqarah (Q2:124) ʿahdì ḏ̣-ḏ̣ālimīna and nothing else. The rest place the fatḥah on the yāʾ whenever it occurs. ʾAbū Šuʿayb [al-Sūsī] is unique in applying the fatḥah and retaining the yāʾ in pause without a vowel (a yāʾ that is absent in the rasm) in al-Zumar (Q39:17–18) fa-baššir ʿibādiya // llaḏīna (and fa-baššir ʿibādī# in pause). The rest removed (the yāʾ) in connected speech and pause.[79] The disagreement concerning the words of the Almighty fa-mā ʾātānì llāhu (Q28:36) will come in its position (in the specific variants section) if God wills it. All of them (i.e., including Ḥamzah) apply the fatḥah to the yāʾ in three phrases regularly (i.e., whenever they occur) and nine individual words. So, the regular phrases are His words: 1. niʿmatiya llatī (Q2:40, 47, 122), 2. ḥasbiya ḷḷāhu (Q9:129; Q39:38), and 3. šurakāʾiya llaḏīna (Q16:27; Q18:52; Q28:62, 74) whenever they occur. The (specific) words are: 1. the first in ʾĀl ʿImrān wa-qad balaġaniya l-kibaru (Q3:40), 2. in al-ʾAʿrāf fa-lā tušmit biya l-ʾaʿdāʾa (Q7:150), 3. mā massaniya s-sūʾu (Q7:188) and 4. ʾinna waliyyiya ḷḷāhu (Q7:196), 5. in al-Ḥiǧr massaniya l-kibaru (Q15:54), 6. in Sabaʾ ʾarūniya llaḏīna (Q34:27), 7. in al-Muʾmin rabbiya ḷḷāhu (Q40:28) and 8. lammā ǧāʾaniya l-bayyinātu (Q40:66), and 9. in al-Taḥrīm nabbaʾaniya l-ʿalīmu l-ḫabīru (Q66:3).

footnotes.text: The Pretzl edition has ‘ ੀඟففتഽنtwo softened hamzahs’, but this is certainly a mistake. It should read ੀචققتഽن instead, correct in the al-Ḍāmin edition (al-Dānī 2008a, 292).

statements.heading: U.20.5. Subsection: [The yāʾ Followed by an ʾalif al-waṣl Which Does Not Belong to the Definite Article]
statements.text: As for each yāʾ with an isolated ʾalif after it, for example, in the words ʾinnì ṣṭafaytuka (Q7:144), ʾaḫì // šdud (Q20:30) and what is like it (the treatment is as follows): Nāfiʿ does not pronounce a vowel after the yāʾ for three of those (but applies fatḥah to all other cases): 1. ʾinnì ṣṭafaytuka (Q7:144), 2. ʾaḫì // šdud (Q20:30–31), 3. yā laytanì ttaḫattu (Q25:27) and nothing else (i.e., all other cases were pronounced with -iya). Ibn Kaṯīr only pronounces (the yāʾ) of yā laytanì ttaḫaḏtu (Q25:27) vowelless in both of his transmissions, and nowhere else (where he applies fatḥah instead). In the transmission of Qunbul (there is also) ʾinna qawmì ttaḫaḏū (Q25:30) and nothing else (i.e., all other cases were pronounced with -iya). ʾAbū ʿAmr applies the fatḥah to the yāʾ whenever it occurs. Šuʿbah applies the fatḥah only to min baʿdiya smuhū (Q61:6). The rest does not apply a vowel to the yāʾ whenever it occurs.

statements.heading: U.20.6. Subsection: [The Remainder]
statements.text: As for what comes with a yāʾ among what remains of the letters of the alphabet (following it), for example, in the words of the Almighty baytī (e.g., Q2:125), waǧhī (Q3:20; Q6:79), mamātī (Q6:162), lī (e.g., Q2:152) and what is like it: Nāfiʿ, in both of his transmissions, applies a fatḥah to seven of these: 1. baytiya in al-Baqarah (Q2:125), 2. and al-Ḥaǧǧ (Q22:26), 3. waǧhiya in ʾĀl ʿImrān (Q3:20) 4. and al-ʾAnʿām (Q6:79), 5. mamātiya li-llāhi in that (same sūrah, Q6:162), 6. māliya in Yā-Sīn (Q36:22), and 7. wa-liya dīni in al-Kāfirūn (Q109:6). Warš, transmitting from him, added to it, and so he applies a fatḥah to four (more words): 1. in al-Baqarah li-yūminū biya (Q2:186), 2. in Ṭā-Hā (Q20:18) wa-liya fīhā, 3. in al-Šuʿarāʾ (Q26:118) wa-man maʿiya, 4. and in al-Duḫān (Q44:21) liya fa-ʿtazilūni. Ibn Kaṯīr applies fatḥah to five words: 1. maḥyāya in al-ʾAnʿām (Q6:162), 2. min warāʾiya in Maryam (Q19:5), 3. māliya in al-Naml (Q28:20), 4. and Yā-Sīn (Q36:22), and 5. ʾayna šurakāʾiya in Fuṣṣilat (Q51:47). Al-Bazzī adds to that with disagreement among his transmitters wa-liya dīni in al-Kāfirūn (Q109:6). ʾAbū ʿAmr applies the fatḥah to two yāʾs: 1. maḥyāya (Q6:162) in al-ʾAnʿām 2. and māliya in Yā-Sīn (Q36:22) and nothing else. Ibn ʿĀmir applies fatḥah—in both of his transmissions—to six words: 1. waǧhiya in the two places (where it occurs) (Q3:20; 2. Q6:79), 3. in al-ʾAnʿām ṣirāṭiya (Q6:153) and 4. maḥyāya (Q6:162), 5. in al-ʿAnkabūt (Q29:56) ʾinna ʾarḍiya 6. and māliya in Yā-Sīn (Q36:22). Hišām adds to this baytiya (e.g., Q2:125) whenever it occurs, māliya in al-Naml (Q28:20) and wa-liya dīni in al-Kāfirūn (Q109:6). Ḥafṣ applies fatḥah to the yāʾ of baytiya (e.g., Q2:125), waǧhiya (Q3:20; Q6:79), maʿiya (e.g., Q7:105) in the whole Qurʾān, maḥyāya in al-ʾAnʿām (Q6:162), liya in ʾIbrāhīm (Q14:22), Ṭā-Hā (Q20:18), al-Naml (Q27:20), Yā-Sīn (36:22), in two places in Ṣād (Q38:23, 69) and in al-Kāfirūn (Q109:6)—in these seven and nothing else. ʾAbū Bakr and Al-Kisāʾī applies the fatḥah (to the yāʾ) in three cases: 1. maḥyāya (Q6:162), 2. liya in al-Naml (Q27:20) and 3. Yā-Sīn (Q36:22) and nothing else. Ḥamzah applies fatḥah to maḥyāya (Q6:162) only. He does not apply fatḥah anywhere else from this group of yāʾs that is disagreed upon. Success comes from God.

statements.heading: U.21. Their Principles Concerning the yāʾs Removed from the rasm
statements.text: Know that the total number of words disagreed upon in this category is 61 yāʾs and no more.

statements.heading: U.21.1. [Specifics of Nāfiʿ]
statements.text: So Nāfiʿ, in the transmission of Warš, retains (the yāʾ) of these in connected speech in 47 cases, but not in pause. In the transmission of Qālūn, he retains (the yāʾ) of these in 20 (cases). There was disagreement in the transmission from Qālūn on two of them: at-talāqi (Q40:15) and at-tanādi (Q40:32) in Ġāfir.

statements.heading: U.21.2. [Specifics of Ibn Kaṯīr]
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr retains (the yāʾ) in both of his transmissions, in connected speech and in pause, in 21 cases. Qunbul and al-Bazzī disagree in their transmission from him at six junctures: 1. wa-taqabbal duʿāʾī̆ (Q14:40) in ʾIbrāhīm, 2. yadʿu d-dāʿī̆ (Q54:6) in al-Qamar, 3. bi-l-wādī̆ (Q89:9), 4. ʾakramanī̆ (Q89:15) and 5. ʾahānanī̆ (Q89:16) in al-Faǧr. Al-Bazzī retains (the yāʾ) of these five in connected speech and pause. Qunbul retains (the yāʾ) of bi-l-wādī (Q89:9) in connected speech and, with disagreement, in pause. He removes (the yāʾ) of the (remaining) four in connected speech and pause. Qunbul retains (the yāʾ) in ʾinnahū man yattaqī wa-yaṣbir (Q12:90) in Yūsuf in connected speech and pause. Al-Bazzī removes (the yāʾ) in connected speech and pause (i.e., yattaqi/yattaq#).

statements.heading: U.21.3. [Specifics of ʾAbū ʿAmr]
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr (retains the yāʾ) of those only in connected speech in 34 cases. He allows both ways in the words of the Almighty ʾakramanī̆ (Q89:15) and ʾahānanī̆ (Q89:16), but what is adopted is the removal of these two, because they are the ends of two verses.

statements.heading: U.21.4. [Specifics of al-Kisāʾī]
statements.text: Al-Kisāʾī retains (the yāʾ) of these in connected speech for two yāʾs: 1. yawma yaʾtī in Hūd (Q11:105) 2. and mā kunnā nabġī in al-Kahf (Q18:64) and nothing else.

statements.heading: U.21.5. [Specifics of Ḥamzah]
statements.text: Ḥamzah retains the yāʾ in connected speech only in the speech of the Almighty taqabbal duʿāʾī (Q14:40) in ʾIbrāhīm. He retains it in connected speech and pause in the speech of the Almighty in al-Naml ʾa-tumiddūnanī (Q27:36) and nothing else.

statements.heading: U.21.6. [Specifics of ʿĀṣim]
statements.text: ʿĀṣim removes all of them in connected speech and pause. But they disagree in transmission from him for two yāʾs. The first of these is in al-Naml fa-mā ʾātāniya ḷḷāhu (Q27:36). Ḥafṣ (retains it) and applies fatḥah to it in connected speech and retains it with no vowel in pause (i.e., ʾātānī#). ʾAbū Bakr removes it in connected speech and pause (i.e., ʾātāni, ʾātān#). The second is in al-Zuḫruf yā ʿibādiya lā ḫawfun (Q43:68). ʾAbū Bakr (retains it) and applies the fatḥah to it in connected speech and retains it with no vowel in pause (i.e., yā ʿibādī#). Ḥafṣ removes it in connected speech and pause (i.e., yā ʿibādi, yā ʿibād#).

statements.heading: U.21.7. [Specifics of Ibn ʿĀmir]
statements.text: Ibn ʿĀmir, in the transmission of Hišām, retains the yāʾ in connected speech and pause in the speech of the Almighty ṯumma kīdūnī(#) (Q7:195) in al-ʾAʿrāf. He removes the yāʾ in connected speech and pause in the transmission of Ibn Ḏakwān with disagreement according to the transmission from al-ʾAḫfaš from him in the speech of the Almighty in al-Kahf fa-lā tasʾalannī(#) (Q18:70) and nothing else. And all of this which has been transmitted of those in terms of disagreement will also return at the end of the sūrahs if God wills it.

statements.heading: U.22. [Conclusion of the ʾUṣūl]
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: We have mentioned these regular principles in order to explain them as much as it is possible in this summary, using few words but conveying the meaning, in order to allow analogous expansion (of the rules) over what has been transmitted and to apply what we have explained. We will now begin to mention the specific wordings sūrah by sūrah from the beginning of the Qurʾān until the end if God Almighty wills it. Success comes from God. F. THE CHAPTER THAT MENTIONS THE SPECIFIC VARIANTS

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: The two of the holy cities and ʾAbū ʿAmr read wa-mā yuḫādiʿūna with an ʾalif, ḍammah on the yāʾ, fatḥah on the ḫāʾ and kasrah on the dāl. The rest read it without the ʾalif, and with fatḥah on the yāʾ and dāl (i.e., yaḫdaʿūna).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: The Kufans read yakḏibūna with fatḥah on the yāʾ and without gemination. The rest read it with ḍammah (on the yāʾ) and gemination (i.e., yukaḏḏibūna).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Al-Kisāʾī and Hišām read qǖla, ġǖḍa, ǧǖʾa with ʾišmām al-ḍamm on the first root letter of those (verbs), whenever they occur. The rest read it with the pure pronunciation of the kasrah (i.e., qīla, ġīḍa, ǧīʾa).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Warš lengthens the yāʾ of šayyyyʾ, šayyyyʾan, ka-hayyyyʾati and what is like it. It is also like that for the wāw of as-sawwwwʾi and sawwwwʾah and what is like it, whenever what stands before it carries a fatḥah, and what comes after it is a hamzah within the same word, except mawʾilan (Q18:85) and al-mawʾūdah (Q81:8). Ḥamzah pauses on the yāʾ of šay<pause>ʾ and šay<pause>ʾan in continuous speech specifically. The rest do not lengthen it nor pause on it.

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Qālūn, ʾAbū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī place no vowel on the hāʾ of huwa and hiya whenever wa-, fa- or la- precedes it (i.e., wa-hwa, fa-hya, la-hwa, etc.). Qālūn and al-Kisāʾī also do not place a vowel on it when ṯumma occurs before it in His speech ṯumma hwa yawmu lqiyāmati (Q28:61). The rest place a vowel on the hāʾ (of both huwa and hiya) (i.e., wa-huwa, fa-hiya, la-huwa, ṯumma huwa, etc.).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah reads fa-ʾazālahumā with ʾalif and without gemination. The rest read it without ʾalif and with gemination (i.e., fa-ʾazallahumā).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr reads fa-talaqqā ʾādama with naṣb, and kalimātun with rafʿ (i.e., fa-talaqqā ʾādama min rabbihī kalimātun). The rest read ʾādamu with rafʿ, and kasrah on the tāʾ (of kalimātin) (i.e., fa-talaqqā ʾādamu min rabbihī kalimātin).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū ʿAmr read wa-lā tuqbalu minhā with tāʾ. The rest read it with yāʾ (i.e., yuqbalu).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr reads wa-ʾiḏ waʿadnā and wa-waʿadnākum without ʾalif whenever it occurs. The rest read it with ʾalif (i.e., wa-ʾiḏ wāʿadnā and wa-wāʿadnākum).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr reads bāriʾĭkum in both cases, yaʾ/āmurŭkum, yaʾ/āmurŭhum, yanṣurŭkum and yušʿirŭkum with ultrashort pronunciation of the vowel for all of these in the manner (ṭarīq) of the Baghdadis (i.e., the transmitters from al-Dūrī). This is the preference of Sībawayh.[1] The manner (ṭarīq) of the Raqqans (i.e., the transmitters from al-Sūsī) and others is the dropping of the vowel (i.e., bāriʾkum, yaʾ/āmurkum, etc.). This is transmitted solely from ʾAbū ʿAmr, and with that I recited it to [ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ǧaʿfar] al-Fārisī according to his recitation to ʾAbū Ṭāhir. The rest pronounce the vowels (of these words) completely (i.e., bāriʾikum(ū), yaʾ/āmurukum(ū), etc.).

footnotes.text: This is a reference to Sībawayh (1988, IV:202) who explicitly tells us that ʾAbū ʿAmr reads it with an ultrashort vowel, not with no vowel.

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads yuġfar lakum with yāʾ that carries a ḍammah and with fatḥah on the fāʾ, and Ibn ʿĀmir with tāʾ (i.e., tuġfar). The rest reads it with nūn that carries a fatḥah and with kasrah on the fāʾ (i.e., naġfir).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʿalayhu/imu/i ḏ-ḏillah and what is related to it has already been mentioned.[2] Nāfiʿ reads an-nabīʾīna, al-(ʾ)anbiʾāʾ, an-nubūʾah and an-nabīʾ with hamzah whenever it occurs. Qālūn drops the hamzah in His speech in al-ʾAḥzāb (Q33): li-n-nabī ʾin ʾarāda (Q33:50) and biyūta n-nabī ʾillā ʾan (Q33:53) in these two places in connected speech only, according to his general principle employed when two hamzahs that both carry a kasrah.[3] The rest reads it without hamzah (i.e., an-nabiyyīna, al-ʾanbiyāʾ, an-nubuwwah, an-nabiyy).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads aṣ-ṣābīna and aṣ-ṣābūna without hamzah whenever they occur. The rest read it with hamzah (i.e., aṣ-ṣābiʾīna and aṣ-ṣābiʾūna).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥafṣ reads huzuwan and kufuwan with ḍammah on the zāy and fāʾ without hamzah. Ḥamzah does not place a vowel on the zāy and fāʾ, and pronounces the hamzah in connected speech. When he pauses on it, he replaces the hamzah with wāw, following the written text as a representation (taqdīran) for the ḍammah of the letter that carries no vowel before it (i.e., in connected speech huzʾan and kufʾan, while in pause huzwā# and kufwā#). The rest read it with ḍammah and hamzah (i.e., huzuʾan, kufuʾan).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr reads the ʿammā yaʿmalūna that is followed by ʾa-fa-taṭmaʿūna (Q2:75) with yāʾ. The two of the holy cities and ʾAbū Bakr read the ʿammā yaʿmalūna (Q2:75) that is followed by ʾulāʾika llaḏīna (Q2:76) with a yāʾ. The rest read both with tāʾ (i.e., ʿammā taʿmalūna in Q2:74, 75).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads ḫaṭīʾātuhū in the plural, while the rest read it in the singular (i.e., ḫaṭīʾatuhū).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read lā yaʿbudūna ʾillà ḷḷāh with yāʾ, and the rest read it with tāʾ (i.e., taʿbudūna). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read li-n-nāsi ḥasanan with fatḥah on the ḥāʾ and sīn, and the rest read it with ḍammah on the ḥāʾ and no vowel on the sīn (i.e., ḥusnan).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: The Kufans read taḏ̣āharūna with no gemination of the ḏ̣āʾ, and it is like that in al-Taḥrīm (Q66:4) wa-ʾin taḏ̣āharā ʿalayhi. The rest read it with gemination (i.e., taḏ̣ḏ̣āharūna, wa-ʾin taḏ̣ḏ̣āharā). Ḥamzah reads ʾasrē without ʾalif according to the pattern faʿlē, and the rest read it with ʾalif according to the pattern fuʿālā/ǟ/ē (i.e., ʾusārā/ǟ/ē). Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read tufādūhum(ū) with ʾalif and ḍammah on the tāʾ. The rest read it without ʾalif and with fatḥah on the tāʾ (i.e., tafdūhum(ū)).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr reads al-quds without an extra vowel whenever it occurs, and the rest read it with an extra vowel (i.e., al-qudus).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū ʿAmr read yunzilu, tunzilu and nunzilu, whenever it occurs in the imperfect, with ḍammah of the first letter and without gemination. Ibn Kaṯīr makes an exception for wa-mimmā nunazziluhū in al-Ḥiǧr (Q15:21), nunazzilu min al-qurāni (Q17:82) and ḥattā tunazzilu ʿalaynā (Q17:93) in Ṣubḥān. ʾAbū ʿAmr makes an exception for ʿalā ʾan yunazzilu ʾāyatan in al-ʾAnʿām (Q6:37) and the one which was in al-Ḥiǧr, which they agree upon. The rest read with gemination (i.e., yunazzilu, tunazzilu, nunazzilu), but Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī make an exception to that for two words in Luqmān, yunzilu l-ġayṯa (Q31:34), and in ʿAyn-Sīn-Qāf,[4] allaḏī yunzilu l-ġayṯa (Q42:28), which they pronounce ungeminated.

footnotes.text: This is one of the alternative names of Sūrat al-Šūrā (Kandil 1992, 51).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr reads ǧabrīl here and in al-Taḥrīm (Q66:4), with fatḥah on the ǧīm and kasra on the rāʾ without hamzah. ʾAbū Bakr reads it with fatḥah on the ǧīm and the rāʾ, and with hamzah that carries kasrah without a (following) yāʾ (i.e., ǧabraʾil). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī are similar, except that they place a yāʾ after the hamzah (i.e., ǧabraʾīl). The rest read it with kasrah on the ǧīm and the rāʾ without a hamzah (i.e., ǧibrīl).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥafṣ and ʾAbū ʿAmr read wa-mīkāla without hamzah and without yāʾ. Nāfiʿ reads it with hamzah and without yāʾ (i.e., mīkāʾila). The rest read it with yāʾ after the hamzah (i.e., mīkāʾīla).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read wa-lākin iš-šayāṭīnu and in al-ʾAnfāl (Q8:17) wa-lākin illāhu qatalahum and wa-lākin illāhu ramā/ē in three places, with kasrah of the nūn and the rafʿ of the word after it. The rest read it with fatḥah on the geminated nūn and naṣb of what is after it (i.e., wa-lākinna š-šayāṭina, wa-lākinna ḷḷāha, wa-lākinna ḷḷāha).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn ʿĀmir reads mā nunsiḫ min ʾāyatin with ḍammah on the nūn and kasrah on the sīn. The rest read it with fatḥah on both (i.e., nansaḫ). Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū ʿAmr read ʾaw nansaʾhā with hamzah and fatḥah on the nūn and sīn. The rest read it without hamzah, with ḍammah on the nūn and kasrah on the sīn (i.e., nunsihā).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn ʿĀmir reads qālù ttaḫaḏa ḷḷāhu without wāw and the rest read wa-qālū with wāw.[5]

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn ʿĀmir reads fa-yakūna here, in ʾĀl ʿImrān at fa-yakūna // wa-nuʿallimuhū[6] (Q3:47), in al-Naḥl (Q16:40), Maryam (Q19:35), Yā-Sīn (Q36:82) and Ġāfir (Q40:68)—in all these six places with the naṣb of the nūn. Al-Kisāʾī follows him in al-Naḥl and Yā-Sīn only. The rest read it with rafʿ (i.e., fa-yakūnu).

footnotes.text: The reading of wa-nuʿallimuhū is also disagreed upon, see F.3:48.

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads wa-lā tasʾal with fatḥah on the tāʾ and ǧazm of the lām. The rest read it with ḍammah of the tāʾ and rafʿ (i.e., wa-lā tusʾalu).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read wa-ttaḫaḏū with fatḥah on the ḫāʾ and the rest read it with kasrah (i.e., wa-ttaḫiḏū).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn ʿĀmir reads fa-ʾumtiʿuhū ungeminated and the rest read it geminated (i.e., fa-ʾumattiʿuhū).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū Šuʿayb [al-Sūsī] read wa-ʾarnā and ʾarnī without vowel on the rāʾ whenever they occur. ʾAbū ʿUmar[7] [al-Dūrī], transmitting from al-Yazīdī, reads with an ultrashort kasrah (i.e., wa-ʾarĭnā and ʾarĭnī), while the rest read it with full pronunciation of the vowel (i.e., wa-ʾarinā, ʾarinī).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Hišām reads ʾibrāhām with ʾalif for all that occur in this sūrah. In al-Nisāʾ there are three occurrences of it and they are at the final ones (Q4:125, 163), in al-ʾAnʿām the last one (Q6:161), in al-Tawbah the last two cases (Q9:114), in ʾIbrāhīm (Q15:35) one case, in al-Naḥl two cases (Q16:120, 123), in Maryam three cases (Q19:41, 46, 58), and in al-ʿAnkabūt the last word (Q29:31). In ʿAyn-Sīn-Qāf there is a case (Q43:13), in al-Ḏāriyāt there is a case (Q51:24), in al-Naǧm there is a case (Q53:37), in al-Ḥadīd there is a case (Q58:26), and in al-Mumtaḥanah the first occurrence (i.e., the first of the two in Q60:4). There are 33 cases in total. Ibn Ḏakwān reads it only in al-Baqarah with both options (ʾibrāhām and ʾibrāhīm). The rest read all of them with yāʾ (i.e., ʾibrāhīm).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read wa-ʾawṣā with ʾalif without gemination, and the rest without ʾalif and with gemination (i.e., wa-waṣṣā).[8]

footnotes.text: This is a regional rasm variant (Sidky 2020, 140).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥafṣ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ʾam taqūlūna with tāʾ, and the rest with yāʾ (i.e., ʾam yaqūlūna).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: The two of the holy cities, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥafṣ read la-raʾūfun with a long vowel whenever it occurs and the rest with a short vowel (i.e., la-raʾufun).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ʿammā taʿmalūna followed by laʾin ʾatayta (as opposed to the occurrence in Q2:149) with tāʾ and the rest read it with yāʾ (i.e., ʿammā yaʿmalūna).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn ʿĀmir reads muwallāhā with ʾalif, and the rest with yāʾ (i.e., muwallīhā).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr reads ʿammā yaʿmalūna followed by wa-man ḥayṯu with yāʾ, and the rest with tāʾ (i.e., ʿammā taʿmalūna).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read wa-man yaṭṭawwaʿ in two places (here and at Q2:184) with yāʾ, gemination of the ṭāʾ and ǧazm of the ʿayn. The rest read it without gemination of the ṭāʾ and with fatḥah on the ʿayn (i.e., wa-man taṭawwaʿa).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read wa-taṣrīfi r-rīḥi here, in al-Kahf (Q18:45) and al-Ǧāṯiyah (Q45:5) in the singular. Ibn Kaṯīr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read it in al-ʾAʿrāf (Q7:57), al-Naml (Q27:63), the second case in al-Rūm (Q30:48) and Fāṭir (Q35:9) in the singular. The rest read it in the plural (i.e., ar-riyāḥ). Ḥamzah also reads it in al-Ḥiǧr (Q15:22) in the singular. Ibn Kaṯīr reads it in al-Furqān (Q25:48) in the singular, and the rest read it in the plural. Nāfiʿ reads it in ʾIbrāhīm (Q14:18) and al-Šūrā (Q42:33) in the plural, and the rest in the singular.

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read wa-law tarà llaḏīna with tāʾ, and the rest with yāʾ (i.e., yarā/ē). Ibn ʿĀmir reads ʾiḏ yurawna with ḍammah on the yāʾ, and the rest read it with fatḥah (i.e., yarawna).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Qunbul, Ḥafṣ, Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾī read ḫuṭuwāt with ḍammah on the ṭāʾ whenever it occurs, while the rest read it without vowel (i.e., ḫuṭwāt).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʿĀṣim, ʾAbū ʿAmr and Ḥamzah place kasrah on the nūn of fa-man iḍṭurra (Q2:173, etc.), ʾan iʿbudū (Q5:117, etc.), ʾan iḥkum (Q5:49), lākin inḏ̣ur (Q7:143), ʾan iġdū (Q68:22) and what is similar to it. They do likewise with the dāl of wa-la-qad istuhziʾa (Q6:10, etc.), the tāʾ of wa-qālat iḫruǧ (Q12:31) and the tanwīn in, for example, fatīlan // inḏ̣ur (Q4:49–50) and mubīnun // iqtulū (Q12:8–9) and what is like it. They do so whenever there is an unvowelled letter followed by another letter that is part of the stem and that carries a ḍammah. If you start on it, you pronounce the ʾalif (al-waṣl) with ḍammah (i.e., #ʾuḍṭurra, etc.). ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah also apply the kasrah to the lām of qul and the wāw of ʾaw in, for example, His speech qul idʿū (Q7:195), ʾaw inquṣ (Q73:3) and what is like it. The rest pronounce these with ḍammah for all of them (i.e., fa-man uḍṭurra, ʾan uʿbudū, wa-la-qad ustuhziʾa, wa-qālat uḫruǧ, qatīlan unḏ̣ur, qul udʿū and ʾaw unquṣ). Ibn Ḏakwān makes an exception with the tanwīn only, thus he applies the kasrah, except for the two words bi-raḥmatin udḫulū (Q7:49) and ḫabīṯatin uǧtuṯṯat (Q14:26). This is the transmission of Muḥammad b. al-ʾAḫram[9] from al-ʾAḫfaš from him (Ibn Ḏakwān). Al-Naqqāš and others report all of that with kasrah whenever it occurs.

footnotes.text: Pretzl has b. al-ʾAḥzam; this is a mistake (al-Dānī 2008a, 33). Note that this ʾisnād is not present in the Taysīr nor in the Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān. It is one of the tilāwah paths for al-Dānī’s teacher ʾAbū al-Ḥasan Ibn Ġalbūn (1991, 27) as well as ʾAbū al-Ṭayyib Ibn Ġalbūn (2015, 185). Both of them indeed explicitly mention this exception (Ibn Ġalbūn 1991, 265; 2015, 436).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥafṣ and Ḥamzah read laysa l-birra with naṣb, and the rest read it with rafʿ (i.e., laysa l-birru). There is no disagreement about the second occurrence (Q2:189) that it is with rafʿ. Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read wa-lākin il-birru in both places (Q2:177, 189) with kasrah on the nūn and rafʿ of the rāʾ. The rest read it with fatḥah on the geminated nūn and with naṣb of the rāʾ (i.e., wa-lākinna l-birra).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʾAbū Bakr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read min muwaṣṣin with fatḥah on the wāw and gemination of the ṣād. The rest read it without gemination (i.e., mūṣin).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ and Ibn Ḏakwān read fidyatu ṭaʿāmi masākīna as a construct phrase and in the plural. The rest read it with tanwīn, with rafʿ of the mīm and in the singular (i.e., fidyatun ṭaʿāmu miskīnin), except for Hišām, who reads masākīna in the plural (i.e., fidyatun ṭaʿāmu masākīna). Whoever makes it plural, applies fatḥah to the mīm and sīn, and adds an ʾalif. Whoever makes it singular, applies kasrah to the mīm and nūn, and tanwīn to it, and removes the ʾalif.

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr reads fīhi l-qurān and qurānan and qurānahū whenever it occurs as a noun (i.e., not the verb qaraʾa) without the hamzah. Upon pausing, Ḥamzah follows him (i.e., qurānā#).[10] Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū Bakr read wa-li-tukammilū with gemination, and the rest without (i.e., wa-li-tukmilū).

footnotes.text: On Ḥamzah’s reading in pause, see U.11.6.2.

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Warš, Ḥafṣ and ʾAbū ʿAmr read al-buyūt, and buyūtvkum with ḍammah on the bāʾ whenever it occurs. The rest read it with kasrah (i.e., al-biyūt, biyūtvkum(ū)).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read wa-lā taqtulūhum, ḥattā yaqtulūkum and fa-ʾin qatalūkum without ʾalif derived from al-qatl (i.e., the stem I form). The rest read it with an ʾalif, derived from al-qitāl (i.e., the stem III form, tuqātilūhum(ū), yuqātilūkum(ū) and qātalūkum(ū)).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū ʿAmr read fa-lā rafaṯun wa-lā fusūqun with rafʿ and tanwīn on both, while the rest read it with naṣb and without tanwīn (i.e., fa-lā rafaṯa wa-lā fusūqa). There is no disagreement on His speech wa-lā ǧidāla.

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: The two of the holy cities and al-Kisāʾī read fì s-salmi with fatḥah on the sīn and the rest read it with kasrah (i.e., as-silmi).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read tarǧiʿu l-ʾumūru with fatḥah on the tāʾ and kasrah on the ǧīm whenever it occurs (Q2:110; Q3:109; Q8:44; Q22:76; Q35:4; Q57:5), and the rest read it with ḍammah on the tāʾ and fatḥah on the ǧīm (i.e., turǧaʿu).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads ḥattā yaqūlu with rafʿ of the lām and the rest with naṣb (i.e., yaqūla).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: [11] Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ʾiṯmun kaṯīrun with ṯāʾ and the rest with bāʾ (i.e., kabīrun). ʾAbū ʿAmr reads qul il-ʿafwu with rafʿ and the rest read it with naṣb (i.e., al-ʿafwa).

footnotes.text: Pretzl has 216 here; this is a mistake.

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Al-Bazzī, according to the transmission of ʾAbū Rabīʿah from him, reads la.aʿnatakumū with softening of the hamzah, while the rest read it with full pronunciation (i.e., la-ʾaʿnatakum).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʾAbū Bakr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ḥattā yaṭṭahharna with gemination of both the ṭāʾ and the hāʾ. The rest read it with no vowel on the ṭāʾ (and no gemination) and with ḍammah on the hāʾ (i.e., yaṭhurna).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah reads ʾillā ʾan yuḫāfā with ḍammah on the yāʾ and the rest read it with fatḥah (i.e., yaḫāfā).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū ʿAmr read lā tuḍārru with rafʿ of the rāʾ, and the rest read it with fatḥah (i.e., lā tuḍārra). Ibn Kaṯīr reads mā ʾataytumū with a short vowel, and likewise in al-Rūm (Q30:39) wa-mā ʾataytumū min riban, and the rest read it lengthened (i.e., ʾātaytum).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read tumāssūhunna in two places here (Q2:236, 237) and in al-ʾAḥzāb (Q33:49) with ḍammah on the tāʾ with ʾalif, and the rest read with fatḥah on the tāʾ without ʾalif (i.e., tamassūhunna). Ḥafṣ, Ibn Ḏakwān, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read qadaruhū in both cases with fatḥah on the dāl, and the rest read it without vowel (i.e., qadruhū).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: The two of the holy cities, ʾAbū Bakr and al-Kisāʾī read waṣiyyatun with rafʿ, and the rest with naṣb (i.e., waṣiyyatan).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read fa-yuḍāʿifahū/fa-yuḍaʿʿifahū here and in al-Ḥadīd (Q57:11) with naṣb of the fāʾ, and the rest read it with rafʿ (i.e., fa-yuḍāʿifuhū/fa-yuḍaʿʿifuhū). Ibn Kaṯīr and Ibn ʿĀmir read fa-yuḍaʿʿifa/uhū, yuḍaʿʿifu and muḍaʿʿif with gemination of the ʿayn and without ʾalif whenever it occurs, and the rest read it with ʾalif and without gemination (i.e., fa-yuḍāʿifa/uhū, yuḍāʿifu and muḍāʿif). Qunbul, Ḥafṣ, Hišām, ʾAbū ʿAmr and Ḥamzah, with disagreement in transmission of Ḫallād (from Ḥamzah), read yabsuṭu here and basṭatun in al-ʾAʿrāf (Q7:69) with sīn, while al-Naqqāš transmits from al-ʾAḫfaš [from Ibn Ḏakwān] here with sīn and in al-ʾAʿrāf with ṣād (i.e., yabsuṭu but baṣṭatun). The rest read it with ṣād in both cases (i.e., yabṣuṭu and baṣṭatun).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads ʿasītum here and in al-Qitāl[12] (Q47:22) with kasrah on the sīn, and the rest read it with fatḥah (i.e., ʿasaytum(ū)).

footnotes.text: A different name for Sūrat Muḥammad (Kandil 1992, 52).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: The Kufans and Ibn ʿĀmir read ġurfatan with ḍammah on the ġayn, and the rest read it with fatḥah (i.e., ġarfatan).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads difāʿu ḷḷāhi here and in al-Ḥaǧǧ (Q22:40) with kasrah on the dāl and ʾalif after the fāʾ, while the rest read it with fatḥah on the dāl and no vowel on the fāʾ without ʾalif (i.e., dafʿu).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū ʿAmr read here lā bayʿa fīhī̆ wa-lā ḫullata wa-lā šafāʿata, in ʾIbrāhīm (Q14:31) lā bayʿa fīhī̆ wa-lā ḫalāla and in al-Ṭūr (Q52:23) lā laġwa fīhā wa-lā taʾ/āṯīma with naṣb and without tanwīn in all these cases. The rest read it with rafʿ and tanwīn (i.e., lā bayʿun fīhi wa-lā ḫullatun wa-lā šafāʿatun, etc.).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads ʾanā ʾuḥyī wa-ʾumītu, ʾanā ʾawwalu, ʾanā ʾunabbiʾukum and what is like it, whenever after ʾana comes a hamzah that carries ḍammah or fatḥah with the addition of an ʾalif in connected speech and pause. ʾAbū Našīṭ also transmits it (i.e., ʾanā in connected speech and pause) from Qālūn when it is followed by a hamzah carrying a kasrah in His speech ʾin ʾanā ʾillā (Q7:188; Q26:115) and mā ʾanā ʾillā (Q46:9). The rest read it with removal of the ʾalif in connected speech only, and all of them add it in pause (i.e., ʾana in connected speech, ʾanā# when pausing).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read lam yatasanna without hāʾ in connected speech only (i.e., yatasannah# in pause). The rest read it with the addition (of hāʾ) in connected speech and pause (i.e., yatasannah(#)). The Kufans and Ibn ʿĀmir read nunšizuhā with zāy and the rest with rāʾ (i.e., nunširuhā). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read qāla ʿlam ʾanna ḷḷāha with ʾalif al-waṣl and ǧazm of the mīm. When they start on the word, it is read with kasrah on the ʾalif as an imperative (i.e., #ʾiʿlam). The rest read it with ʾalif al-qaṭʿ both in connected speech and when starting on the word (fī al-ḥālayn), and with rafʿ of the mīm according to the indicative (i.e., ʾaʿlamu).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah reads fa-ṣirhunna with kasrah on the ṣād and the rest read it with ḍammah (i.e., fa-ṣurhunna). ʾAbū Bakr reads ǧuzuʾan and ǧuzuʾun with ḍammah on the zāy whenever it occurs and the rest read it without vowel (i.e., ǧuzʾan, ǧuzʾun).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read bi-rabwatin here and in al-Muʾminūn (Q23:50) with fatḥah on the rāʾ. The rest read it with ḍammah (i.e., bi-rubwatin). The two of the holy cities read ʾuklv̆hā, ʾuklv̆hū and al-(ʾ)uklv̆ whenever it occurs without extra vowel. ʾAbū ʿAmr only follows them when it is suffixed by the feminine pronoun (i.e., ʾuklv̆hā but ʾukulv̆hū and al-ʾukulv̆). The rest read it with an extra vowel (i.e., ʾukulv̆hā, ʾukulv̆hū and al-ʾukulv̆).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Al-Bazzī reads tāʾ with gemination in connected speech when it is the first letter of a verb in the prefix conjugation in 31 places: 1. here lâ ttayammamū, 2. in ʾĀl ʿImrān (Q3:103) wa-lâ ttafarraqū, 3. in al-Nisāʾ (Q4:97) ʾinna llaḏīna ttawaffāhumū, 4. in al-Māʾidah (Q5:2) wa-ttaʿāwanū, 5. in al-ʾAnʿām (Q6:153) fa-ttafarraqa bikumū, 6. in al-ʾAʿrāf (Q7:117) fa-ʾiḏā hiya ttalaqqafu, 7. and likewise in Ṭāhā (Q20:69) (i.e., yamīnika ttalaqqaf), 8. and al-Šuʿarāʾ (Q26:45) (i.e., hiya ttalaqqafu), 9. and in al-ʾAnfāl (Q8) wa-lâ ttawallaw (Q8:20), 10. and wa-lâ ttanāzaʿū (Q8:46), 11. in al-Tawbah (Q9:52) qul hal ttarabbaṣūna, 12. in Hūd (Q11) wa-ʾin ttawallaw (Q11:3), 13. and fa-ʾin ttawallaw (Q11:57), 14. and lâ ttakallamu nafsin (Q11:105), 15. in al-Ḥiǧr (Q15:8) mâ ttanazzalu, 16. in al-Nūr (Q24) ʾiḏ ttalaqqawnahū (Q24:15), 17. and fa-ʾin ttawallaw faʾinnamā (Q24:54), 18. in al-Šuʿarāʾ (Q26) ʿalā man ttanazzalu š-šayāṭīnu (Q26:221), 19. // ttanazzalu (Q26:222), 20. in al-ʾAḥzāb (Q33) wa-lâ ttabarraǧna (Q33:33), 21. wa-lā ʾan ttabaddala (Q33:52), 22. in al-Ṣāffāt (Q37:25) lâ ttanāṣarūna, 23. in al-Ḥuǧurāt wa-lâ ttanābazū (Q49:11), 24. wa-lâ ttaǧassasū (Q49:12), 25. and li-ttaʿārafū (Q49:13), 26. in al-Mumtaḥanah (Q60:9) ʾan ttawallawhumū, 27. in al-Mulk (Q67:8) takādu ttamayyazu, 28. in al-Qalam (Q68:38) lammâ ttaḫayyarūna, 29. in ʿAbasa (Q80:10) ʿanhû ttalahhā, 30. in al-Layl (Q92:14) nāran ttalaḏ̣ḏ̣ā, 31. and in al-Qadr (Q97:4) min ʾalfi šahrin // ttanazzalu. ʾAbū al-Faraǧ al-Naǧǧād, the teacher of recitation adds, transmitting from his recitation to ʾAbū al-Fatḥ b. Budhun from ʾAbū Bakr al-Zaynabī from ʾAbū Rabīʿah from al-Bazzī[13] two more places: ʾĀl ʿImrān (Q3:143) wa-la-qad kuntumû ttamannawna l-mawta and al-Wāqiʿah (Q56:65) faḏ̣altumû ttafakkahūna—he added gemination to the tāʾ of these too.[14] This is by analogy of the words of ʾAbū Rabīʿah: “If I start on these tāʾs, they are ungeminated.” If there is a long vowel before them, add to it extra length (i.e., make them overlong, as if the geminate followed within a word). The rest read the tāʾ without gemination for all the words in this section (i.e., tayammamū, etc.).

footnotes.text: This ʾisnād does not occur in U.4.2.2. nor in the ʾisnād section of Ǧāmiʿ al-bayān.

With these two added to the list, the gemination of initial tāʾ is completely regular. It occurs on every single verb which starts with a single tāʾ in the rasm which must be interpreted as a simplification of tata- by haplology rather than assimilation (e.g., Q2:280 تصدقوا taṣṣaddaqū). But these two are only added in this isolated transmission that does not seem to be confirmed by any other transmission (see also the discussion in al-Dānī 2007, 933; Ibn al-Ǧazarī 2018, §2804).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr, Warš and Ḥafṣ read fa-niʿimmā here and in al-Nisāʾ (Q4:58) with kasrah on the nūn and on the ʿayn. Qālūn, ʾAbū Bakr and ʾAbū ʿAmr with kasrah on the nūn and an ultrashort vowel on the ʿayn (ʾiḫfāʾ ḥarakat al-ʿayn, i.e., niʿĭmmā), and it is allowed to pronounce no vowel (i.e., niʿmmā). This is how it is transmitted in written works from them, but the first is more regular (ʾaqyas). The rest read it with fatḥah on the nūn and kasrah on the ʿayn (i.e., naʿimmā). Ibn Kaṯīr, ʾAbū Bakr and ʾAbū ʿAmr read nukaffiru with nūn and with rafʿ of the rāʾ. Ḥafṣ and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with yāʾ and rafʿ (i.e., yukaffiru), and the rest with nūn with ǧazm (i.e., nukaffir).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamzah read yaḥsabuhum, yaḥsabūna, yaḥsabu and yaḥsabanna when it is a verb in the prefix conjugation with a fatḥah on the sīn. The rest read it with a kasrah (i.e., yaḥsibuhum(ū), yaḥsibūna, yaḥsibu and yaḥsibanna).[15]

footnotes.text: This description is more restrictive than it should be. Unlike what the wording might suggest, not just 3sg.m. and 3pl.m. forms, but all forms of the prefix conjugation are meant here, including, e.g., Q25:44 taḥsabu, and Q3:87 li-taḥsa/ibūhū̆.

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʾAbū Bakr and Ḥamzah read fa-ʾāḏinū with length and kasrah on the ḏāl, and the rest with shortness and fatḥah on the ḏāl (i.e., fa-ʾḏanū/fāḏanū).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads ʾilā maysuratin with ḍammah on the sīn, and the rest with fatḥah (i.e., maysaratin). ʿĀṣim reads wa-ʾin taṣaddaqū without gemination of the ṣād, and the rest read it with gemination (i.e., taṣṣaddaqū).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr reads tarǧiʿūna fīhi with fatḥah on the tāʾ and kasrah on the ǧīm, while the rest read it with ḍammah on the tāʾ and fatḥah on the ǧīm (i.e., turǧaʿūna).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah reads min aš-šuhadāʾi ʾin taḍilla with kasrah of the hamzah, and the rest read it with fatḥah (i.e., ʾan). Ḥamzah reads fa-tuḏakkiru with rafʿ and gemination. Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū ʿAmr read it with naṣb without gemination (i.e., fa-tuḏkira). The rest read it with naṣb and gemination (i.e., fa-tuḏakkira). ʿĀṣim reads tiǧāratan ḥāḍiratan with naṣb and the rest with rafʿ (i.e., tiǧāratun ḥāḍiratun).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ibn Kaṯīr and ʾAbū ʿAmr read fa-ruhunun with ḍammah on the rāʾ and the hāʾ without ʾalif. The rest read it with kasrah on the rāʾ, fatḥah on the hāʾ and an ʾalif after it (i.e., fa-rihānun).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read fa-yaġfiru and yuʿaḏḏibu, both with rafʿ. The rest read it with ǧazm (fa-yaġfir, yuʿaḏḏib).

statements.heading: F.2. Sūrat al-Baqarah
statements.text: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read wa-kitābihī with ʾalif in the singular, and the rest without ʾalif in the plural (i.e., kutubihī). ʾAbū ʿAmr reads ruslvnā, ruslvkum, ruslvhum and sublvnā whenever after the lām (of rusul and subul) come two letters (i.e., -nā, -kum, -hu/im) with no vowel on the sīn and bāʾ whenever it occurs. The rest read it with ḍammah (i.e., rusulvnā, subulvnā, etc.).

statements.heading: F.2.1. [Yāʾs of Q2]
statements.text: There are eight yāʾs: 1. ʾinniya ʾaʿlamu (Q2:30) and 2. ʾinniya ʾaʿlamu (Q2:33) with fatḥah on both by the two of the holy cities and ʾAbū ʿAmr (the rest read it as ʾinnī). 3. ʿahdì ḏ̣-ḏ̣ālimīna (Q2:124) carries no vowel for Ḥafṣ and Ḥamzah (it is ʿahdiya for the rest). 4. baytiya li-ṭ-ṭāʾifīna (Q2:125) with fatḥah for Nāfiʿ, Ḥafṣ and Hišām (the rest read it as baytī). 5. fa-ḏkurūniya ʾaḏkurkumū (Q2:152) with fatḥah for Ibn Kaṯīr (fa-ḏkurūnī for the rest). 6. biya laʿallahum (Q2:186) with fatḥah for Warš (the rest read bī). 7. minniya ʾillā man (Q2:249) with fatḥah for Nāfiʿ and ʾAbū ʿAmr (the rest read minnī). 8. rabbì llaḏī (Q2:258) with no vowel for Ḥamzah (the rest read rabbiya).

statements.heading: F.2.2. [Removed yāʾs of Q2]
statements.text: There are three removed ones:[16] 1. ad-dāʿī ʾiḏā 2. daʿānī (Q2:186): in connected speech Warš and ʾAbū ʿAmr maintain (the yāʾ) (the rest removes it: ad-dāʿi ʾiḏā daʿāni). 3. wa-ttaqūnī yā ʾulì l-ʾalbāb (Q2:197): in connected speech ʾAbū ʿAmr maintains (the yāʾ) (the rest removes it: wa-ttaqūni). ʾAbū ʿAmr [al-Dānī] said: I will proceed like this at the end of the sūrahs with regard to the yāʾs. I will (mention the minority reading and) leave out what the rest of them read, be it a fatḥ or no vowel, and be it a case of maintenance or removal (of the yāʾ), because ambiguity is removed for all of that (because when fatḥah is given, the ʾiskān form is what everybody else reads, and vice versa and when the maintenance is given, what everybody else reads is with the removal of yāʾ and vice versa). Success comes from God.

footnotes.text: ‘Removed ones’ refers to word-final yāʾs which, especially in verse-final position, are often unwritten in the Qurʾānic text where classical orthography would expect them. Readers different on whether and when these yāʾs are reconstituted in recitation or not.

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: ʾAbū ʿAmr, Ibn Ḏakwān and al-Kisāʾī read at-tawrēh with ʾimālah in all the Qurʾān. Nāfiʿ and Ḥamzah read it in between the two sounds (i.e., at-tawrǟh), and the rest read it with fatḥah (i.e., at-tawrāh). For Qālūn I recited it like that too.

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read sa-yuġlabūna wa-yuḥšarūna with yāʾ and the rest with tāʾ (i.e., sa-tuġlabūna wa-tuḥšarūna).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads tarawnahum with tāʾ and the rest read it with yāʾ (i.e., yarawnahum(ū)).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: ʾAbū Bakr reads wa-ruḍwān with ḍammah of the rāʾ everywhere except for the second occurrence in al-Māʾidah (Q5:16), and that is His speech man ittabaʿa riḍwānahū. The rest read it with kasrah on the rāʾ (i.e., riḍwān).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Al-Kisāʾī reads ʾanna d-dīna ʿinda ḷḷāhi with fatḥah on the hamzah and the rest with kasrah (i.e., ʾinna).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Ḥamzah reads wa-yuqātilūna llaḏīna with an ʾalif, ḍammah on the yāʾ and kasrah of the tāʾ as al-qitāl (i.e., stem III verb). The rest read it without ʾalif, with fatḥah on the yāʾ and ḍammah on the tāʾ as al-qatl (i.e., stem I verb, so yaqtulūna).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Nāfiʿ, Ḥafṣ, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read al-ḥayya min al-mayyiti, al-mayyita min al-ḥayyi, ʾilā baladi mayyitin and what is like it when someone has died, with an extra vowel (i.e., with a bisyllabic stem mayyit). The rest read it without an extra vowel (i.e., mayt).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: ʾAbū Bakr and Ibn ʿĀmir read bi-mā waḍaʿtu with no vowel on the ʿayn and ḍammah on the tāʾ. The rest read it with fatḥah on the ʿayn and no vowel on the tāʾ (i.e., waḍaʿat).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: The Kufans read wa-kaffalahā with gemination of the fāʾ and the rest read it without gemination (i.e., wa-kafalahā). ʾAbū Bakr reads zakariyyāʾa with naṣb of the hamzah, and Ḥafṣ, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī drop the case vowels of zakariyyā and its hamzah, here and throughout the whole Qurʾān. The rest applies the rafʿ here (i.e., zakariyyāʾu), and apply case vowels to it whenever it occurs. If it is adjacent to a hamzah, ʾAbū Bakr and Ibn ʿĀmir pronounce the hamzah strongly (i.e., Q19:2–3 zakariyyāʾa // ʾiḏ), whereas the two of the holy cities and ʾAbū ʿAmr pronounce it softly (i.e., zakariyyā.a ʾiḏ).[17]

footnotes.text: The details of this softening of the hamzah have already been discussed in U.11.2.

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read fa-nādēhu l-malāʾikatu with ʾalif with ʾimālah and the rest with tāʾ without the ʾalif (i.e., fa-nādathu l-malāʾikatu). Ḥamzah and Ibn ʿĀmir read ʾinna ḷḷāha yubašširuka/yabšuruka bi-yaḥyā/ē with kasrah on the hamzah, and the rest with fatḥah (i.e., ʾanna ḷḷāha). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read yabšuruka in two places here (Q3:39, 45), and in Subḥān[18] (Q17:9) and Kahf (Q18:2) wa-yabšuru with fatḥah on the yāʾ, no vowel on the bāʾ, ḍammah on the šīn and no gemination in these four places. Ḥamzah reads in al-Tawbah (Q9:21) yabšuruhum, in al-Ḥiǧr (Q15:53) ʾinnā nabšuruka and in Maryam (Q19) ʾinnā nabšuruka (Q19:7) and li-tabšura bihī (Q19:97) with this derivation in these four places as well. The rest read it with ḍammah of the first letter, a kasrah on a geminate šīn for all of these (i.e., yubašširuhum(ū), etc.).

footnotes.text: Pretzl has ୚ඤن (al-Dānī 2008a, 35). Subḥān is an alternative name for Sūrat al-ʾIsrāʾ (Kandil 1992, 50).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: kun fa-yakūnu has already been mentioned.[19]

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Nāfiʿ and ʿĀṣim read wa-yuʿallimuhū with yāʾ and the rest with nūn (i.e., wa-nuʿallimuhū).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Nāfiʿ reads ʾinnī ʾaḫluqu with kasrah on the hamzah. The rest has fatḥah (i.e., ʾannī ʾaḫluqu). Nāfiʿ reads fa-yakūnu ṭāʾiran here and in al-Māʾidah (Q5:110) with ʾalif and hamzah according to the singular. The rest read it without ʾalif or hamzah according to the plural (i.e., according to the collective ṭayran).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Ḥafṣ reads fa-yawaffāhum with yāʾ and the rest read it with nūn (i.e., fa-nawaffā/ē/ǟhum(ū)).

statements.heading: F.3. Sūrat ʾĀl ʿImrān
statements.text: Nāfiʿ and ʾAbū ʿAmr read hā .antum whenever it occurs with length without a hamzah. Warš is lesser in length (i.e., ha-.antum).[20] Qunbul reads it with hamzah without ʾalif after the hāʾ (i.e., ha-ʾantumū). The rest read it with length and hamzah (i.e., hâ ʾantum), but al-Bazzī shortened the overlong vowel in accordance with his general principle (i.e., hā ʾantumū).[21] As for the hāʾ in the manner of ʾAbū ʿAmr, Qālūn and Hišām, it is possible for it to be taken as a demonstrative or as the replacement of the hamzah (as an interrogative)[22] (i.e., hā ʾantum with demonstrative hā- or ʾa-ʾantum → ʾā-.antum[23] → hā-.antum). For Qunbul (ʾa-ʾantumū → ha-ʾantumū) and Warš (ʾa-ʾantum → ʾa-.antum → ha-.antum) it is only possible to take it as the replacement (of hamzah) and nothing else. In the manner of the Kufans, al-Bazzī and Ibn Ḏakwān, it can only be a demonstrative.
